subject: english
note: Descriptor text: Australian Curriculum v9 (ACARA, CC BY 4.0). Waypoints and prior knowledge: Learning Waypoints. Made by tools/import-curriculum.mjs; do not edit by hand.

descriptors.title: Language formality and social distance
descriptors.description: understand that language varies as levels of formality and social distance increase
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that language is selected for social contexts and that it helps to signal social roles and relationships (AC9E5LA01). They have not yet examined how formality and social distance interact as a continuum, or how formal address protocols function at institutional or ceremonial levels.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that language choices vary systematically with levels of formality and social distance, and can identify and apply appropriate language for a given context.

nodes.label: Formality as a continuum
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that language exists along a continuum from informal to formal and name the key registers (slang, colloquial, conversational, formal).
criteria: Names and correctly applies the four register labels (slang, colloquial, conversational, formal) to provided examples
Identifies at least one language feature (e.g. vocabulary choice, contraction use) that signals register
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate 'polite' with 'formal' or treat formality as binary cannot correctly reason about social distance in Node 2 — the two-variable model breaks down without a working continuum.

width.minimum: Identify at least three points on the formality continuum using provided examples; label each as slang, colloquial, conversational or formal.
width.typical: Discuss and sort a range of spoken and written examples across the full continuum; explain what features (vocabulary, sentence structure, tone) signal each register.
wider: Compare the same message expressed across all four registers (e.g. a request for help) and analyse how meaning and relationship signal shift
Examine how digital communication (texts, emails, social media posts) creates new registers that blend formal and informal features

modes.reason: Students often conflate 'polite' with 'formal' or assume formality is binary. Exposure to a range of register examples across spoken and written modes helps students build a more nuanced continuum model.

nodes.label: Social distance and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how social distance (familiarity, power relationship, audience) determines appropriate register choice.
criteria: Explains why a specific register is appropriate for a given social relationship using at least two contextual cues (familiarity, power, audience)
Identifies an example where register mismatch would be inappropriate and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot hold familiarity and power as two separate variables, their Node 3 register choices will rest on single-cue guessing — producing register mismatches in formal production tasks.

width.minimum: Explain the register appropriate for one contrasting pair of social relationships (e.g. talking to a friend vs. a principal) and justify why using at least one language feature.
width.typical: Analyse several social contexts (peer, teacher, community leader, ceremonial) and explain how both familiarity and relative power shape register expectations; identify how audience affects language selection.
wider: Investigate how social distance operates differently in cultures where respect is marked differently (e.g. formal pronoun systems in other languages compared with English address terms)
Compare formal address protocols across institutions (school, government, royalty) and identify what social values they encode

modes.reason: Students need to hold two variables simultaneously (familiarity AND power/status) to make register judgements. Making the reasoning chain explicit — 'I know this is formal because the relationship is distant AND the status differential is high' — prevents over-reliance on a single cue.

nodes.label: Applying register appropriately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use language appropriate to a given level of formality and social distance, and evaluate their choices.
criteria: Produces spoken or written language that consistently fits the specified register level
Explains at least one specific language choice (vocabulary, sentence structure, or tone) and how it signals the intended register

width.minimum: Present or write an idea at one specified register level appropriate to a given audience; identify one choice made and explain why it suits the context.
width.typical: Present ideas or opinions in at least two contrasting register contexts (e.g. peer discussion and a formal presentation); reflect on choices made and how they serve different audiences.
wider: Analyse a formal public speech or ceremonial address and identify specific language features that signal institutional formality
Draft the same argument for two different audiences (e.g. a class debate and a letter to a local council) and compare register choices

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate understanding of continuum, social distance, and language features into a production and evaluation act — the components from Nodes 1 and 2 come together in a situated, purposeful language choice.

descriptors.title: Objective and subjective language; bias
descriptors.description: understand the uses of objective and subjective language, and identify bias
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how to move beyond making bare assertions by taking account of differing ideas or perspectives (AC9E5LA02). They have not yet examined the distinction between objective and subjective language, or how language choices construct bias in texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand the distinction between objective and subjective language, and can identify how language choices construct bias in a range of texts.

nodes.label: Objective vs subjective language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and distinguish objective language (factual, verifiable) from subjective language (opinion, feeling, judgement) in texts.
criteria: Correctly classifies provided sentences or text extracts as objective or subjective
Names at least one language feature that indicates subjectivity (e.g. emotive vocabulary, judgement word, first person)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate written text with objectivity cannot identify emotive positioning (Node 2) or construct bias (Node 3) — both require the ability to see subjective language choices as choices, not neutral reporting.

width.minimum: Sort a set of provided sentences or text extracts as objective or subjective; identify one feature that signals each.
width.typical: Analyse both factual recounts and opinion pieces to identify objective and subjective language; explain what features (verifiable claims, emotive vocabulary, judgement words) distinguish them.
wider: Compare a factual news report with an editorial on the same event and annotate where the language shifts from objective to subjective
Examine science or informational texts from the curriculum and identify when objective reporting shifts into authorial interpretation

modes.reason: Students commonly assume all written text is objective, or conflate 'formal' with 'objective'. Comparing texts in multiple genres — news reports, editorials, personal recounts, information reports — reveals that the objective/subjective distinction cuts across register, not with it.

nodes.label: Emotive language and persuasion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how emotive language and judgement words are used to position audiences and create persuasive effects.
criteria: Identifies specific emotive or judgement vocabulary in a persuasive text
Explains how at least one word or phrase positions the audience or evokes a particular response
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reason from vocabulary choice to audience effect cannot analyse how bias is constructed in Node 3 — identifying bias requires the vocabulary→positioning reasoning chain established here.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of emotive or judgement vocabulary in a provided persuasive text and explain how each positions the audience.
width.typical: Analyse how language choices in persuasive texts (reviews, editorials, advertisements) evoke emotion and judgement; explain how these choices work directly and indirectly to persuade audiences to take a position.
wider: Analyse how the same event or product is described using different emotive language choices for different target audiences
Compare print and visual advertising and identify how emotive language and image choices work together to persuade

modes.reason: Students need to move from identifying emotive words to explaining how they position a reader — the reasoning chain from vocabulary choice → reader effect requires explicit scaffolding before students can do it independently.

nodes.label: Identifying bias
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify bias in a text — the selective or slanted use of language that advantages one perspective — and explain how it is constructed.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific language choice that contributes to bias in a provided text
Explains how the language choice advantages one perspective over another

width.minimum: Identify one example of bias in a provided text (e.g. a news report or factual recount) and explain how the language choices create it.
width.typical: Differentiate between reporting facts and providing commentary in a range of texts (factual recounts, editorials, unedited vs edited representations); explain how word selection, inclusion/exclusion of information, and point of view construct bias.
wider: Compare news reports of the same event from two different publications and analyse where bias is evident through language choices
Examine how an unedited photograph vs. a cropped or captioned version can construct different perspectives on the same event

modes.reason: Bias is most visible in comparison. Students who read only one account often cannot see its bias without a contrasting perspective. Multiple text contexts help students recognise bias as constructed rather than inherent.
Identifying bias requires integrating knowledge of objective/subjective distinction (Node 1) and understanding of how emotive language positions (Node 2) into a single critical reading act.

descriptors.title: Text structure: stages, phases and adaptation
descriptors.description: explain how texts across the curriculum are typically organised into characteristic stages and phases depending on purposes, recognising how authors often adapt text structures and language features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how spoken, written and multimodal texts use language features and are typically organised into stages for different purposes (AC9E5LA03). They have not yet examined the internal phase structure within stages, or the ways authors deliberately adapt typical structures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can explain the characteristic stages and phases of texts across the curriculum and identify and explain when authors adapt typical structures and language features.

nodes.label: Stages and phases within texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that texts are organised into stages and that stages can be further divided into phases, and name the stages and phases in a familiar text type.
criteria: Names the stages of at least one text type accurately
Identifies at least one phase within a stage and explains its purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify stages across a range of text types arrive at Node 2 without the structural vocabulary needed to compare characteristic structures — N2 presupposes that stage/phase concepts are stable across text types.

width.minimum: Identify the stages of one familiar text type (e.g. narrative) and name at least one phase within a stage (e.g. the hook as a phase within the introduction).
width.typical: Examine a range of text types (narrative, review, discussion, historical recount) and identify their stages; identify how introductions and other stages may be divided into phases with distinct purposes.
wider: Map the stage and phase structure of a film or picture book narrative, comparing visual and written structural signals
Compare stage and phase structures across curriculum areas (e.g. a science report vs a history recount) and identify shared and distinct structural features

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate examples of stage/phase structures across multiple text types before the underlying concept of structural organisation becomes generalisable. Exposure to a range of text types — not just narrative — builds the repertoire needed to recognise and explain the concept across the curriculum.

nodes.label: Characteristic structures across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the characteristic stages and phases of multiple text types including reviews, discussions and historical recounts.
criteria: Names and explains the characteristic stages of at least two text types, including one non-narrative type
Identifies at least one language feature associated with a specific stage in a text type

width.minimum: Identify and explain the characteristic stages of at least two different text types, including at least one from outside narrative (e.g. review or discussion).
width.typical: Explain characteristic stages and phases across the range of text types encountered in curriculum — including reviews, discussions of alternative positions, historical recounts, and narratives; identify language features that accompany each stage.
wider: Examine a range of curriculum-area texts (science, history, geography) and explain how structural stages serve the discipline's purposes
Investigate how humour texts use stage structures differently — for example, how exaggeration functions within a structural stage

modes.reason: Students typically build strong understanding of narrative structure but underestimate the structural regularity of non-narrative texts. Extending across reviews, discussions and recounts prevents the misconception that text structure is primarily a literary concern.

nodes.label: Author adaptation of text structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and explain when and why authors adapt or subvert the characteristic stages and language features of a text type.
criteria: Identifies a specific structural adaptation in a text and names what the conventional structure would be
Explains what effect the adaptation creates for the reader

width.minimum: Identify one example where an author has adapted a typical text structure (e.g. a narrative that opens with a flashback rather than a scene-setting introduction) and explain the effect.
width.typical: Analyse at least two examples of authors adapting text structures or language features across different text types; explain what effect the adaptation creates and why an author might choose it.
wider: Compare two texts of the same type by different authors and evaluate how structural adaptations shape audience experience or argument
Create a short text that deliberately adapts a typical structural feature and explain the choice in an author's note

modes.reason: Recognising adaptation requires holding the conventional structure in mind simultaneously with the actual structure — a metacognitive comparison move. Scaffolding the reasoning ('What is the typical structure? What has changed? What effect does that create?') prevents students from either accepting deviation as arbitrary or missing it entirely.
This node integrates knowledge of stages (Node 1), knowledge of characteristic structures across text types (Node 2), and applies both to the analytic question of intentional adaptation.

descriptors.title: Cohesion: repetition and word associations
descriptors.description: understand that cohesion can be created by the intentional use of repetition, and the use of word associations
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how texts can be made cohesive by using the starting point of a sentence or paragraph as a signal of its theme (AC9E5LA04). They have not yet examined how repetition of key words and word associations (general/specific substitution, synonyms, antonyms) build cohesion across a text.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how cohesion is built through intentional repetition and word associations, and can identify these devices and explain their effect in texts.

nodes.label: Repetition as a cohesion device
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify repetition of key words and synonyms in a text and explain how this repetition creates cohesive links across sentences.
criteria: Identifies at least two cohesive links created by repetition or synonym use in a provided text
Explains how one example of repetition connects ideas across sentences or paragraphs

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of key word repetition or synonym use in a provided text and explain how each creates a connection between sentences or paragraphs.
width.typical: Recognise how cohesion is developed through repeating key words, synonyms and antonyms across a text; explain how this threading of language choices holds a text together thematically.
wider: Analyse how repetition functions differently in literary texts (for effect) vs. informational texts (for clarity)
Examine a speech or persuasive text where repetition is used structurally (e.g. anaphora) and explain its rhetorical effect beyond cohesion

nodes.label: Word associations and lexical cohesion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify word associations — where a general word stands in for a more specific word previously mentioned — and explain how this creates cohesion.
criteria: Identifies an example of general-for-specific word association in a text and names both the general term and the specific word it refers to
Explains how the association creates cohesion between two sentences
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify the general-for-specific substitution move cannot deploy word associations in Node 3 production — the integration task requires this concept to be operational, not just named.

width.minimum: Identify one example of lexical cohesion via word association in a provided text (e.g. 'Look at those apples. Granny Smiths are my favourite.') and explain the cohesive link.
width.typical: Identify and explain multiple examples of word associations (general-for-specific substitution) in a range of text types; explain how word associations work alongside repetition and synonyms to build cohesion.
wider: Write a short informative paragraph that deliberately uses word associations alongside synonyms, then annotate the cohesive devices used
Compare how word associations function in a formal information report vs. an informal narrative — identifying where each is more or less appropriate

modes.reason: The general-for-specific substitution move is conceptually subtle — students often read past it. Making the reasoning explicit ('What does the general word refer back to? How do we know?') prevents the misconception that word choice is arbitrary.

nodes.label: Using cohesive devices in own writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use repetition, synonyms and word associations intentionally to build cohesion in their own writing.
criteria: Produces a paragraph that uses at least one cohesive device intentionally
Names the device and explains how it connects ideas across sentences

width.minimum: Write a short paragraph that deliberately uses at least one cohesion device (key word repetition, synonym, or word association); identify the device used and explain how it connects ideas.
width.typical: Compose extended writing in which cohesion is built through a combination of key word repetition, synonyms and word associations; review and edit own writing to identify and improve cohesive links.
wider: Edit a provided text with weak cohesion and rewrite it using repetition, synonyms and word associations to improve coherence
Compare the cohesion strategies used in a literary text and an information report on the same topic, explaining how the purpose shapes the choice of cohesive device

modes.reason: Using repetition, synonyms and word associations in combination requires integrating knowledge of all three devices (Nodes 1 and 2) into a purposeful production and editing act.

descriptors.title: Embedded clauses in complex sentences
descriptors.description: understand how embedded clauses can expand the variety of complex sentences to elaborate, extend and explain ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that the structure of a complex sentence includes a main clause and at least one dependent clause (AC9E5LA05). They have not yet examined how embedded (relative) clauses are inserted within a main clause to expand noun groups, as distinct from adverbial dependent clauses that follow or precede the main clause.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how embedded clauses expand noun groups within complex sentences and can use them to elaborate, extend and explain ideas.

nodes.label: What an embedded clause is
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an embedded (relative) clause within a sentence and distinguish it from a trailing dependent clause.
criteria: Correctly identifies the embedded clause in at least two provided sentences
Explains how an embedded clause differs in position from a trailing dependent clause
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish embedded from trailing clauses cannot attempt the Node 2 construction task — they will produce trailing dependent clauses and believe they have met the requirement.

width.minimum: Identify the embedded clause in at least two provided example sentences (e.g. 'The town that was flooded suffered extensive damage'); explain how it is positioned inside the main clause rather than following it.
width.typical: Identify and explain embedded clauses across a range of provided sentences; distinguish between adverbial dependent clauses (e.g. 'Because it rained, the game was cancelled') and embedded clauses that expand noun groups within the main clause.
wider: Analyse a paragraph from a curriculum-area text (science, history) and identify where embedded clauses are used and what noun groups they expand
Compare the effect of an embedded clause vs a trailing clause in conveying the same information (e.g. 'The dog that bit me...' vs 'The dog bit me, and it...')

modes.reason: Students who have only encountered trailing dependent clauses will classify all complex sentences as having the same structure. Encountering embedded clauses in multiple sentence contexts helps students build a more complete model of complex sentence variety.

nodes.label: Using embedded clauses to elaborate ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct complex sentences using embedded clauses to elaborate, extend and explain ideas, and explain why they have used an embedded clause in preference to other constructions.
criteria: Constructs a grammatically accurate sentence with an embedded clause
Identifies the embedded clause and names the noun group it expands
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot produce accurate embedded clauses cannot deploy them in extended writing (Node 3 and AC9E6LY06) — the production skill must be established before the integration task is attempted.

width.minimum: Construct at least one sentence using an embedded clause to expand a noun group (e.g. 'Hamish studied the rock samples that he had collected on the excursion'); identify the embedded clause and what noun group it expands.
width.typical: Create and use complex sentences with embedded clauses in writing, selecting conjunctions that enable the clauses to elaborate, extend or explain; revise sentences to evaluate whether an embedded clause improves precision and variety.
wider: Experiment with stacking multiple clauses in a sentence and evaluate where embedded clauses create clarity vs. awkwardness
Edit a piece of own writing to introduce embedded clauses where they add precision, and reflect on the effect

modes.reason: Constructing embedded clauses accurately requires mechanical precision — students need practice producing them in varied sentences before they can deploy them fluently in extended writing. Fluency here enables transfer to AC9E6LY06.

nodes.label: Embedded clauses in extended writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deploy embedded clauses in extended writing as part of a varied repertoire of complex sentence structures.
criteria: Produces at least one grammatically accurate embedded clause within a piece of extended writing
Demonstrates at least two different complex sentence structures in the same piece of writing

width.minimum: Produce a short piece of extended writing (at least one paragraph) that uses at least one embedded clause accurately within a varied sentence structure.
width.typical: Write extended texts that use embedded clauses alongside other complex sentence structures; evaluate the variety and precision of complex sentences in own writing; edit to improve sentence variety where needed.
wider: Analyse a paragraph from a curriculum-area information report and identify all complex sentence types used, including any embedded clauses
Rewrite a provided paragraph using a greater variety of complex sentence structures, including embedded clauses, and evaluate the improvement

modes.reason: Deploying embedded clauses fluently in extended writing requires integrating identification knowledge (Node 1) with production skills (Node 2) in sustained compositional context — the transfer to extended writing is the integration challenge.

descriptors.title: Verbs, tense and adverb groups for precision
descriptors.description: understand how ideas can be expanded and sharpened through careful choice of verbs, elaborated tenses and a range of adverb groups
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how noun groups can be expanded in a variety of ways to provide a fuller description (AC9E5LA06). They have not yet examined the precision available through verb selection, tense elaboration, or adverb groups as tools for sharpening ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how careful verb choice, elaborated tenses and adverb groups expand and sharpen ideas in texts, and can apply these choices in their own writing.

nodes.label: Precise verb selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how selecting a precise verb sharpens meaning and reduces the need for additional words.
criteria: Selects a more precise verb than the general alternative in a given sentence
Explains what additional meaning the precise verb contributes
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without a repertoire of precise verbs arrive at Node 3 unable to make meaningful verb-precision choices in their writing — the integration task requires accessible vocabulary stock, not just conceptual understanding.

width.minimum: Replace at least two general verbs (e.g. 'cut', 'say') with more precise alternatives in provided sentences and explain how the meaning changes.
width.typical: Analyse how precise verb choices (e.g. 'slice', 'dice', 'fillet' vs 'cut') sharpen meaning across different text types; explain how verb precision reduces reliance on adverbs to convey the same information.
wider: Compare verb choices in two information reports on the same topic and analyse how verb precision affects the authority and clarity of the text
Examine verbs of saying in narratives (e.g. 'whispered', 'demanded', 'muttered') and explain what each adds beyond the neutral 'said'

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of precise verb choices before they can deploy them fluently in writing. Accumulating alternatives to common general verbs (cut, say, walk, look) across multiple contexts builds the vocabulary stock needed for AC9E6LY06.

nodes.label: Elaborated tenses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the different ways English refers to time using simple present, simple past, and future time expressions, and select the appropriate form for a given purpose.
criteria: Identifies whether a sentence uses simple present for a present state, habitual action, or timeless truth
Names at least two ways of expressing future time in English and provides an example of each

width.minimum: Identify and explain the difference between simple present tense for present states vs. habitual actions in at least two provided sentences; identify at least one way of referring to future time (using 'will', present tense, or adverbials).
width.typical: Understand and use the simple present tense for present states, habitual actions, and 'timeless' happenings (as in information reports); understand the range of future time expressions and select the appropriate form for different text types and purposes.
wider: Analyse how tense choices function in information reports vs. narratives vs. procedure texts and explain why different text types use different tense conventions
Investigate how authors deliberately shift tense within a text for effect (e.g. a historical recount that shifts to present tense for dramatic immediacy)

modes.reason: Students often treat the simple present as a single tense with one function. The three distinct uses (present state, habitual action, timeless truth) are revealed through varied contexts — each text type makes a different use dominant.

nodes.label: Adverb groups for precision
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how adverb groups expand and sharpen ideas by adding information about manner, place, time or degree, and can use them to improve the precision of their own writing.
criteria: Identifies and classifies adverb groups by type (manner, place, time, degree) in provided text
Uses at least one adverb group appropriately in own writing to add precision

width.minimum: Identify adverb groups in at least two provided sentences and explain what type of information each adds (manner, place, time, degree); use one adverb group to improve a provided sentence.
width.typical: Analyse how adverb groups work alongside precise verb and tense choices to sharpen ideas across a range of text types; use adverb groups in writing to add precision about when, where, how and to what extent actions occur.
wider: Edit a piece of own writing to evaluate whether each adverb group adds necessary precision or is redundant given a precise verb choice
Compare adverb group use in procedure texts vs. narratives and explain how the type and placement of adverb groups differs by purpose

modes.reason: This node integrates verb precision (Node 1) and tense understanding (Node 2) with adverb group selection — the authoring challenge is coordinating all three to produce precise, varied writing. The components come together in the editing act.

descriptors.title: Images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps and graphs
descriptors.description: identify and explain how images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps and graphs contribute to meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how the sequence of images in print, digital and film texts has an effect on meaning (AC9E5LA07). They have not yet examined how a range of non-narrative visual representations (tables, diagrams, maps, graphs, flowcharts) contribute to meaning in informational and procedural texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and explain how a range of visual representations — images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps and graphs — contribute to meaning in different text types.

nodes.label: Sequential visual representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how sequential visual representations (timelines, flowcharts, procedure diagrams, life-cycle diagrams) represent order and process.
criteria: Identifies the type of sequential visual representation and names the type of information it conveys
Explains at least one way the visual contributes to meaning differently from the accompanying written text

width.minimum: Explain how one type of sequential visual representation (e.g. a flowchart or procedure diagram) represents order or process in a provided text; identify what information it adds that the written text alone does not.
width.typical: Identify and explain how a range of sequential visual representations (timelines, flowcharts, procedure diagrams, life-cycle diagrams, photo stories) convey sequence and process; compare how different sequential types suit different purposes.
wider: Create a visual sequential representation (flowchart, timeline or diagram) for a curriculum-area process and evaluate whether it adds meaning more efficiently than prose
Compare how comic strips and scientific procedure diagrams both use sequential images — and identify what is the same and what differs in their conventions

nodes.label: Conceptual visual representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how tables, maps, graphs and diagrams represent concepts, information and relationships visually.
criteria: Names the type of conceptual visual representation and identifies the kind of information or relationship it displays
Explains how the visual adds to meaning beyond what the accompanying written text provides

width.minimum: Explain how one type of conceptual visual (table, map, graph, or diagram) contributes to meaning in a provided text; identify at least one relationship or pattern it makes visible.
width.typical: Analyse how tables, maps, graphs and diagrams represent different kinds of information and relationships; explain why a visual representation may communicate certain information more effectively than prose.
wider: Compare the same data presented as a table vs. a graph and explain which is more effective for different purposes
Analyse a map from a curriculum-area text (geography, history) and explain how its design choices (scale, symbols, orientation) affect meaning

modes.reason: Students typically have more experience with graphs than with tables, maps or diagrams. Encountering all types across curriculum areas helps students build a generalised understanding of how visual representations work, rather than a graph-specific one.

nodes.label: Cultural sensitivity in visual texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that images and maps may hold cultural significance or sensitivity for First Nations Australians, and can apply appropriate judgement when using or sharing such materials.
criteria: Identifies that visual materials including maps may hold cultural significance for First Nations Australians
Explains why a disclaimer or judgement about cultural appropriateness is relevant when using such materials

width.minimum: Identify that some images and maps may be sensitive for First Nations Australians and explain why a disclaimer or careful judgement may be required when using them.
width.typical: Discuss examples of images or maps that may be culturally sensitive for First Nations Australians; explain the concept of cultural appropriateness and how this should shape decisions about using or reproducing visual texts.
wider: Research how First Nations Australian communities manage the use and sharing of culturally significant images and maps, and compare with general copyright practices
Examine the difference between an image that is legally available and one that is culturally appropriate to share, and develop a set of questions to ask before using visual materials

modes.reason: Students need explicit reasoning support to navigate the distinction between legal availability and cultural appropriateness — the reasoning chain from 'I can access this image' to 'I should consider whether it is appropriate to use it' requires scaffolding.

descriptors.title: Figurative and emotive vocabulary
descriptors.description: identify authors' use of vivid, emotive vocabulary, such as metaphors, similes, personification, idioms, imagery and hyperbole
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how vocabulary is used to express greater precision of meaning, including through metaphor, simile and personification (AC9E5LA08). They have not yet examined idioms, hyperbole, or the way figurative language creates shades of meaning that are less predictable than literal vocabulary.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and explain authors' use of vivid and emotive vocabulary — metaphors, similes, personification, idioms, imagery and hyperbole — and discuss how these create meaning and effect.

nodes.label: Figurative language devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name the range of figurative language devices — metaphor, simile, personification, idiom, imagery, hyperbole — and explain what each does.
criteria: Names at least three figurative language device types correctly when presented with examples
Explains the literal meaning of one figurative example and how it differs from its figurative meaning
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably identify and name the full device set — particularly idioms and hyperbole — cannot perform the explanation task in Node 2 or deploy metalanguage accurately in Node 3.

width.minimum: Identify and correctly name at least three figurative language devices in provided texts; explain the literal vs. figurative meaning of one example.
width.typical: Identify and name all six device types in provided texts; explain the difference between idioms (fixed phrases with non-literal meanings) and other figurative devices; explain how hyperbole creates emphasis through exaggeration.
wider: Research the origins of several common English idioms and explain how their literal meanings relate to their figurative use
Compare how idioms and metaphors function in texts from different cultural contexts, including texts by First Nations Australian authors

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of examples of each device — particularly idioms and hyperbole, which are newer at Y6 — before they can reliably identify and distinguish them. A range of text types builds this repertoire more effectively than a single text.

nodes.label: Figurative language for vivid and unexpected meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how figurative language creates vivid and less predictable shades of meaning compared with more literal vocabulary choices.
criteria: Explains what effect a specific figurative language choice creates that a literal equivalent would not
Identifies at least one reason why an author might choose figurative language at a particular point in a text
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can only identify devices without explaining their effect cannot use metalanguage accurately in Node 3 — the explanation move ('this device creates this effect') is the basis for all metalinguistic discussion.

width.minimum: Compare a provided sentence using figurative language with a literal equivalent and explain what meaning or effect is added by the figurative choice.
width.typical: Analyse how metaphors, personification and idioms create vivid, unexpected or emotionally resonant meanings in literary and persuasive texts; explain why an author might choose figurative language over literal vocabulary at a particular point.
wider: Examine how figurative language choices in a poem or story create an extended or sustained impression rather than isolated effects
Analyse the figurative language in a persuasive text (e.g. a review) and explain how it affects the reader's emotional response to the subject

modes.reason: The move from 'this is a metaphor' to 'this metaphor creates this particular shade of meaning, which a literal word would not' requires explicit scaffolding. Students who have only been asked to identify devices rarely develop the explanatory move without a structured reasoning prompt.

nodes.label: Using subject metalanguage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the correct vocabulary (metalanguage) to name text structures, literary devices and language features when discussing and analysing texts.
criteria: Uses at least two figurative language metalanguage terms accurately when discussing a text
Pairs the metalanguage term with an explanation of its effect, not just its identification

width.minimum: Use at least two figurative language terms accurately in a written or spoken response about a text.
width.typical: Discuss texts using vocabulary to name text structure, literary devices and language features accurately; use metalanguage (metaphor, simile, personification, idiom, hyperbole, imagery) fluently in written analysis.
wider: Write a short analytical paragraph about a poem that uses at least three metalanguage terms accurately and explains the effect of each device
Compare two texts of the same type using metalanguage to discuss both similarities and differences in language choices

modes.reason: Accurate and fluent use of metalanguage in discussion and writing requires practice. Students who know the terms in isolation often revert to vague language ('it makes it more interesting') under the pressure of producing extended writing or spoken analysis.

descriptors.title: Comma use
descriptors.description: understand how to use the comma for lists, to separate a dependent clause from an independent clause, and in dialogue
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use commas to indicate prepositional phrases, and apostrophes where there is multiple possession (AC9E5LA09). They have not yet systematically examined all three conventional comma uses — for lists, for separating clauses, and in dialogue.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how the comma is used for lists, to separate a dependent clause from an independent clause, and in dialogue, and can apply these uses accurately in their own writing.

nodes.label: Three uses of the comma
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the three main uses of the comma covered at Year 6: for lists, to separate a dependent clause from an independent clause, and in dialogue.
criteria: Names the three comma uses covered at Year 6
Correctly identifies which use applies in at least three out of four provided examples
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat commas as pause markers rather than grammatical signals apply them inconsistently in Nodes 2 and 3 — producing systematic punctuation errors in both controlled practice and extended writing.

width.minimum: Identify which of the three comma uses applies in each of at least four provided sentences; explain the rule for each use in own words.
width.typical: Identify and explain all three comma uses in a range of example sentences; identify different uses of commas including between independent clauses with conjunctions in compound sentences.
wider: Analyse a professional writer's use of commas in a passage and classify each use, including noting any uses that go beyond the three taught
Research the Oxford comma debate and form a reasoned opinion about whether it should be used

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse clause-separation commas with list commas when encountering compound sentences. Encountering the three uses in diverse sentence contexts prevents the misconception that commas mark natural pauses rather than grammatical relationships.

nodes.label: Applying comma use in writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use commas accurately for all three purposes in their own writing.
criteria: Produces at least one sentence demonstrating each of the three comma uses correctly
Uses commas accurately in a short piece of own writing including at least one dialogue exchange
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably place commas in controlled sentence production will not apply them accurately in the sustained composition required by Node 3 — errors established here propagate directly into extended writing.

width.minimum: Produce at least three sentences — one demonstrating each comma use — with the comma placed correctly.
width.typical: Use commas accurately across all three purposes in extended writing; demonstrate comma use in dialogue correctly (including placement relative to speech marks and dialogue tags).
wider: Edit a provided passage with comma errors, correct them, and explain the reasoning behind each correction
Compare how dialogue punctuation conventions differ in different published texts and discuss whether authors sometimes deliberately break conventions

modes.reason: Comma use requires precision through practice — students who understand the rules conceptually frequently revert to guessing or avoidance under the pressure of extended writing. Accuracy comes from repeated application in varied writing contexts.

nodes.label: Comma accuracy in extended writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students use commas accurately across all three purposes consistently in extended writing across different text types.
criteria: Uses commas accurately for at least two purposes in a piece of extended writing
Identifies and corrects at least one comma error in own or peer writing

width.minimum: Produce a short piece of extended writing (including narrative or persuasive text with dialogue) in which commas are used accurately for at least two of the three purposes.
width.typical: Use commas accurately across all three purposes in extended writing across different text types (narrative, informative, persuasive); self-edit for comma accuracy as part of the writing process.
wider: Peer-edit a classmate's writing for comma accuracy, identifying and explaining any errors found
Analyse how published authors use commas in complex sentences and identify any comma choices that go beyond the three rules taught

modes.reason: Applying all three comma rules accurately under extended writing conditions requires integrating rule knowledge (Node 1) with production practice (Node 2) simultaneously — the integration pressure of composing and punctuating together is the learning challenge.

descriptors.title: Responses to characters and events across contexts
descriptors.description: identify responses to characters and events in literary texts, drawn from historical, social or cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify aspects of literary texts that represent details or information about historical, social and cultural experiences (AC9E5LE01). They have not yet examined how the historical, social or cultural context of a text shapes responses to its characters and events, nor read widely across First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify their own and others' responses to characters and events in literary texts from diverse historical, social and cultural contexts, and explain how context shapes those responses.

nodes.label: Context shapes response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the historical, social or cultural context of a text may influence how readers respond to characters, actions and events.
criteria: Identifies at least one way that a text's context shapes a reader's response to a character or event
Explains how a reader from a different time or context might respond differently to the same character or event
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat their own response as universal cannot engage meaningfully with diverse authors in Node 2 or evaluate others' responses in Node 3 — both require the foundational understanding that response is contextually situated.

width.minimum: Identify at least one way that the historical, social or cultural context of a provided text shapes how readers respond to a character or event; explain why a response might differ from a reader of a different time or context.
width.typical: Discuss how historical, social and cultural experiences embedded in a text may produce different responses to characters and events; explain how a reader's own context also shapes their response.
wider: Compare responses to the same character from a contemporary reader and a reader from the historical context of the text
Examine how responses to heroes in texts from different cultural contexts (e.g. First Nations Australian texts vs. Western adventure narratives) reflect different values

modes.reason: Moving from 'I respond to this character in this way' to 'I respond this way because of my context, and someone from a different context might respond differently' requires explicit scaffolding. Students often treat their response as universal without prompting to consider its situatedness.

nodes.label: Reading across diverse authors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors and describe features of the literary contexts they represent.
criteria: Names the cultural, historical or social context of at least one text by a First Nations Australian or world author
Shares a personal response to a character or event and connects it to the text's context

width.minimum: Identify and describe the context (historical, social, or cultural) represented in at least one text from a First Nations Australian author or a world author from a different cultural context.
width.typical: Read and respond to texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors; discuss how the contexts represented in these texts shape their characters, events and themes; share personal responses and connect them to the texts' contexts.
wider: Compare how two authors from different cultural backgrounds represent a shared theme (e.g. family, belonging, courage) and analyse what the similarities and differences reveal
Explore reviews of Australian films and identify how reviewers interpret cultural contexts in their responses

modes.reason: Reading across diverse authors requires accumulating a range of textual encounters — responses to diverse contexts cannot be built from analysis of a single text. The wider the reading repertoire, the more textured students' understanding of how context shapes response becomes.

nodes.label: Sharing and evaluating responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share and evaluate responses to characters and events in texts from diverse contexts, explaining how context shapes their own and others' readings.
criteria: Shares a personal response to a character or event and connects it to the text's context
Explains how a reader from a different context might respond differently to the same character or event

width.minimum: Share a personal response to a character or event from a text by a First Nations Australian or world author and connect the response to one aspect of the text's context.
width.typical: Share and evaluate responses to texts from diverse historical, social and cultural contexts; explain how own and others' responses are shaped by context; compare responses across the class and discuss how different readers may respond differently to the same character or event.
wider: Compare personal responses to a First Nations Australian text with those of a classmate and discuss how different contexts produce different readings
Evaluate a published review of a text from a different cultural context and analyse how the reviewer's context shapes their response

modes.reason: Sharing and evaluating responses requires integrating understanding of how context shapes meaning (Node 1) and reading experience from diverse authors (Node 2) into a reflective, socially situated act of literary discussion.

descriptors.title: Comparing literary texts on similar topics
descriptors.description: identify similarities and differences in literary texts on similar topics, themes or plots
descriptors.knowledge: Students can present an opinion on a literary text using specific terms about literary devices, text structure and language features (AC9E5LE02). They have not yet systematically compared texts on similar topics or themes, examining how narrator, narrative structure, voice, and language choices differ and influence readers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in literary texts on similar topics, themes or plots, and explain how differences in narrator, narrative structure, voice, and language and visual features influence readers.

nodes.label: Identifying shared and different features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in the use of structural and language features between two texts on a similar topic, theme or plot.
criteria: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference in the structural features of two compared texts
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference in the language or visual features of two compared texts

width.minimum: Identify at least two similarities and two differences between two provided texts on a similar topic or theme, using at least one structural feature and one language feature.
width.typical: Compare at least two texts on a similar topic or theme across a range of features — topic, theme, narrative structure, characterisation, language choices, visual features — and organise comparisons systematically.
wider: Compare two fantasy quest novels or two realistic novels on a specific theme from different authors or cultural contexts
Compare texts on the same theme with very different styles — for example, a picture book and a chapter book on the same theme — to identify what stylistic differences do to the reader experience

nodes.label: How differences influence readers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how differences in narrator, narrative structure, voice, and language and visual features between texts influence readers or viewers.
criteria: Names at least one difference in narrator, voice or narrative structure between two compared texts
Explains how that difference influences the reader's interpretation or experience
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can only identify differences without connecting them to reader effect cannot form an evaluative preference in Node 3 — the evaluation requires the difference→effect reasoning chain established here.

width.minimum: Identify one difference in narrator or voice between two texts on a similar topic and explain how that difference changes the reader's experience.
width.typical: Analyse how differences in the use of narrator, narrative structure, voice, and language and visual features between two texts influence how readers interpret the topic or theme; explain which features best serve the texts' respective purposes.
wider: Analyse how the choice of first-person vs. third-person narrator shapes reader identification with characters across two texts on the same theme
Compare how visual features in picture books vs. chapter books on the same topic influence younger vs. older reader experiences

modes.reason: Moving from 'these texts are different' to 'this difference produces this reader effect' requires a reasoning scaffold. Students often identify differences without connecting them to audience experience — the reasoning chain needs to be made explicit.

nodes.label: Evaluating texts and forming preferences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate texts on similar topics and form and explain a preference based on how effectively structural and language features serve the text's purpose.
criteria: States a preference between two compared texts with at least one reason grounded in textual evidence
Uses at least one literary metalanguage term accurately in the explanation

width.minimum: State a preference for one of two compared texts and give at least one reason that refers to a structural or language feature.
width.typical: Form and explain a preference between two compared texts based on an analysis of how effectively narrator, structure, voice and language features serve the texts' respective purposes; use literary metalanguage in the explanation.
wider: Write a comparative review of two texts on the same theme, evaluating which is more effective for the purpose and audience and why
Evaluate which text from two compared would be more appropriate for a specific reader or purpose, and justify the recommendation

modes.reason: Forming an evaluative preference requires integrating feature identification (Node 1) with understanding of how differences influence readers (Node 2) into a reasoned aesthetic judgement — the integration is the literary thinking act.

descriptors.title: Author's individual style
descriptors.description: identify and explain characteristics that define an author's individual style
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise that the point of view in a literary text influences how readers interpret and respond to events (AC9E5LE03). They have not yet examined the concept of an individual author's style — the distinctive combination of choices (theme, structure, voice, vocabulary, technique) that characterises a particular author's work across texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify and explain characteristics that define an individual author's style, drawing on analysis of multiple texts by the same author.

nodes.label: What constitutes author style
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the elements that collectively constitute an author's style — subject/theme, characterisation, text structure, plot development, tone, vocabulary, voice, grammatical structures, and visual techniques.
criteria: Names at least four elements that constitute author style
Identifies at least two style elements in a provided text extract with evidence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name and identify the style element vocabulary cannot perform the cross-text pattern recognition required in Node 2 — they have no analytical categories to apply.

width.minimum: Name at least four elements that can characterise an author's style; identify examples of two of these elements in a provided text extract.
width.typical: Examine a text and identify examples of the full range of style elements: subject, theme, characterisation, text structure, plot development, tone, vocabulary, voice, grammatical structures, and visual techniques; discuss which elements seem most defining for a given author.
wider: Compare a list of style elements for two contrasting authors and analyse which elements are universal and which are distinctive
Investigate how illustrators also develop individual styles in picture books — identifying characteristic visual features across multiple works

modes.reason: Students need to encounter the full range of style elements across multiple texts before the concept of 'style as a pattern across texts' becomes visible. A single text only shows one data point; style emerges from accumulation.

nodes.label: Style as a cross-text pattern
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similarities across two or more texts by the same author that define the qualities characterising that author's style.
criteria: Identifies at least two characteristics that appear across two or more texts by the same author
Names these as defining features of the author's style, not just features of a single text
nodes.hinge_reason: Without cross-text pattern recognition, Node 3's explanatory task has no data — students cannot explain a style they have not identified across texts.

width.minimum: Identify at least two similarities across two texts by the same author and explain what these reveal about the author's characteristic style.
width.typical: Explore two or more texts by the same author; identify similarities in subject, theme, characterisation, structure, plot, tone, vocabulary, voice and grammatical structures; articulate the qualities that characterise the author's individual style.
wider: Explore two or more texts by a First Nations Australian author and identify characteristic elements of their writing, including images, themes and language choices
Compare illustrations across two or more picture books by the same illustrator and identify the characteristic visual features that define their style

modes.reason: The concept of style as a cross-text pattern is invisible with a single text. Reading two texts by the same author is the minimum for identifying style — reading more texts (and different authors) strengthens the concept by showing what persists vs. what varies.

nodes.label: Explaining style choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the characteristics that define a specific author's individual style using literary metalanguage.
criteria: Identifies and names at least three style elements with specific textual evidence from the author's work
Explains how these elements work together to create the author's distinctive style

width.minimum: Write or speak a brief explanation of one author's style, using at least three style elements with textual evidence.
width.typical: Produce an explanation of an author's individual style that identifies multiple characteristic elements with specific textual evidence; discuss how these choices create the author's distinctive voice and effect on readers.
wider: Compare the defining style features of two authors who write in the same genre and explain what makes each distinctive
Write a short piece in the style of a chosen author, then annotate the choices made to reflect the style elements identified

modes.reason: Producing an explanation of an author's style integrates knowledge of style elements (Node 1) with cross-text pattern recognition (Node 2) into a coherent explanatory act — the components come together in the writer's own analytical production.

descriptors.title: Sound and imagery in poetry
descriptors.description: explain the way authors use sound and imagery to create meaning and effect in poetry
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine the effects of imagery including simile, metaphor and personification, and sound devices such as alliteration and onomatopoeia in literary texts (AC9E5LE04). They have not yet examined assonance, the combined effect of multiple sound devices, rhythm in ballads, or how imagery builds emotional connection and engagement in poetry.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can explain how authors use sound devices (alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia) and imagery to create meaning, emotional effect and engagement in poetry.

nodes.label: Sound devices in poetry
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the effects of alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia in poetry.
criteria: Correctly identifies and names alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia in provided examples
Explains the effect of at least one sound device example on mood, pace or meaning
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify and name all three sound devices — particularly assonance — cannot perform the integration analysis required in Node 4, which depends on naming devices to explain how they work together.

width.minimum: Identify and name alliteration, onomatopoeia and assonance in provided poems; explain the effect of one example of each.
width.typical: Describe the effects of alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia in a range of poems; explain how each sound device contributes to the mood, pace or meaning of the poem.
wider: Analyse how multiple sound devices work together in the same poem to create a cumulative effect
Compare two poems on the same theme where one uses extensive sound devices and one does not, and evaluate the difference in effect

modes.reason: Students who have encountered only alliteration need to build familiarity with assonance (internal vowel rhyme) through a range of examples before the concept solidifies. Assonance is less perceptually obvious than alliteration and benefits from multiple exposures.

nodes.label: Imagery for emotional engagement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how imagery builds emotional connections and engagement with the story or theme in poetry.
criteria: Identifies a specific image in a poem and describes the emotional response it evokes
Explains how the image creates that response (what associations or sensory details produce the effect)

width.minimum: Identify one image in a poem and explain how it builds emotional connection or engagement for the reader.
width.typical: Explain how imagery in poems builds emotional connections and engagement; analyse examples where imagery evokes a specific emotional response; identify imagery in narratives or poetry about First Nations Australians' Country/Place.
wider: Identify the imagery used in poetry about First Nations Australians' Country/Place and discuss how it reflects relationships between people, land and story
Compare how imagery functions in a poem vs. an information text on the same subject and explain what poetry makes possible that prose does not

modes.reason: Explaining how imagery creates an emotional response (rather than simply naming the image) requires students to reason from image content → association → emotional effect. This chain is not obvious and benefits from explicit modelling.

nodes.label: Rhythm and effect in ballads
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the effect of rhythm in ballads and how regular rhythm contributes to meaning and oral tradition.
criteria: Identifies a regular rhythmic pattern in a ballad
Explains at least one effect the rhythm creates for the reader or listener

width.minimum: Identify regular rhythmic patterns in a provided ballad; explain at least one effect of the rhythm (e.g. it creates a sense of pace, makes the poem memorable, suits oral performance).
width.typical: Explain the effect of rhythm in ballads — including how regular rhythm contributes to the oral and performative tradition of the ballad form, suits storytelling, and creates predictability that reinforces theme or mood.
wider: Compare the rhythmic effect in two ballads with different tempos and explain how rhythm choice suits each poem's content
Perform a ballad aloud and evaluate how performing the rhythm affects the poem's meaning and emotional impact

nodes.label: How sound and imagery work together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how sound devices and imagery work together in a poem to create its overall meaning and effect.
criteria: Identifies at least one sound device and one image in a poem and names each correctly
Explains how they work together to create a specific meaning or emotional effect in the poem

width.minimum: Identify at least one sound device and one image in a poem and explain how they work together to create meaning or effect.
width.typical: Analyse a poem identifying how the combination of sound devices and imagery constructs the poem's meaning, mood and emotional engagement; explain why the author has made specific sound and imagery choices.
wider: Compare how an Australian poem and a poem from another cultural context use sound and imagery to convey a theme, identifying cross-cultural similarities and differences
Write a short poem that deliberately employs at least two sound devices and one sustained image, then annotate the choices

modes.reason: Explaining how sound and imagery work together requires integrating Nodes 1–3 into a coherent reading of a whole poem — the components only show their full meaning in coordination.

descriptors.title: Create and edit literary texts adapting from sources
descriptors.description: create and edit literary texts that adapt plot structure, characters, settings and/or ideas from texts students have experienced, and experiment with literary devices
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and edit literary texts, experimenting with figurative language, storylines, characters and settings (AC9E5LE05). They have not yet deliberately adapted specific elements (plot structure, characters, settings) from texts they have read, or consciously experimented with named literary devices in their own writing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can create and edit literary texts that deliberately adapt elements from source texts and experiment with literary devices, and explain the choices made.

nodes.label: Adaptation as a literary strategy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how adaptation works — taking specific elements (character, setting, plot structure) from a known text and reimagining them — and distinguish adaptation from retelling.
criteria: Identifies at least two elements adapted from a source text in a provided example
Explains how the adaptation differs from retelling the same story
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat adaptation as retelling cannot plan deliberate element choices in Node 2 — the planning task requires understanding that adaptation involves purposeful selection and transformation, not reproduction.

width.minimum: Identify at least two elements that have been adapted in a provided example of a literary adaptation; explain how the adaptation differs from the source.
width.typical: Discuss how literary adaptation works across a range of forms (reimagined characters, altered settings, shifted plot structures); identify what has been kept, changed and added in an example adaptation; distinguish adaptation from retelling.
wider: Compare an original text and its adaptation and analyse what the adapter's choices reveal about their perspective or context
Examine how an autobiography of a character from a known text requires inferring from the source while adding a new interpretive layer

modes.reason: Students need to understand that adaptation involves deliberate choice — not random change — and that choices must be justified against the source. The reasoning chain from 'I am changing this' to 'I am changing this because...' requires scaffolding before the production task.

nodes.label: Planning an adaptation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a literary text that adapts elements from a source text, making deliberate choices about which elements to keep, change or add.
criteria: Produces a planning document that identifies at least two elements adapted from a source text
Identifies at least one literary device to be used and explains what effect it is intended to create

width.minimum: Plan an adaptation of one element (e.g. reimagining the hero) from a text experienced, noting which elements are kept and which are changed; identify at least one literary device to experiment with.
width.typical: Plan a literary adaptation that adapts multiple elements (character, setting, plot structure, ideas) from a source text; identify and plan for literary devices (figurative language, narrative structure, dialogue) to be used in the text.
wider: Plan an adaptation that deliberately shifts the cultural or social context of the source text (e.g. reimagining a Western adventure story in an Australian context)
Plan a character autobiography that requires deep reading of the source text to infer characterisation details not stated directly

nodes.label: Creating and editing the adaptation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create, edit and discuss a literary text that adapts source material and experiments with literary devices, explaining choices made.
criteria: Produces a literary text that demonstrably adapts at least one element from a source text
Identifies and explains at least one literary device used and the effect intended

width.minimum: Create a short literary text (written, spoken or multimodal) that adapts at least one element from a source text and uses at least one literary device; edit using at least one stated criterion; explain one choice made.
width.typical: Create and edit a literary text that adapts plot structure, characters, settings and/or ideas from a source text; experiment with literary devices; discuss setting choices with a peer during editing; explain editing choices against the text's purpose.
wider: Create a literary text adapting from a First Nations Australian text experienced, engaging respectfully with cultural elements and explaining the choices made
Present the adaptation alongside a reflection on how the literary devices used enhance the setting, character or plot

modes.reason: Creating an adaptation integrates understanding of literary devices (from LA strand), knowledge of text structure (AC9E6LA03), and the adaptation strategy from Nodes 1-2 — all in a single production and editing act.

descriptors.title: Texts reflecting context of creation
descriptors.description: examine texts including media texts that represent ideas and events, and identify how they reflect the context in which they were created
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe the ways in which a text reflects the time and place in which it was created (AC9E5LY01). They have not yet examined media texts specifically, or analysed how context shapes representation through comparison of multiple texts from different times or places.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can examine texts including media texts that represent ideas and events, and identify and explain how those representations reflect the context in which the texts were created.

nodes.label: Context shapes representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the context in which a text was created (time, place, culture, purpose) shapes how it represents ideas and events.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific feature of a text that reflects the context of its creation
Explains why a text from a different context might represent the same ideas or events differently
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat their own cultural context as neutral cannot analyse how creator context shapes media representation in Node 2 — the N2 analysis presupposes that context is an active force, not a neutral background.

width.minimum: Identify at least one way a provided text reflects the context of its creation; explain why a text from a different context might represent the same event or idea differently.
width.typical: Analyse how context — including time, place, cultural values and purpose — shapes how a text represents ideas and events; discuss the relationship between creator context and text representation across a range of text types.
wider: Compare news reports of the same type of event from different time periods and identify how the representations reflect their historical contexts
Identify how advertisements for the same product from different decades reflect changing social values and contexts

modes.reason: Students who analyse only contemporary texts can mistake their own cultural context as neutral or universal. Comparing texts from different times and places reveals context as an active force in representation — preventing the misconception that texts simply describe reality.

nodes.label: Media texts and context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how media texts including advertising and news media represent ideas and events in ways that reflect their context of creation.
criteria: Identifies how a specific representation choice in a media text reflects the context of its creation
Explains the impact of that choice on how ideas or events are understood by the intended audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reason from 'this choice was made' to 'this choice was made because of this context' cannot evaluate representation choices in Node 3 — the evaluation depends on the creator-context→choice reasoning chain.

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of how context shapes representation in a provided media text (e.g. a news report, advertisement, or film poster); explain what the choice reveals about the context.
width.typical: Examine and compare media texts (news reports, advertisements, film promotions) from different contexts; identify how the same event, product, or theme is represented differently across different cultural or national contexts; explain the impact of these choices on audience expectations.
wider: Compare advertising posters for the same animated film in different countries and explain how cultural context shapes audience appeal
Examine how the same news story is represented in two different media outlets and identify how institutional context shapes the representation

modes.reason: Media text analysis requires students to hold creator context and representation choice simultaneously — reasoning from 'this choice was made' to 'this choice was made because of this context'. The reasoning chain needs scaffolding before students can apply it independently.

nodes.label: Evaluating representation choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the impact of representation choices in texts and media texts, explaining how context-shaped choices affect audience understanding or response.
criteria: Evaluates the impact of at least one representation choice in a media text
Explains whether the choice is effective, misleading or limited given the context of the text's creation

width.minimum: Evaluate the impact of at least one representation choice in a media text and explain whether the choice is effective or misleading given its context.
width.typical: Evaluate how context-shaped representation choices in a range of texts and media texts affect how audiences understand ideas and events; explain the impact on audience expectations; consider how more transparent representation of context could change audience response.
wider: Evaluate a news report or advertisement for the transparency of its contextual representations and explain what a critical reader should consider
Compare how representation choices in two media texts from different contexts could lead audiences to different understandings of the same event or product

modes.reason: Evaluating representation choices integrates understanding of how context shapes texts (Node 1) and how media texts function (Node 2) into a critical evaluative stance — the synthesis of context knowledge and evaluative judgement is the integration challenge.

descriptors.title: Interaction skills and formality
descriptors.description: use interaction skills and awareness of formality when paraphrasing, questioning, clarifying and interrogating ideas, developing and supporting arguments, and sharing and evaluating information, experiences and opinions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use appropriate interaction skills including paraphrasing and questioning to clarify meaning and make connections to their own experiences (AC9E5LY02). They have not yet applied formality awareness to their interaction choices, or developed and supported arguments through structured oral exchange.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use interaction skills with awareness of formality across a range of spoken contexts — paraphrasing, questioning, clarifying, developing arguments, and sharing and evaluating ideas.

nodes.label: Formality in spoken interaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt their spoken interaction style to the level of formality required by the context.
criteria: Uses language that consistently matches the expected formality level of the spoken context
Identifies at least one specific language choice made for formality reasons

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two different levels of formality in a spoken exchange; identify one language choice that signals the formality level.
width.typical: Participate in informal conversations, discussions and formal presentations; adjust vocabulary, tone and interaction style to match the formality of the context; identify when formality shifts are required.
wider: Participate in a formal debate or structured discussion and reflect on how formality requirements shaped language choices
Analyse a transcript of a formal vs. informal spoken exchange and identify the specific language features that signal each
