modes.reason: Formality in spoken interaction requires practised flexibility — students who understand the concept of formality levels (AC9E6LA01) still need repeated spoken practice to deploy appropriate register naturally under the pressure of real-time interaction.

nodes.label: Questioning and clarifying strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use paraphrasing, questioning, rephrasing and clarifying strategies purposefully in spoken interaction.
criteria: Uses at least two distinct interaction strategies (e.g. open question, paraphrase, clarifying question) in a discussion
Explains the purpose of at least one strategy used

width.minimum: Use at least two questioning or clarifying strategies (e.g. paraphrasing, asking a clarifying question, rephrasing) in a discussion; explain why each was used.
width.typical: Use the full range of interaction strategies — pausing, questioning (open and closed), rephrasing, repeating, summarising, reviewing and asking clarifying questions — when discussing topics; recognise that closed questions ask for precise responses while open questions prompt elaboration.
wider: Analyse a recorded discussion and identify where different questioning strategies were used effectively and where missed opportunities for clarification occurred
Practise using open questions to probe and extend a speaker's ideas, and reflect on how this shapes the conversation

modes.reason: Students who have only practised paraphrasing and one type of questioning need to build a broader repertoire of interaction strategies before they can deploy them flexibly. Practice across multiple spoken contexts is the path to flexible, context-sensitive use.

nodes.label: Developing and evaluating arguments in interaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop and support arguments and share and evaluate information, experiences and opinions through spoken interaction.
criteria: States an argument and supports it with at least one reason or piece of evidence
Evaluates at least one argument or opinion from another speaker, explaining whether and why they agree or disagree

width.minimum: Develop at least one argument orally and support it with a reason or evidence; evaluate one argument or opinion offered by another speaker.
width.typical: Develop, support and extend arguments in structured spoken contexts (discussions, debates); share and evaluate information, experiences and opinions using appropriate evidence and reasoning; interrogate ideas offered by others with relevant questions.
wider: Lead a structured group discussion on a topic, ensuring all participants contribute and arguments are developed and evaluated
Participate in a formal debate and reflect on how the structured format shaped argument development compared with informal discussion

modes.reason: Developing arguments in real-time spoken interaction requires integrating formality awareness (Node 1), questioning strategies (Node 2), and substantive content reasoning simultaneously — the coordination challenge is the learning.

descriptors.title: Text structures and language features serving purpose
descriptors.description: analyse how text structures and language features work together to meet the purpose of a text, and engage and influence audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain characteristic features used in imaginative, informative and persuasive texts to meet the purpose of the text (AC9E5LY03). They have not yet analysed how structures and language features work together as a system to meet purpose, nor explicitly considered how this system engages and influences audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can analyse how text structures and language features work together to meet the purpose of a text and engage and influence audiences.

nodes.label: Structures and language features as a system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how text structures and language features work together (not in isolation) to serve a text's purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least one structural feature and one language feature in a text
Explains how both contribute to the same purpose — not just lists them independently
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can only identify features in isolation cannot perform the audience-engagement analysis in Node 2 or the effectiveness evaluation in Node 3 — both require the systems-level reasoning established here.

width.minimum: Identify one structural feature and one language feature in a provided text and explain how both contribute to the same purpose.
width.typical: Analyse how text structures and language features work together across a range of text types — noting that structures organise content and language features realise meaning within those structures — to produce a coherent text that meets its purpose.
wider: Compare the structural and language feature choices in two texts with the same purpose (e.g. two information reports on the same topic) and evaluate which combination is more effective
Analyse a multimodal text and explain how layout, image and language features work together to meet purpose

modes.reason: Students who can identify features in isolation often struggle to explain how they interact. The reasoning move from 'this text has X structure and Y language feature' to 'X and Y work together because...' requires explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Engaging and influencing audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how text structures and language features are chosen to engage a specific audience and influence how they respond.
criteria: Identifies a specific structural or language feature choice that engages or influences the audience
Explains how that choice affects the reader's engagement or response

width.minimum: Identify at least one structural or language feature choice in a text that is designed to engage or influence the audience, and explain the effect on the reader.
width.typical: Compare print and digital sources on similar topics and evaluate which structural and language features best aid navigation and clear communication; analyse how texts use structure and language choices to engage specific audiences and influence response.
wider: Compare two texts on the same topic aimed at different audiences and analyse how structural and language feature choices differ to suit each audience
Evaluate a digital text's use of navigation features (headings, links, images) and explain how these choices serve the audience's reading purpose

modes.reason: The concept of texts 'designed for audiences' is most visible in comparison — when students see that the same content is structured differently for different audiences, the intentionality of the choices becomes clear.

nodes.label: Evaluating text effectiveness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of a text's structural and language feature choices for its purpose and audience, and explain what improvements could be made.
criteria: Evaluates the effectiveness of at least one structural or language feature choice in a text for its purpose
Suggests a specific improvement and explains how it would better serve the purpose or audience

width.minimum: Evaluate whether the structural and language feature choices in a provided text effectively serve its purpose; identify at least one improvement and explain why it would help.
width.typical: Evaluate texts across a range of purposes and audiences for how effectively their structural and language feature combinations serve purpose and engage audience; suggest specific improvements where features are ineffective or missing.
wider: Design an improved version of a poorly structured text, identifying which features to add, remove or change and explaining each decision
Compare a student-written text with a professional example on the same topic and evaluate which combination of structural and language features is more effective and why

modes.reason: Evaluating effectiveness integrates systems-thinking about how features interact (Node 1) and audience awareness (Node 2) into a critical judgement — the evaluative act requires both components working together.

descriptors.title: Select, navigate and read texts for purpose
descriptors.description: select, navigate and read texts for a range of purposes, monitoring meaning and evaluating the use of structural features; for example, table of contents, glossary, chapters, headings and subheadings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can navigate and read texts for specific purposes, monitoring meaning using strategies such as adjusting reading rate and re-reading (AC9E5LY04). They have not yet systematically evaluated structural features (table of contents, glossary, headings) for their effectiveness in serving navigation and comprehension purposes, or applied research skills to locate and evaluate multiple texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can select, navigate and read texts for a range of purposes, monitoring meaning and evaluating how structural features serve those purposes.

nodes.label: Using structural features to navigate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use structural features of texts (table of contents, glossary, chapters, headings, subheadings) to locate specific content for a purpose.
criteria: Locates specific information in a text using at least two structural features
Identifies which structural feature was most useful for the stated purpose

width.minimum: Use at least two structural features (e.g. table of contents, headings) to locate specific information in a provided text for a stated purpose.
width.typical: Use knowledge of text structure to navigate a range of print and digital texts; use structural features including table of contents, glossary, chapters, headings and subheadings to locate specific literal content for a given research or reading purpose.
wider: Compare navigation features in a print text vs. a digital text on the same topic and evaluate which features better serve a specific reading purpose
Navigate a multi-source research task using structural features across several texts and evaluate which texts best serve the purpose

nodes.label: Evaluating structural features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the use of structural features in a text — assessing how well they serve navigation, comprehension and the reader's purpose.
criteria: Evaluates the effectiveness of at least one structural feature in a text with a stated reason
Identifies whether the feature effectively serves the reader's purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate evaluation criteria for structural features cannot make principled source selections in Node 3 — the research task requires evaluation criteria, not just navigation skill.

width.minimum: Evaluate the effectiveness of at least one structural feature (e.g. a glossary, heading system, or table of contents) in a provided text; explain whether it aids navigation and why.
width.typical: Evaluate how structural features in a range of print and digital texts serve navigation and comprehension; assess whether features are clearly designed, consistently applied and useful for the reader's purpose; identify where features are missing or poorly designed.
wider: Design an improved structural feature (e.g. a revised heading hierarchy, a more detailed table of contents) for a provided text and explain how the improvement serves the reader
Compare structural feature use across curriculum-area texts (e.g. a science textbook, a geography atlas) and evaluate what each subject's conventions reveal about how its readers use texts

modes.reason: Evaluating structural features requires students to articulate criteria for 'good' navigation design — reasoning from reader purpose through feature design to effectiveness. Without a reasoning scaffold, evaluations remain vague ('this heading is clear').

nodes.label: Selecting and evaluating texts for research
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select, evaluate and use texts for their relevance to a task and the accuracy of their information, applying research skills including locating, gathering and organising information.
criteria: Selects a text for a research task and explains why it is relevant and likely accurate
Locates specific information within the text using at least one structural feature

width.minimum: Select at least one text for a given research task, explain why it was selected (relevance, accuracy), and locate specific information within it using structural features.
width.typical: Apply research skills — locating, gathering, organising and evaluating texts — for a research task; bring subject and technical vocabulary to new reading; evaluate texts for pertinence to the task and accuracy of information.
wider: Compare two texts on the same topic for accuracy and relevance, explaining why one is a better source for a specific research purpose
Evaluate a digital source for indicators of credibility (author, publication, date, evidence) and explain the reasoning

modes.reason: Research-based reading integrates navigation skills (Node 1), evaluation of structural features (Node 2), and comprehension monitoring into a purposeful, multi-text reading act — the coordination is the learning.

descriptors.title: Comprehension strategies
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning to build literal and inferred meaning, and to connect and compare content from a variety of sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use comprehension strategies including visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning (AC9E5LY05). They have not yet applied these strategies specifically to building inferred meaning, or to connecting and comparing content across multiple sources.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies to build both literal and inferred meaning, and to connect and compare content from a variety of sources.

nodes.label: Building literal meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comprehension strategies to locate and construct literal meaning from a text.
criteria: Uses at least two comprehension strategies to locate literal information in a text
Distinguishes between information stated explicitly in the text and information that requires inference

width.minimum: Apply at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. questioning, summarising) to extract literal meaning from a provided text; identify where in the text the information is explicitly stated.
width.typical: Use the full range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning — to build literal meaning from a text; locate specific literal content accurately.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to a complex multimodal text and identify which strategies were most useful for extracting different types of literal information
Use graphic organisers to visualise and organise literal information from a text, demonstrating hierarchical or categorical relationships

nodes.label: Building inferred meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use prior knowledge and textual information to make inferences, going beyond what is explicitly stated.
criteria: Makes an inference and names the textual evidence that supports it
Distinguishes the inference from what is explicitly stated in the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot make supported inferences cannot connect and compare across sources in Node 3 — multi-source comparison relies on inferred meaning as much as literal retrieval, and without the inference skill, cross-source synthesis collapses to surface matching.

width.minimum: Identify at least one inference made during reading and explain what textual information and prior knowledge supported it.
width.typical: Use prior knowledge and textual information to make inferences; connect information in print and images to construct inferred meaning; ask and answer questions that require inference rather than literal retrieval.
wider: Identify a point in a text where inference is required due to ambiguity or implied meaning, and evaluate two different possible inferences against the textual evidence
Compare inferences made by different readers of the same text and discuss what prior knowledge or experience shaped different interpretations

modes.reason: Inference requires students to articulate the two-part reasoning move: 'the text says X; I know Y; therefore Z'. Students who have not had the inference process made explicit often guess rather than infer — scaffolding the distinction between evidence and guessing is productive here.

nodes.label: Connecting and comparing across sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect and compare content from a variety of sources using comprehension strategies.
criteria: Connects information from at least two sources and identifies a similarity or difference
Summarises content from one source accurately in own words

width.minimum: Connect information from at least two sources on the same topic and identify one similarity and one difference in what they say.
width.typical: Apply comprehension strategies to connect and compare content across a range of sources — print and digital, images and text; use graphic organisers to visualise connections, categories and hierarchies across sources; summarise and synthesise information from multiple texts.
wider: Compare the claims made by three or more sources on the same topic and evaluate which is best supported by evidence
Investigate a topic using sources from different disciplines (e.g. a science article, a historical account, an Indigenous knowledge source) and compare what each perspective reveals

modes.reason: Connecting and comparing across sources requires deploying literal comprehension (Node 1) and inferencing (Node 2) simultaneously on multiple texts — the integration challenge is managing meaning across sources, not just within one.

descriptors.title: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts
descriptors.description: plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts whose purposes may be imaginative, informative and persuasive, using paragraphs, a variety of complex sentences, expanded verb groups, tense, topic-specific and vivid vocabulary, punctuation, spelling and visual features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts across imaginative, informative and persuasive purposes, using paragraphs, complex sentences, expanded noun and verb groups, tense, vocabulary choices, punctuation and spelling (AC9E5LY06). They have not yet specifically deployed embedded clauses, elaborated tenses, adverb groups, or explicitly rhetorical devices in their writing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts for imaginative, informative and persuasive purposes, using paragraphs, complex sentences (including embedded clauses), expanded verb groups, tense, topic-specific and vivid vocabulary, appropriate punctuation and spelling, and visual features.

nodes.label: Planning for purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a written or multimodal text that identifies the purpose, audience, text structure and key language choices to be made.
criteria: Produces a plan that identifies purpose, audience and text structure
Identifies at least two language choices appropriate to the purpose and audience

width.minimum: Produce a plan for a written text identifying purpose, intended audience, text structure, and at least two key language choices (e.g. vocabulary register, sentence type) suited to that purpose and audience.
width.typical: Plan texts for imaginative, informative and persuasive purposes with attention to audience; identify text structure, vocabulary register, language features and visual elements appropriate to purpose and audience; note how the plan will use language choices taught in the Language strand.
wider: Plan the same text for two different audiences (e.g. a persuasive text for peers and for a council), identifying what language choices would differ
Plan a multimodal text and evaluate how digital tools and visual elements will work alongside the written text to serve purpose

nodes.label: Creating with varied complex sentences and precise vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create written texts that deploy a variety of complex sentences (including embedded clauses), expanded verb groups, tense choices, and topic-specific and vivid vocabulary.
criteria: Produces a paragraph that includes at least one embedded clause and at least one precise verb choice
Uses vocabulary that is appropriate to the purpose and audience of the text

width.minimum: Produce a paragraph that includes at least one embedded clause, at least one precise verb choice, and vocabulary appropriate to the text's purpose.
width.typical: Create written texts that use a variety of complex sentences including embedded clauses; use expanded verb groups, appropriate tense, topic-specific and vivid vocabulary; use rhetorical devices, images and modal verbs for persuasive effects where relevant.
wider: Create an informative text for two different audiences, adjusting text structure and language choices for each, and note the changes required
Use digital tools to combine written and multimodal elements, evaluating how the combination serves the purpose

modes.reason: Writing with embedded clauses, precise vocabulary, tense control and vivid language simultaneously requires integrating the conceptual knowledge from multiple LA strand descriptors into a coherent production act — the integration is the learning challenge.

nodes.label: Editing for structure, meaning and accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can re-read and edit their own and others' work against negotiated criteria for text structure, meaning, grammar, spelling and punctuation, and explain editing choices.
criteria: Makes at least two edits to a piece of writing and identifies what criterion each addresses
Explains at least one editing choice in terms of how it improves the text's purpose, meaning or accuracy

width.minimum: Re-read own writing and make at least two edits against a stated criterion (e.g. punctuation accuracy, vocabulary precision); explain at least one editing choice.
width.typical: Re-read and edit own and others' work using negotiated criteria across text structure, meaning, accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation; explain editing choices; use knowledge of comma rules, embedded clauses and word choice to improve writing.
wider: Edit a provided piece of writing against multiple criteria and write a brief editor's note explaining each significant change and why it improves the text
Use the editing process to deliberately introduce a literary device and evaluate whether it improves the text

modes.reason: Editing accuracy — particularly comma use, embedded clause structure and spelling — requires repeated practice to become reliable. Students who understand the rules conceptually still need editing practice to apply them consistently under production pressure.

descriptors.title: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations
descriptors.description: plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that include information, arguments and details that develop a theme or idea, organising ideas using precise topic-specific and technical vocabulary, pitch, tone, pace, volume, and visual and digital features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that include relevant information, facts, arguments and details using appropriate vocabulary, pace, volume and visual features (AC9E5LY07). They have not yet specifically developed a sustained theme or idea across a presentation, deployed pitch and tone deliberately, or used technical vocabulary for persuasive effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that develop a theme or idea with information, arguments and details, using precise vocabulary, voice delivery features, and visual and digital elements.

nodes.label: Planning and organising ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a spoken or multimodal presentation that organises information, arguments and details to develop a theme or idea, selecting appropriate vocabulary and structural choices.
criteria: Produces a plan that identifies a theme or idea and organises at least three supporting points logically
Identifies at least two key vocabulary choices appropriate to the topic and audience

width.minimum: Produce a plan for a spoken or multimodal presentation that identifies the theme or idea, organises at least three supporting points logically, and notes key vocabulary choices.
width.typical: Plan a report or argument that sequences ideas logically and provides supporting detail; select precise topic-specific and technical vocabulary for key concepts; plan how graphics, sound and visuals will enhance audience engagement and understanding.
wider: Plan an argument on a curriculum content issue, identifying claims, evidence and persuasive techniques appropriate to the audience
Plan and set goals for a presentation in a written or digital journal, and monitor progress against those goals

nodes.label: Voice delivery for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliberately use pitch, tone, pace and volume in spoken delivery and explain the effect on audience understanding.
criteria: Demonstrates deliberate variation in at least two voice features during a presentation
Explains the intended effect of at least one voice choice on the audience

width.minimum: Demonstrate deliberate variation in at least two voice features (pitch, tone, pace, or volume) in a practice delivery; explain one effect on audience understanding.
width.typical: Experiment with pitch, tone, volume and pace effects in formal presentations; recognise and demonstrate how voice effects aid audience understanding; rehearse and reflect on voice delivery choices.
wider: Record and review own delivery, identifying where voice features supported or undermined the presentation's purpose
Compare delivery of the same content at different pace and volume settings and evaluate which best serves the audience and content

modes.reason: Voice delivery requires repeated rehearsal practice — students who understand voice features conceptually still need iterative practice before deliberate control is available under the pressure of live delivery.

nodes.label: Delivering a complete presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver a spoken and/or multimodal presentation that develops a theme or idea using precise vocabulary, deliberate voice features, and effective visual and digital elements.
criteria: Delivers a presentation that develops a clear theme with at least three supporting points
Demonstrates at least one deliberate voice delivery choice and uses at least one piece of precise topic vocabulary

width.minimum: Deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation that develops one theme or idea with at least three supporting points, uses at least one piece of precise topic vocabulary, and demonstrates at least one deliberate voice delivery choice.
width.typical: Deliver a structured spoken or multimodal presentation that develops a theme or idea through information, arguments and details; use precise technical vocabulary; apply deliberate voice delivery features; integrate visual and digital elements to enhance communication.
wider: Present an argument on a learning area content issue with claims supported by evidence, careful topic vocabulary and audience-appropriate persuasive techniques
Evaluate the presentation against stated goals (from the planning journal) and identify specific improvements for a future presentation

modes.reason: Delivery integrates planning (Node 1), voice control (Node 2), content knowledge, vocabulary precision, and visual integration simultaneously — the whole-presentation act is where all components must coordinate.

descriptors.title: Spelling: word origins, morphology and letter patterns
descriptors.description: use knowledge of known words, word origins including some Latin and Greek roots, base words, prefixes, suffixes, letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell new words including technical words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can build and spell new words from knowledge of known words, base words, prefixes and suffixes (AC9E5LY09). They have not yet applied specific Latin and Greek root knowledge (beyond the most common), or used etymology systematically to access the spelling and meaning of technical words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use knowledge of word origins (including Latin and Greek roots), base words, prefixes, suffixes, letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell new words including technical words.

nodes.label: Latin and Greek roots for spelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use knowledge of some Latin and Greek roots to spell and understand the meaning of words derived from those roots.
criteria: Identifies the Greek or Latin root in at least two provided words
Explains how knowing the root meaning helps with both spelling and word meaning
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without a working repertoire of root meanings cannot apply morphemic strategies to prefixes and suffixes in Node 2 — the prefix/suffix application presupposes that base word origins are recognisable.

width.minimum: Identify the root (Greek or Latin) in at least three provided words and explain how knowledge of the root helps with spelling and meaning.
width.typical: Use a dictionary to explore word origins; apply knowledge of Greek roots (e.g. 'ath' — outstanding skill, 'pent' — five, 'dec' — ten) to spell and understand words including technical vocabulary; explain how root knowledge helps decode and spell unfamiliar words.
wider: Research the meanings of five or more Greek or Latin roots and generate a family of words for each, explaining meaning connections
Investigate the meanings of words in languages of First Nations Australians using dictionaries or online resources from state libraries or universities

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of root meanings before the strategy of using etymology to spell and decode becomes productive. Building a small but well-understood set of roots is more effective than a superficial encounter with many.

nodes.label: Prefixes, suffixes and meaning relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can expand knowledge of prefixes and suffixes and explore meaning relationships between words in the same morphemic family.
criteria: Identifies at least one prefix or suffix and explains how it modifies the base word's meaning
Spells at least two words correctly using morphemic knowledge

width.minimum: Identify the prefix or suffix in at least three provided words and explain how each affix changes the word's meaning.
width.typical: Expand knowledge of prefixes and suffixes by exploring meaning relationships between words; use morphemic knowledge to spell and understand technical vocabulary (e.g. 'metaphorical', 'biology', 'biodegradable'); apply prefix and suffix knowledge to spell new words accurately.
wider: Build a morphemic word map showing a family of words sharing a root, prefix or suffix, showing meaning connections
Apply morphemic knowledge to spell technical vocabulary from curriculum-area learning (science, mathematics, history) and explain the morphemic components

nodes.label: Applying spelling generalisations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply accumulated knowledge of letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell new words, including irregular and technically complex words.
criteria: Correctly spells at least three provided words requiring application of a spelling generalisation
Names the generalisation applied in at least one case

width.minimum: Correctly spell at least three provided words that require applying a spelling generalisation (e.g. doubling rules, y-to-i changes, -ible/-able patterns); identify the generalisation applied.
width.typical: Apply accumulated knowledge of a wide range of letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell new words; use knowledge of common patterns to spell words including 'ratio', 'synthesis', 'reliability', 'handkerchief', 'receive', 'lollies', 'trolleys', 'climbing', 'designed', 'emergency'.
wider: Compare sets of words that seem to break a spelling rule and identify the underlying pattern that explains the 'exceptions'
Apply spelling generalisation knowledge to read and write technical words encountered in curriculum-area texts, explaining the generalisation used

modes.reason: Spelling accuracy requires overlearning — students who know the generalisation still need repeated encounter with its application in diverse words before accurate spelling becomes automatic. Targeted practice with words that consistently cause errors is the productive investment here.

descriptors.title: Language and identity
descriptors.description: Understand how language expresses and creates personal and social identities
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how language varies with formality and social distance (AC9E6LA01) and how objective and subjective language can reveal bias (AC9E6LA02). They have not yet examined how language actively constructs identity — the idea that identity is not just expressed but created through language choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how language expresses and creates personal and social identities.

nodes.label: Language as identity expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ways that language choices express aspects of personal or social identity
criteria: Identifies at least two language features that express aspects of identity
Explains what each feature signals about personal or social identity
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify how language choices signal identity, Node 2's conceptual shift — that language creates rather than just reflects identity — is inaccessible. The creation argument depends on students already seeing the expression relationship clearly.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of language use (vocabulary, dialect, register, idiom) that signal something about a speaker's or writer's identity; explain what each signals
width.typical: Examine a range of language examples and identify what each reveals about personal identity (individual personality, values) and social identity (group membership, cultural background, age, region)
wider: Examine local idioms and discuss their connection to community identity — what does using or not using a particular expression signal about belonging?
Compare how the same person uses language differently in different social contexts (family, friends, teachers) and discuss what this reveals about shifting identities

modes.reason: Students commonly treat language-as-identity-expression as a matter of accent or slang only. Seeing examples across vocabulary choice, register, dialect, idiom and code-switching across varied social contexts builds a broader and more nuanced understanding of the relationship.

nodes.label: Language as identity creation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand that language does not just reflect identity but actively creates and shapes it
criteria: Explains how a language choice constructs (not just describes) an aspect of identity
Distinguishes between language that expresses an existing identity and language that creates one

width.minimum: Given an example (e.g. dialogue that reveals character, a social media profile, a speech), explain how the language choices are doing more than reporting — they are constructing how the speaker or character is perceived and understood
width.typical: Compare two versions of a character or speaker represented through different language choices; discuss how the language creates a different identity in each case, not just describes it differently
wider: Examine how developing dialogue for a character in a comic, cartoon or animation requires making active language choices that construct — not just reflect — who that character is
Discuss how names, titles and honorifics create social identity and position within a relationship or community

modes.reason: The shift from 'language reflects identity' to 'language creates identity' is conceptually significant and students commonly don't make it without scaffolding. An explicit reasoning scaffold — what would this character/person be like if these language choices were different, and why does changing the language change the identity rather than just the description — is needed to make the distinction productive.

descriptors.title: Evaluative language and substantiation
descriptors.description: Recognise language used to evaluate texts including visual and multimodal texts, and how evaluations of a text can be substantiated by reference to the text and other sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how objective and subjective language can reveal bias (AC9E6LA02). They have not yet developed a systematic vocabulary for evaluative language across the three dimensions (affect, judgement, appreciation) or examined how textual reference and outside sources function as substantiation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise evaluative language and understand how evaluations of a text can be substantiated by reference to the text and other sources.

nodes.label: Vocabulary of evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify evaluative language and classify it across emotional response, judgement of behaviour, and aesthetic appreciation
criteria: Identifies evaluative language in a given text
Classifies evaluative words into at least two categories (emotional response, judgement, or aesthetic appreciation)
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify and classify evaluative vocabulary, Node 2's substantiation work loses its analytical grounding — students cannot examine how evaluations are supported without first being able to identify what counts as an evaluative claim.

width.minimum: Given a short evaluative text, identify words that express evaluation; sort them into at least two categories (e.g. emotional response vs judgement)
width.typical: Examine evaluative vocabulary across three domains — emotional responses to texts, judgement of characters and their actions, and appreciation of aesthetic qualities — and identify examples of each in a range of texts
wider: Build a word bank of evaluative vocabulary across the three domains and explore how the same event or character can be evaluated very differently depending on word choice
Compare evaluative language in a student review vs a published critic's review of the same text — what vocabulary differences signal the difference in authority and register?

modes.reason: Evaluative vocabulary is a resource students draw on — a wider repertoire directly improves their ability to recognise and produce nuanced evaluations. Building the word bank across the three domains (affect, judgement, appreciation) is the core work here, not just understanding the concept.

nodes.label: Substantiating evaluations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how evaluations are substantiated by reference to the text and to other sources
criteria: Identifies whether an evaluative claim is substantiated by textual reference, outside source, or neither
Explains how substantiation strengthens an evaluative claim

width.minimum: Given an evaluative claim about a text, identify whether it is supported by textual reference, outside source, or neither; explain why the unsupported claim is less persuasive
width.typical: Examine how evaluative language is used in a review or critical response and trace the substantiation strategy — which claims are supported by textual evidence, which by external sources, and which are bare assertions; discuss the effect of each
wider: Examine how evaluative language is used to critically assess the validity of evidence and the reliability of sources — moving from evaluating literary texts to evaluating informational texts and source quality
Compare two evaluations of the same text that reach different conclusions and identify how different substantiation strategies produce different persuasive effects

modes.reason: Students commonly produce evaluative claims without understanding that a claim requires support, or they treat any reference to the text as adequate substantiation. An explicit reasoning scaffold — what is the claim, what is the evidence, and how does the evidence support the claim — builds the connection between evaluation and substantiation that is not intuitive.

descriptors.title: Text structure varies by purpose
descriptors.description: Identify and describe how texts are structured differently depending on their purpose and how language features vary in texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how texts are organised into characteristic stages and phases depending on purpose, and how authors adapt text structures and language features (AC9E6LA03). They have not yet worked at the level of identifying and describing structural variation across a wider range of text types including reviews, persuasive texts, and analytical responses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and describe how text structure and language features vary by purpose.

nodes.label: Purpose drives structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a text's purpose determines the structural choices a writer makes
criteria: Identifies at least one structural difference between two texts with different purposes
Explains how the structure serves the purpose of each text
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot connect purpose to structure, Node 2's work on language feature variation loses its anchoring principle — explaining why language features differ requires first understanding that purpose drives all textual choices.

width.minimum: Given two texts with different purposes (e.g. a recount and a persuasive text), identify at least one structural difference and explain how each structure serves its purpose
width.typical: Compare the structural logic of three or more text types — how the stages of a review (context → summary → judgement) differ from those of a persuasive text, and why each structure serves its purpose
wider: Examine how the structure of a book or film review moves from description of context to summary to judgement — and why reversing that order would undermine the purpose
Identify the social purpose of a text type and trace how that purpose is embedded in its structural stages

modes.reason: Students commonly describe structural features without connecting them to purpose — they can list 'introduction, body, conclusion' without explaining why that sequence serves the text's goal. Seeing the purpose-structure connection across several distinct text types helps students internalise the principle rather than memorising formats.

nodes.label: Language features vary with purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe how language features vary across texts with different purposes
criteria: Identifies at least one language feature that varies between two texts with different purposes
Describes how the language feature serves the purpose of the text

width.minimum: Given two texts with different purposes, identify at least one language feature difference (e.g. use of first vs third person, evaluative vs factual vocabulary, modality) and describe how it serves the purpose
width.typical: Examine language features across a range of text types — how persuasive texts use high modality and evaluative language; how recounts use past tense and first person; how explanations use present tense, technical vocabulary and logical connectives — and explain the relationship between language choices and purpose
wider: Analyse the structure and language features of advertising posters as persuasive texts — how do visual and verbal language work together to serve the purpose?
Describe how literary texts, arguments, and analytical responses each use language features differently, and discuss why each set of choices suits its purpose

modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of language feature–purpose pairings to draw on when analysing and creating texts. Building this repertoire across multiple text types — not just one — gives students the comparative knowledge that makes the variation visible and meaningful.

descriptors.title: Cohesion devices guide readers
descriptors.description: Understand that the cohesion of texts relies on devices that signal structure and guide readers, such as overviews and initial and concluding paragraphs
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how cohesion can be created through intentional repetition and word associations (AC9E6LA04). They have not yet worked at the level of structural cohesion devices — how overviews, topic sentences, and concluding paragraphs function to guide readers through a text's logic.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how cohesion devices including overviews and paragraph structure guide readers.

nodes.label: Cohesion at the paragraph level
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how topic sentences and paragraph structure guide readers through a text
criteria: Identifies the topic sentence in a given paragraph
Explains how the topic sentence signals the paragraph's direction and connects to the text
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot reliably identify topic sentences at the paragraph level, Node 2's whole-text structural logic is inaccessible — recognising how overviews and conclusions function requires first being able to track cohesion at the paragraph level.

width.minimum: In a given text, identify the topic sentence of at least two paragraphs; explain how each signals what the paragraph is about and connects to the text's overall direction
width.typical: Examine how topic sentences, sentence openers and text connectives work together to create cohesion across paragraphs — how a reader can follow the text's logic by reading the opening of each paragraph
wider: Identify how authors foreshadow how a text will unfold through sentence openers and text connectives — trace the signposting across a whole text
Compare two versions of the same text — one with strong topic sentences, one without — and discuss the difference in readability

modes.reason: Topic sentence identification is a precision skill students use repeatedly across their schooling. Students commonly identify any first sentence as a topic sentence, or miss topic sentences that don't appear first. Practice with varied paragraph structures builds reliable recognition.

nodes.label: Structural cohesion devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how overviews, initial paragraphs and concluding paragraphs function as cohesion devices that guide readers through the whole text
criteria: Identifies the overview/introduction and conclusion in a given text
Explains how each structural device guides the reader

width.minimum: Identify the overview or introductory paragraph and the concluding paragraph in a given text; explain what job each does in guiding the reader
width.typical: Examine how the introduction (overview of what's coming), body paragraphs (developed with topic sentences), and conclusion (synthesis or restatement) work as a cohesive system — and how each part signals its function to the reader
wider: Compare and analyse the structure of media texts such as digital news sites or print media — how do structural devices create cohesion in texts that may not have traditional paragraph structure?
Examine how the absence or disruption of cohesion devices affects readability — what happens when a text omits an overview or has no concluding paragraph?

modes.reason: Students commonly understand paragraph-level cohesion but don't extend it to whole-text structural logic. Seeing how overviews and conclusions function across different text types — including non-traditional structures like digital news — helps students understand cohesion as a principle rather than a formula.

descriptors.title: Complex and compound-complex sentences
descriptors.description: Understand how complex and compound-complex sentences can be used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how embedded clauses can expand complex sentences to elaborate and explain ideas (AC9E6LA05). They have not yet worked with compound-complex sentences — the combination of coordination and subordination in a single sentence — or examined how sentence structure choices serve rhetorical purposes (elaborating, extending, explaining).
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how complex and compound-complex sentences can be used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas.

nodes.label: Clause types and relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify independent and dependent clauses and explain the relationship between them in a complex sentence
criteria: Correctly identifies the independent and dependent clause in a given complex sentence
Explains what the dependent clause contributes to the meaning of the sentence
nodes.hinge_reason: Clause identification errors here propagate directly into Nodes 2 and 3 — students who cannot reliably distinguish independent from dependent clauses cannot identify compound-complex structure or explain elaboration/extension/explanation relationships.

width.minimum: Label the independent and dependent clauses in a given complex sentence; explain what the dependent clause adds to the independent clause
width.typical: Identify clause relationships across several complex sentences; explain how the dependent clause elaborates, extends or qualifies the main idea in each case
wider: Examine how the position of the dependent clause (before or after the independent clause) changes emphasis — 'Although it was raining, we went ahead' vs 'We went ahead, although it was raining'
Identify clause relationships in sentences from a range of text types (narrative, explanation, argument) and discuss how subordination serves different purposes in each

modes.reason: Clause identification is a precision skill with a high error rate — students commonly mislabel the dependent clause as the main idea, or treat any long clause as 'complex'. Fluency here is the prerequisite for everything that follows; practice with varied sentence structures (not just textbook examples) builds the reliable recognition the later nodes depend on.

nodes.label: Compound-complex sentence structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and construct compound-complex sentences, distinguishing them from complex sentences
criteria: Identifies the independent and dependent clauses in a compound-complex sentence
Distinguishes a compound-complex sentence from a complex sentence and explains the structural difference

width.minimum: Given a compound-complex sentence, identify its independent clauses and at least one dependent clause; explain how it differs from a complex sentence
width.typical: Construct compound-complex sentences by combining coordination and subordination; discuss how adding a second independent clause changes what the sentence can express compared to a complex sentence alone
wider: Compare a complex and compound-complex version of the same idea — 'When dinosaurs roamed the earth, vegetation depleted' vs 'When dinosaurs roamed the earth, weather patterns shifted significantly and as a result vegetation depleted' — and explain what the compound-complex version adds
Identify compound-complex sentences in published texts and discuss why the author chose that structure over a simpler alternative

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse compound-complex sentences with long or complicated sentences generally. The distinction between coordination and subordination — and what happens when both operate in the same sentence — only becomes clear when students see the structure across enough varied examples to isolate the pattern. A single textbook example produces surface recognition; breadth across sentence types and contexts builds the structural understanding.

nodes.label: Elaborating, extending and explaining
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how complex and compound-complex sentence structures are used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas
criteria: Identifies whether a given complex or compound-complex sentence elaborates, extends or explains the main idea
Explains how the clause structure signals the purpose

width.minimum: For a given sentence, identify whether the structure elaborates, extends or explains the main idea; give a reason
width.typical: Examine several sentences and match each to the purpose it serves (elaborating — adding detail; extending — adding a related idea; explaining — giving a reason or condition); discuss how the clause relationship signals the purpose
wider: Examine how the same base clause can be developed in different directions depending on the subordinating conjunction chosen — 'because', 'although', 'when', 'so that' each signal a different relationship and serve a different purpose
Compare how elaboration, extension and explanation are distributed differently across text types — argument texts tend toward explanation structures; narratives tend toward elaboration and extension

modes.reason: Students can correctly label clause types without being able to explain what purpose the structure serves. The elaboration/extension/explanation distinction requires students to reason about the semantic relationship between clauses, not just the grammatical label. An explicit reasoning scaffold — what does the dependent clause add, and what word signals that relationship — is what makes the distinction productive rather than a new set of labels to memorise.

The three purposes (elaborate, extend, explain) are not always cleanly distinct — a clause can extend and explain simultaneously. Seeing the structure across a range of text types and sentence examples helps students develop a flexible understanding of how clause relationships serve purpose, rather than treating the three categories as fixed boxes.

nodes.label: Sentence structure as a deliberate choice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how writers choose between simple, complex and compound-complex sentences to serve different expressive purposes
criteria: Identifies where a writer has used a complex or compound-complex sentence and gives a reason for the choice
Explains why varying sentence structure serves the text's purpose better than using one sentence type throughout

width.minimum: Given a short passage, identify where the writer has used a complex or compound-complex sentence and explain why a simpler sentence would have been less effective at that point
width.typical: Examine how a writer varies sentence structure across a passage — when they choose simple sentences for impact and when they choose complex or compound-complex sentences to carry more meaning; discuss the cumulative effect
wider: Explore the ACARA elaboration insight that a simple sentence can express sophisticated ideas and a complex sentence need not express 'complex' ideas — find examples in published texts that challenge the assumption that longer = more sophisticated
Examine how writers use sentence structure variation for rhythm and reader engagement, not just logical development of ideas

modes.reason: The misconception that sentence sophistication equals sentence length is persistent and cuts across the whole descriptor. Students need to see enough counterexamples — powerful simple sentences alongside unwieldy complex ones — across varied text types before this understanding sticks. A single example is not enough to dislodge the length-equals-sophistication assumption.

descriptors.title: Tense consistency
descriptors.description: Understand how consistency of tense through verbs and verb groups achieves clarity in sentences
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how verb choice, elaborated tenses and adverb groups sharpen and expand ideas (AC9E6LA06). They have not yet focused on tense consistency as a clarity mechanism — how maintaining tense across compound, complex and compound-complex sentences prevents reader confusion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how consistent tense through verbs and verb groups achieves clarity.

nodes.label: Verb tense forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify verb tense forms and explain what each communicates about time
criteria: Correctly identifies the tense of verbs in given sentences
Names at least three distinct tense forms
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot reliably identify tense forms, Node 2's consistency work is impossible — identifying inconsistency requires first being able to name the tense of each verb encountered.

width.minimum: Identify the tense of verbs in given sentences; distinguish at least three tense forms (simple past, simple present, present continuous)
width.typical: Identify and name a range of verb tense forms across compound, complex and compound-complex sentences; explain what each communicates about the timing of events
wider: Examine how different tense forms interact in compound-complex sentences — e.g. 'I organise the cake stall every week, and I am running the meeting this weekend' — and explain why both tenses are correct
Compare how tense choices differ across text types — present tense in explanations vs past tense in recounts

modes.reason: Tense identification is a precision skill with consistent error patterns — students confuse present continuous with simple present, and struggle with perfect tenses. Consolidation across varied sentence structures builds the reliable identification that tense-consistency work requires.

nodes.label: Consistency of tense for clarity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how maintaining tense consistency across a sentence or passage achieves clarity, and identify where inconsistency creates confusion
criteria: Identifies a tense inconsistency in a given sentence or passage
Explains why the inconsistency creates confusion for the reader

width.minimum: Given a sentence or short passage with a tense inconsistency, identify the error and explain why it creates confusion for the reader
width.typical: Examine how tense is maintained across compound, complex and compound-complex sentences; identify intentional tense shifts (e.g. flashback, quoted speech) and distinguish them from errors
wider: Examine how tense consistency operates differently in different text types — narrative (past tense maintained), explanation (present tense maintained), and mixed texts where intentional tense shifts occur
Discuss cases where tense inconsistency is deliberate — stream of consciousness, historical present — and explain how context signals intentionality

modes.reason: Tense inconsistency in student writing is a high-frequency error that responds to practice rather than broader contexts. Students understand the concept but lose tense tracking in longer sentences and passages. Sustained practice identifying and correcting inconsistency across varied sentence structures is the remedy.

descriptors.title: Visual perspective techniques
descriptors.description: Analyse how techniques such as vectors, angle and/or social distance in visual texts can be used to create a perspective
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and explain how visual elements including images, tables and graphs contribute to meaning (AC9E6LA07). They have not yet worked with the specific technical vocabulary of visual grammar — vectors, angle, social distance — or analysed how these techniques deliberately construct a viewer's perspective.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how vectors, angle and social distance in visual texts create perspective.

nodes.label: Visual grammar: vectors, angle, social distance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify vectors, angle and social distance in visual texts and explain what each communicates
criteria: Correctly identifies at least one visual technique (vector, angle, or social distance) in a given image
Explains what the technique communicates about the viewer-subject relationship
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify and name the individual techniques, Node 2's combined-techniques analysis is inaccessible — explaining how techniques work together to create perspective requires first being able to identify each technique reliably.

width.minimum: In a given visual text, identify at least one of: a vector (line of gaze or gesture directing attention), an angle (high/low/eye-level), or social distance (close/medium/long shot); explain what it communicates
width.typical: Identify all three techniques in a visual text and explain how each positions the viewer in relation to the subject
wider: Examine how illustrations in picture books, graphic novels and advertisements use size, colour, angle, proximity, vector and salience to influence the reader — building a complete visual grammar vocabulary
Compare how the same subject photographed at different angles (high, low, eye-level) creates a different relationship between viewer and subject

modes.reason: Visual grammar is a technical vocabulary students need to accumulate before they can analyse perspective. Building the repertoire — vector, angle, social distance, salience, proximity — across multiple visual examples gives students the language tools the analysis requires.

nodes.label: Techniques construct perspective
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how visual techniques work together to create a perspective in a visual text
criteria: Identifies at least two visual techniques in a given image
Explains how the techniques work together to create a perspective

width.minimum: In a given visual text, identify at least two techniques being used and explain how they work together to position the viewer and create a perspective
width.typical: Analyse how multiple visual techniques combine to construct a specific perspective — e.g. a low angle + close social distance + direct gaze together create intimacy and power; compare two images of the same subject that use different technique combinations to create different perspectives
wider: Compare how perspectives are created in animations and advertisements — examine how technique choices differ between a children's animation (where perspective creates safety and warmth) and an advertisement (where perspective creates aspiration or urgency)
Analyse how different advertisements for the same product use different technique combinations to target different audiences

modes.reason: Students commonly analyse techniques in isolation — noting that an angle is low without explaining what perspective that creates in combination with other techniques. Seeing how technique combinations produce perspective across varied visual text types (advertisements, animations, graphic novels) builds the integrative understanding the descriptor's 'analyse' command requires.

descriptors.title: Specialist and technical vocabulary
descriptors.description: Investigate the role of vocabulary in building specialist and technical knowledge, including terms that have both everyday and technical meanings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how authors use figurative and emotive vocabulary (AC9E6LA08). They have not yet investigated how specialist and technical vocabulary functions to build disciplinary knowledge, or examined the particular challenge of terms that carry both everyday and technical meanings.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how vocabulary builds specialist knowledge, including terms with everyday and technical meanings.

nodes.label: Specialist and technical vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specialist and technical vocabulary in a text and explain what role it plays in building knowledge in that field
criteria: Identifies specialist or technical vocabulary in a given text
Explains why precise vocabulary is needed in that field

width.minimum: In a given specialist or technical text, identify at least three technical terms and explain why precise vocabulary is needed in this field
width.typical: Identify technical vocabulary across two different subject areas and discuss how specialist vocabulary enables precision and shared understanding within a discipline — what would be lost if everyday language were used instead?
wider: Investigate high utility academic vocabulary — words like 'factor', 'hypothesise', 'issue' and 'critique' — that appear across multiple disciplines and carry specific meanings in each
Examine vocabulary used to discuss a specific topic (e.g. poetic devices) and explore how the technical terms enable more precise discussion than everyday language would allow

modes.reason: Students commonly treat technical vocabulary as jargon to memorise rather than as a knowledge-building tool. Seeing specialist vocabulary functioning across different disciplines — and understanding that precision enables shared understanding — shifts the conception from rote learning to purposeful investigation.

nodes.label: Terms with everyday and technical meanings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify terms that carry both everyday and technical meanings and explain how context determines which meaning applies
criteria: Identifies at least one term with both everyday and technical meanings
Explains both meanings and gives an example of each in context

width.minimum: Given a term with both everyday and technical meanings (e.g. 'power', 'force', 'argument'), explain the everyday meaning and at least one technical meaning; give a sentence example of each
width.typical: Investigate several terms with dual everyday/technical meanings across different disciplines; explain how context signals which meaning applies and discuss what confusion can arise when the distinction is not made
wider: Examine how the same term ('critique', 'analyse', 'evaluate') carries different technical meanings in English compared to other subjects, and discuss how students learn to shift between them
Investigate how misunderstanding a technical term as its everyday counterpart leads to disciplinary misunderstanding — trace a specific example of this in a student-facing text

modes.reason: The everyday/technical distinction is a persistent source of confusion across subjects — students apply everyday meanings to technical terms across all their learning. Seeing this pattern across multiple disciplines (not just English) helps students develop a generalised awareness of the distinction rather than just learning specific word definitions.

descriptors.title: Colons and brackets
descriptors.description: Understand the use of punctuation including colons and brackets to support meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how commas are used in lists, to separate clauses and in dialogue (AC9E6LA09). They have not yet worked with colons or brackets — punctuation marks that introduce, expand or parenthesise information rather than separating clauses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how colons and brackets support meaning.

nodes.label: Colon uses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the uses of colons and explain what each use signals to the reader
criteria: Identifies a colon in a given sentence
Explains what the colon signals in that specific context

width.minimum: Identify a colon in a given sentence and explain what it signals — introduction of a list, elaboration of a preceding clause, or introduction of a quotation or example
width.typical: Examine colons in several sentences across different uses and explain how each signals a specific relationship between what comes before and after the colon
wider: Examine the impact of information added to sentences when colons are used — compare a sentence with and without the colon-introduced elaboration and discuss how meaning changes
Experiment with writing sentences where a colon introduces a list, an elaboration, and a quotation — discuss how the reader's expectation changes depending on what follows the colon

modes.reason: Colon usage is a precision skill with a small set of rules that students apply inconsistently — particularly confusing colon-before-list with comma-before-list. Practice across the distinct uses builds reliable application.

nodes.label: Bracket uses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how brackets are used to add parenthetical information and explain what effect this has on meaning
criteria: Identifies bracketed information in a given sentence
Explains why the information is parenthetical and what it adds to meaning

width.minimum: Identify brackets in a given sentence and explain what the bracketed information adds — clarification, aside, example, or attribution; explain why the information is parenthetical rather than integrated into the main clause
width.typical: Compare sentences that use brackets with versions where the parenthetical content is removed or integrated into the main clause; discuss how the choice to bracket information affects the reader's experience of it
wider: Examine how the impact of bracketed information differs from information added through commas or dashes — when does a writer choose brackets over other parenthetical punctuation?
Investigate how brackets are used in academic and informational writing vs creative writing — do the purposes differ?

modes.reason: Students commonly add brackets without understanding why information is parenthetical — they treat brackets as interchangeable with commas. The reasoning scaffold — why is this information outside the main clause rather than inside it, and what effect does that have on how the reader processes it — is what makes bracket use purposeful rather than mechanical.

descriptors.title: Ideas and context in literature
descriptors.description: Identify and explore ideas, points of view, characters, events and/or issues in literary texts, drawn from historical, social and/or cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify responses to characters and events in literary texts drawn from historical, social or cultural contexts (AC9E6LE01). They have not yet moved from identifying responses to exploring ideas, points of view and issues — the shift from response to analysis of the ideas themselves.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and explore ideas, viewpoints and issues in literary texts across historical, social and cultural contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying ideas and issues in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the ideas, issues or points of view present in a literary text and connect them to the text's historical, social or cultural context
criteria: Identifies at least one significant idea, issue or point of view in a literary text
Connects the idea to the historical, social or cultural context of the text
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot connect ideas to context, Node 2's comparative work collapses — comparison across contexts requires first being able to situate ideas within a single context.

width.minimum: In a given literary text, identify at least one significant idea, issue or point of view; explain how it connects to the context in which the text was created
width.typical: Identify multiple ideas, issues and points of view in a literary text and examine how each is shaped by the historical, social or cultural context — what does the text reveal about the world it came from?
wider: Explore ideas about heroism in literary texts by wide-ranging world authors — how does context shape what counts as heroic?
Explore depictions of the city or the bush in Australian poems and short stories from different eras — how has the representation of these settings changed across historical contexts?

modes.reason: Students commonly read literary texts as universal without recognising how context shapes what ideas are foregrounded, what counts as a problem, and whose perspective is centred. Reading across genuinely different historical, social and cultural contexts — including First Nations Australian texts and wide-ranging world authors — is what builds the understanding that all texts are contextually situated.

nodes.label: Exploring across texts and contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how the same idea or issue is represented differently across literary texts from different contexts
criteria: Compares how the same idea or issue is represented in two texts from different contexts
Explains at least one difference in terms of the texts' different contexts

width.minimum: Compare how the same idea or issue (e.g. heroism, belonging, justice) is represented in two texts from different contexts; identify at least one difference and explain it in terms of context
width.typical: Explore how ideas, points of view and issues are represented across multiple texts from different historical, social or cultural contexts — discussing what the differences reveal about how context shapes literary representation
wider: Discuss similarities and differences in character representations in film adaptations of novels and plays — how does the shift in context and medium affect the representation?

Explore representations of characters and events in literary texts by First Nations Australians alongside mainstream Australian texts on similar themes — what does comparison reveal about different perspectives?

modes.reason: Exploring ideas across contexts is not just reading more texts — it is building comparative awareness of how context shapes representation. Each genuinely different context (First Nations, historical, world literature) reveals something that a single context cannot. The breadth is the analytical tool.

descriptors.title: Form and justify opinions
descriptors.description: Form an opinion about characters, settings and events in texts, identifying areas of agreement and difference with others' opinions and justifying a response
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify similarities and differences in literary texts on similar topics, themes or plots (AC9E6LE02). They have not yet formed personal opinions about characters, settings and events and justified them — or explicitly engaged with the tension between their own and others' interpretations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students form and justify opinions about texts, identifying agreement and difference with others.

nodes.label: Forming and justifying a personal response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form an opinion about characters, settings or events in a text and justify it by reference to the text
criteria: States a personal opinion about a character, setting or event
Justifies the opinion with at least one reference to the text
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot justify an opinion with textual reference, Node 2's dialogic work has no foundation — engaging with others' opinions requires first being able to anchor one's own position in the text.

width.minimum: Form an opinion about a character, setting or event in a given text; justify it with at least one reference to what the text shows or says
width.typical: Form opinions about multiple aspects of a text (character, setting, events) and justify each with textual evidence; explain what in the text led to each opinion
wider: Compare personal opinions on texts and justify responses with reference to specific textual evidence — including reasoning about character behaviours such as integrity and loyalty
Establish criteria for discussing the relative merits of characters, settings and events before forming opinions — discuss how having criteria makes justification more rigorous

modes.reason: Students form opinions readily but rarely justify them with textual evidence — they describe their feeling (I liked/disliked the character) without connecting it to what the text actually shows. The reasoning scaffold — opinion → textual evidence → connection between evidence and opinion — is the core move this node develops.

nodes.label: Engaging with others' opinions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify areas of agreement and difference between their own and others' opinions about a text and respond to those differences
criteria: Identifies at least one point of agreement or difference with another's opinion
Justifies their own position in response to the difference, with reference to the text

width.minimum: Given another person's opinion about a character, setting or event, identify whether you agree or disagree and explain why — reference both your own response and what the text says
width.typical: Participate in a discussion of a literary text where multiple opinions are present; identify specific points of agreement and difference, justify your own position, and respond to at least one point of difference by engaging with the other person's reasoning
wider: Establish forums for discussing the relative merits of characters, settings and events — practise structured literary discussion where opinions are presented, challenged and refined

Compare opinions on a text where characters exhibit complex behaviours (integrity, loyalty, moral ambiguity) — discuss how different readers can reach different justified conclusions from the same text

modes.reason: Engaging with interpretive difference requires genuine interpretive diversity — students need to encounter opinions that differ from their own in non-trivial ways to develop the habit of identifying and responding to difference rather than dismissing it. A range of text types and discussion contexts provides the varied perspectives that make this learning possible.

descriptors.title: Literary devices create character
descriptors.description: Explain the ways that literary devices and language features such as dialogue, and images are used to create character, and to influence emotions and opinions in different types of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and explain characteristics that define an author's individual style (AC9E6LE03). They have not yet examined how specific literary devices and language features — dialogue, imagery, description — work to construct character and influence the reader's emotional and evaluative response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how literary devices and language features create character and influence emotions and opinions.

nodes.label: How literary devices construct character
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify literary devices and language features used to create character and explain how each constructs the reader's understanding of that character
criteria: Identifies at least one literary device or language feature used to create a character
Explains what the device reveals about the character
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot explain how a device constructs character, Node 2's work on influencing emotions and opinions is inaccessible — both require the same explanatory move (device → effect on reader), and without it at the character level, students cannot extend it to emotional influence.

width.minimum: In a given text, identify at least one literary device or language feature (e.g. dialogue, description, imagery) used to create a character; explain what it reveals about the character
width.typical: Examine how multiple devices and features work together to construct a character — dialogue that reveals personality, description that establishes appearance and setting, imagery that signals values or inner life — and explain how each contributes
