criteria: Produces sentences with correctly formed embedded clauses that add information to a noun phrase.
Explains how embedded clauses contribute to concision or information density in a given text.

width.minimum: Write two sentences using embedded clauses to add information about a noun phrase, and explain how embedding is more concise than using a separate sentence for the same information.
width.typical: Examine how embedded clauses allow writers to pack information into sentences concisely across a range of text types; write extended sentences using embedded clauses and evaluate their effect on the text's tone and density.
wider: Rewrite a passage from an academic text by removing all embedded clauses, substituting separate sentences, and analyse the effect on register and density
Investigate how nominalisation (AC9E8LA06) and embedded clauses work together to create high-density formal prose in informative texts
Create a short formal piece that deliberately exploits embedding to create an authoritative, dense register appropriate for an academic audience

modes.reason: Students need to connect their understanding of embedded clause structure to an understanding of writerly choice — when embedding serves the text and when it overloads a sentence. This integration of structure knowledge into purposeful writing is the descriptor's endpoint.

descriptors.title: Nominalisation
descriptors.description: understand the effect of nominalisation in texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand how word choice constructs meaning and how different grammatical categories function (AC9E7LA05, AC9E7LA08). They have not yet examined nominalisation — the process of converting verbs and other word classes into nouns — and its effect on tone, abstraction and register.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how nominalisation works and what effects it creates in texts, including changes to tone, abstraction and formality.

nodes.label: What nominalisation is
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify nominalisations in texts and explain the grammatical transformation involved (verb or adjective converted to noun).
criteria: Identifies a nominalised noun in a text and names the verb or adjective it was derived from.
Explains what grammatical role the nominalised form plays in the sentence (subject, object, etc.).

width.minimum: Identify at least two nominalisations in a provided informative text and name the original verb or adjective form each has been derived from.
width.typical: Identify nominalisations across a range of informative texts, explaining the grammatical process and comparing the nominalised form with its verbal equivalent in terms of grammatical role in the sentence.
wider: Investigate how nominalisation density varies across text types — compare a newspaper report, an academic article and an informal blog on the same topic
Identify nominalisations in a First Nations or multicultural community text and consider how nominalisation conventions may differ across language backgrounds
Examine how government or bureaucratic documents use nominalisation to create abstract, impersonal official language

modes.reason: Identifying nominalisations requires students to work backwards from noun form to verbal origin — a grammatical analysis move that is not obvious. Without explicit attention to the transformation (verb → noun), students may simply note 'formal words' without understanding the grammatical mechanism, which limits the tone analysis at Node 2.

nodes.label: Effect of nominalisation on tone and register
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how nominalisation affects the tone and register of a text — creating abstraction, formality and impersonality — and can discuss the impact of nominalisation on content and potential audiences.
criteria: Explains how nominalisation makes a text more formal or abstract, using a specific example from a provided text.
Discusses how nominalisation affects the relationship between writer and audience in at least one text.

width.minimum: Nominalise the verbs in two or three sentences and explain how the change in tone (more formal/abstract) could affect how the text is perceived by a reader.
width.typical: Examine how nominalisation in a range of informative texts creates a formal, abstract or impersonal tone; explain how this affects the content and the relationship constructed with the audience; discuss where nominalisation is appropriate vs where it may obscure meaning.
wider: Rewrite a formal passage using verbal rather than nominalised forms and analyse how this changes the perceived formality, agency and accessibility of the text

Investigate how critical reading of nominalisation can reveal hidden agency — nominalisation often removes the actor from a sentence, which can have ideological effects in political or institutional writing
Create two versions of the same informational content for different audiences (academic vs general public) and use nominalisation as a deliberate register-shifting tool

modes.reason: The effects of nominalisation are best understood through contrast across registers. Students who only see nominalisation in academic texts may not grasp its ideological dimension (hidden agency) or the deliberate formality it signals. Multiple text contexts surface the range of effects.

descriptors.title: Intertextual references in visual texts
descriptors.description: investigate how visual texts use intertextual references to enhance and layer meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand how images and visual elements create meaning and position viewers (AC9E7LA07). They have not yet examined how visual texts deliberately reference other texts — in the form of intertextuality — to create additional layers of meaning that depend on a viewer's prior cultural knowledge.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can investigate how visual texts use intertextual references to enhance and layer meaning, including how words and images interact in the creation of intertextual meaning.

nodes.label: What intertextuality is in visual texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an intertextual reference in a visual text and explain that its meaning depends on a viewer's knowledge of the original source text.
criteria: Identifies a specific intertextual reference in a visual text and names the source it draws on.
Explains how a viewer's recognition of the source text affects the meaning they make from the visual text.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to explain how intertextual references layer meaning — a task that depends on understanding that meaning is audience-dependent (requires prior knowledge of the source). Students who arrive at Node 2 still treating textual meaning as intrinsic to the image will produce surface-level description rather than intertextual analysis.

width.minimum: Identify one intertextual reference in a provided visual text (e.g. an advertisement or image) and explain what source text or cultural knowledge it draws on.
width.typical: Identify and explain intertextual references in advertisements, images or other visual texts; explain how these references depend on viewer knowledge and what effect is created for viewers who recognise vs do not recognise the reference.
wider: Compare two visual texts that reference the same source text (e.g. two advertisements referencing the same cultural icon) and analyse how the same reference can be used to different effects
Investigate how visual parody relies on intertextual recognition — how the comedy or critique only works if the viewer knows the source
Examine how visual texts from different cultural contexts use intertextual references to cultural materials that may not translate across audiences

modes.reason: The concept that intertextual meaning is audience-dependent (not intrinsic to the image) can be abstract. Seeing examples where some students get the reference and others don't — or comparing references that span cultural contexts — makes this contingency concrete.

nodes.label: How intertextual references layer meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how intertextual references in visual texts enhance and layer meaning — particularly how the interrelationship of words and images in advertisements creates layered meaning through cultural allusion.
criteria: Explains how the intertextual reference in a visual text adds layers of meaning beyond the literal content.
Analyses the interrelationship of words and images in a visual text to show how they work together to create the intertextual effect.

width.minimum: Investigate how one advertisement uses a combination of words and images to create a layered intertextual meaning — identifying what the reference adds that a literal reading of the text would not contain.
width.typical: Investigate how visual texts including advertisements use intertextual references — through images, words or their interrelationship — to enhance meaning by activating cultural associations that go beyond what is literally depicted or written.
wider: Analyse how a series of advertisements from one brand use a consistent intertextual strategy to build cumulative cultural associations over time
Investigate how intertextual references in visual art (e.g. contemporary painting or photography referencing historical artworks) create dialogue between past and present
Create a visual text that deliberately uses an intertextual reference to layer meaning, then explain the choices made and the effect intended

modes.reason: The breadth of intertextual strategies across visual media — advertising, art, meme culture, film — helps students see that intertextuality is a pervasive feature of contemporary visual communication, not confined to one text type.

descriptors.title: Academic vocabulary
descriptors.description: identify and use vocabulary typical of academic texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify specialist and technical vocabulary and understand how vocabulary choices shape meaning and register (AC9E7LA08). They have not yet focused specifically on the cross-disciplinary vocabulary of academic writing — words that are not subject-specific but are characteristic of formal academic register across disciplines.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify vocabulary typical of academic texts and use it in their own writing, understanding how academic vocabulary creates precise information and conveys abstract ideas.

nodes.label: Identifying academic vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify vocabulary typical of academic texts — words used across disciplines to discuss evidence, reasoning and abstraction — and distinguish this from subject-specific technical vocabulary.
criteria: Identifies specific academic vocabulary words in a text and explains that they are typical of formal academic register.
Distinguishes academic vocabulary (cross-disciplinary) from technical vocabulary (subject-specific) with at least one example of each.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires accurate use of academic vocabulary in own writing. Students who have not grasped that academic vocabulary is cross-disciplinary will substitute subject-specific technical terms or informal equivalents — producing writing that fails to meet the academic register the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Identify at least four academic vocabulary words in a provided academic text (e.g. 'evidence', 'consequence', 'contradiction', 'acknowledge') and explain that they are cross-disciplinary rather than subject-specific.
width.typical: Identify academic vocabulary across a range of academic texts on different topics; compare and contrast vocabulary choices in academic texts, considering how they create precise information or convey abstract ideas; distinguish academic vocabulary from technical vocabulary.
wider: Investigate how academic vocabulary differs across disciplines — comparing the language of a science report, a history essay and a literary analysis to identify shared academic vocabulary vs discipline-specific register
Examine how academic vocabulary items (e.g. 'evidence', 'analysis', 'significance') carry implicit disciplinary assumptions about what counts as valid knowledge
Compare the academic vocabulary in a text written for an expert audience with a version of the same content written for a general audience, and analyse what changes

modes.reason: Academic vocabulary is best understood as cross-disciplinary — it appears in science, history and English writing alike. Students who only encounter it in English contexts may not recognise its transferable nature. Multiple disciplinary contexts build this generalised understanding.

nodes.label: Using academic vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use vocabulary typical of academic texts in their own writing to create precise information and convey abstract ideas.
criteria: Uses at least three academic vocabulary items accurately in a piece of own writing.
Word choices are appropriate to the academic register of the task — neither informal substitutes nor technical jargon used inappropriately.

width.minimum: Write one paragraph on an academic topic that uses at least three academic vocabulary items accurately and appropriately.
width.typical: Select and use academic vocabulary appropriately in own writing across different topics, demonstrating understanding that academic vocabulary choices create a formal, precise register and convey abstract ideas accurately.
wider: Revise a piece of informal writing to use academic vocabulary appropriately, and analyse what changes in tone, precision and register as a result
Investigate how using academic vocabulary accurately signals membership in a discourse community — how vocabulary choices mark a writer as credible within academic contexts
Explore how students from language backgrounds other than English may have different relationships to academic vocabulary, and consider what strategies support vocabulary acquisition

modes.reason: Accurate use of academic vocabulary in writing requires repeated practice in authentic writing contexts. Students can identify academic vocabulary before they can deploy it fluently. Consolidation through multiple writing tasks — with feedback on precision of usage — builds the fluency needed.

descriptors.title: Semicolons and dashes
descriptors.description: understand and use punctuation conventions including semicolons and dashes to extend ideas and support meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can understand and use a range of punctuation conventions including colons and brackets (AC9E7LA09). They have not yet examined semicolons and dashes specifically — marks used to extend ideas within sentences and to create effects such as interruption, aside and pause in both formal and creative writing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand and use semicolons and dashes to extend ideas and support meaning in their own writing.

nodes.label: Semicolons and dashes — function and effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify semicolons and dashes in texts and explain the function each performs (linking closely related independent clauses; marking interruption, aside or pause).
criteria: Identifies a semicolon in a text and explains that it links two closely related independent clauses.
Identifies a dash in a text and explains the specific effect it creates (interruption, aside, pause or emphasis).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires purposeful use of semicolons and dashes in own writing. Students who cannot distinguish the function of each mark — or who conflate them — will deploy them randomly rather than purposefully at Node 2, producing errors that undermine the intended effect.

width.minimum: Identify one example of a semicolon and one example of a dash in provided texts and explain what function each performs in that sentence.
width.typical: Understand and explain the conventions for using semicolons (to link related independent clauses without a conjunction) and dashes (to create interruptions, asides, pauses or emphasis) across a range of text types including formal prose and drama.
wider: Compare how semicolons are used differently in formal academic prose vs how dashes are used in informal or creative writing — and discuss why each punctuation mark is suited to its typical register
Investigate how creative writers deliberately use dashes in dialogue to create interruptions, hesitations and asides that reveal character or dramatic tension
Examine how the same content can be punctuated differently using semicolons, colons, brackets or dashes, and how each choice creates a different effect

modes.reason: Students often learn punctuation rules in isolation. Seeing semicolons and dashes in varied contexts — formal prose, drama, informal writing — helps students understand that punctuation choice is rhetorical (creates effect) not merely grammatical (follows rules).

nodes.label: Using semicolons and dashes in own writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use semicolons and dashes accurately and purposefully in their own writing to extend ideas and create intended effects.
criteria: Uses a semicolon correctly to link two related independent clauses in own writing.
Uses a dash to create an intended effect (interruption, aside, pause or emphasis) in own writing.

width.minimum: Write two sentences — one using a semicolon correctly and one using a dash correctly — and explain the effect each creates.
width.typical: Use semicolons and dashes purposefully in a piece of own writing (e.g. creative dialogue or a formal analytical paragraph), demonstrating awareness of the register and effect each mark creates.
wider: Create a piece of dramatic dialogue that uses dashes deliberately to show interruptions, asides and pauses, and annotate the effect of each dash choice
Revise a formal analytical paragraph by introducing a semicolon to improve sentence variety and flow, and explain the revision

Limited width — these punctuation marks do not vary meaningfully across further contexts at this year band. Extension goes deeper: examining how cumulative punctuation choices across a text create a consistent authorial voice.

modes.reason: Accurate punctuation use requires repeated practice across varied writing contexts. Understanding the rule and correctly applying it under pressure are different skills. Multiple writing tasks that require deliberate punctuation choices build reliable usage.

descriptors.title: Ideas, values and contexts in literary texts
descriptors.description: explain the ways that ideas and points of view may represent the values of individuals and groups in literary texts, drawn from historical, social and cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how ideas and points of view in literary texts reflect social and cultural contexts, including First Nations Australian perspectives (AC9E7LE01). They have not yet explained how values are embedded in these representations or systematically connected contextual knowledge to meaning-making in texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how ideas and points of view in literary texts represent the values of individuals and groups in relation to their historical, social and cultural contexts, including texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Values embedded in representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ideas or points of view in a literary text and explain what values they reflect — including whose values and what context those values belong to.
criteria: Identifies a specific idea or point of view in a text and names the values it reflects.
Connects those values to a specific historical, social or cultural context with reference to the text.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to explain how First Nations and diverse authors represent distinct values shaped by their cultural contexts — a move that depends on the conceptual scaffold built at Node 1 (linking textual evidence to contextual claim). Students who have not built this reasoning structure produce vague contextual claims at Node 2 rather than grounded textual explanation.

width.minimum: Identify one idea or point of view in a literary text and explain what values it reflects about the individual or group it represents, connecting those values to a specific historical, social or cultural context.
width.typical: Explain how ideas and points of view in a literary text represent the values of particular individuals or groups in their historical, social or cultural context; draw on contextual knowledge to explain why those values appear in the text.
wider: Explain how values represented in a text from a historical context (e.g. the romantic representation of the Australian swagman) differ from contemporary values about the same subject
Examine how a literary text by a First Nations Australian author represents values, ways of being and knowing that differ distinctly from mainstream Australian literary traditions
Compare how the same historical period is represented in texts from different cultural perspectives, examining whose values each text prioritises

modes.reason: The move from 'what ideas are in this text' to 'these ideas reflect these specific values from this context' requires explicit scaffolding. Students tend to make general contextual claims rather than grounding them in specific textual evidence. Structured reasoning support at this node builds the habit of linking textual detail to contextual claim.

nodes.label: First Nations and diverse author perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how literary texts by First Nations Australian authors represent unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing, and how texts by wide-ranging Australian and world authors offer diverse perspectives shaped by their contexts.
criteria: Explains how a text by a First Nations Australian or diverse author represents a perspective or set of values shaped by a specific cultural context.
Identifies at least one specific way the representation differs from or challenges mainstream representations.

width.minimum: Explain how one text by a First Nations Australian or culturally diverse author represents a perspective or set of values shaped by the author's cultural context, identifying at least one specific way it differs from mainstream representations.
width.typical: Explain how texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors from a range of cultural contexts represent distinct values and perspectives; explain how these representations reflect the social and cultural contexts from which the texts emerge.
wider: Compare how two authors from different cultural backgrounds (e.g. a First Nations Australian and a British author) represent the natural world, examining what values about land, country and environment each text encodes
Investigate how a First Nations Australian text represents ways of being, knowing and doing that are absent from or marginalised in mainstream Australian literature
Examine how reading texts from unfamiliar cultural contexts challenges or expands a reader's own values and perspectives

modes.reason: Understanding that perspective is always culturally situated — and that different contexts produce genuinely different ways of understanding the world — requires exposure to texts from multiple diverse contexts. A single text cannot establish the comparative understanding the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Opinions about literary style
descriptors.description: share opinions about the language features, literary devices and text structures that contribute to the styles of literary texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can form and express opinions about literary texts with reasoning, and evaluate the opinions of others (AC9E7LE02). They have not yet focused specifically on how language features, literary devices and text structures collectively constitute a text's style — or on evaluating and comparing opinions about stylistic choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share and evaluate opinions about how language features, literary devices and text structures contribute to the styles of literary texts.

nodes.label: Style as the sum of language choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language features, literary devices and text structures that contribute to a literary text's style and form an opinion about their effectiveness.
criteria: Identifies specific language features, literary devices or text structures in a literary text.
Forms a clear opinion about how at least one of these contributes to the text's overall style.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate and compare different opinions about literary style. Without the holistic concept of style as the cumulative effect of multiple language choices built at Node 1, students cannot evaluate competing stylistic interpretations — they can only agree or disagree with individual feature observations.

width.minimum: Identify at least two elements (language features, literary devices or text structures) in a literary text and form an opinion about how they contribute to the text's style.
width.typical: Identify and explain how a combination of language features, literary devices and text structures creates the distinctive style of a literary text; form an opinion about the effectiveness of those stylistic choices.
wider: Compare the styles of two literary texts from different periods or genres and explain which stylistic choices are most effective and why
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use distinct language features and structures to create styles that draw on cultural traditions not typically represented in mainstream literary criticism
Investigate how a specific author's style is consistent across multiple works and what signature features constitute that style

modes.reason: Students typically comment on single features in isolation. The concept of 'style' as the cumulative effect of many language choices requires explicit instruction in how to build a holistic stylistic reading from individual observations.

nodes.label: Evaluating opinions about style
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and evaluate different opinions about the stylistic features of literary texts, including opinions that challenge or support their own view.
criteria: Compares at least two different opinions about a text's style, identifying the evidence each opinion relies on.
Evaluates which opinion is better supported, with reasoning connected to specific language features, devices or structures.

width.minimum: Compare two opinions about the style of a literary text (e.g. from two reviews or class discussion) and evaluate which is better supported with reference to language features, devices or structure.
width.typical: Compare and evaluate a range of opinions about the stylistic features of literary texts, including opinions about characterisation, setting and plot; share and refine own opinions in response to opinions that challenge them.
wider: Research critical responses to a literary text and evaluate how different critics have interpreted the same stylistic features differently, examining what assumptions underlie each reading
Engage in structured academic discussion or debate where opinions about literary style are challenged and defended with reference to textual evidence
Reflect on how one's own cultural background or experience shapes the stylistic features one notices or values in a text

modes.reason: Evaluating opinions about literary style requires a repertoire of critical perspectives and metalanguage. Encountering multiple critical viewpoints — including ones that prioritise different stylistic features — builds the evaluative range needed to hold and defend a position.

descriptors.title: Language and images positioning readers
descriptors.description: explain how language and/or images in texts position readers to respond and form viewpoints
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how language choices and visual features shape reader responses (AC9E7LE03). They have not yet explained the positioning function systematically — how specific language and image choices lead readers toward particular responses and viewpoints rather than others.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how language and/or images in texts position readers to respond in particular ways and form specific viewpoints.

nodes.label: How texts position readers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that specific language and image choices in a text are designed to guide readers toward particular responses and viewpoints — not as neutral description but as positioning.
criteria: Identifies a specific language or image choice in a text.
Explains how that choice is designed to guide the reader toward a particular response or viewpoint, rather than describing the choice neutrally.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 applies the positioning concept to film and multimodal texts. Students who have not established the critical stance — that specific choices are designed to guide responses — will approach film analysis as plot summary or personal reaction rather than as analysis of design choices. The conceptual shift must be established in print before it can travel to multimodal contexts.

width.minimum: Explain how at least two specific language or image choices in a provided text are designed to guide the reader toward a particular response or viewpoint.
width.typical: Explain how language choices (e.g. word choice, tone, narrative perspective, figurative language) and/or visual features in texts work together to position readers to respond in particular ways and form specific viewpoints.
wider: Analyse how a complex picture book combines words and images to position readers to respond emotionally or morally to a character
Compare how two texts on the same subject use different language and visual choices to position readers toward opposing viewpoints on that subject
Examine how First Nations or multicultural authors use positioning strategies to invite non-Indigenous or monocultural readers to adopt unfamiliar perspectives

modes.reason: The concept of 'positioning' requires students to adopt a critical stance toward texts that usually feel transparent — to ask 'why is this word chosen rather than another?' Explicit scaffolding of the from-effect-to-cause reasoning is needed: notice the effect first, then reverse-engineer the choices that created it.

nodes.label: Positioning in film and multimodal texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how film and multimodal texts position viewers to respond to characters and events through the interaction of language, image and other modalities.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific choices in a film or multimodal text (e.g. camera angle, word choice, colour, music) and explains how each positions the viewer.
Explains the cumulative effect of these choices on the viewer's response to a character or event.

width.minimum: Share an opinion about how a film positions the viewer to respond to at least one character, identifying the specific choices (camera angle, music, dialogue, colour, etc.) that create that positioning.
width.typical: Explain how film and multimodal texts use a combination of language, image, sound and structural features to position viewers to respond to characters, events and issues in particular ways.
wider: Analyse how a film or TV episode uses a sustained combination of visual and linguistic choices to position the viewer to sympathise with one character and distrust another
Compare how the same narrative event is positioned differently in two film adaptations of the same story — examining what choices create different viewer responses
Investigate how documentary filmmakers use visual and language choices to position viewers toward particular conclusions about a real-world subject

modes.reason: The positioning concept needs to travel across modalities — from print to image to film. Students who only practise it in print texts may struggle to apply the same critical lens to visual and multimodal texts. Multiple modality contexts build the generalised critical reading skill.

descriptors.title: Intertextuality in literary texts
descriptors.description: identify intertextual references in literary texts and explain how the references enable new understanding of the aesthetic quality of the text
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify connections between texts and discuss how one text draws on or responds to another (AC9E7LE04). They have not yet examined intertextuality in literary texts specifically — how allusion or quotation in written texts enables new understanding of aesthetic quality through the meaning generated by the connection between texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify intertextual references in literary texts and explain how those references enable new understanding of the text's aesthetic quality.

nodes.label: Identifying literary intertextuality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an intertextual reference (allusion or quotation) in a literary text and explain what source it draws on.
criteria: Identifies a specific intertextual reference in a literary text.
Names the source text the reference draws on and explains what prior knowledge is needed to recognise it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to explain how an intertextual reference enables new understanding of aesthetic quality — a task that is impossible if students cannot reliably identify references and name their source texts. Without solid identification at Node 1, Node 2 analysis is speculative rather than grounded.

width.minimum: Identify one intertextual reference (allusion or direct quotation) in a literary text and name the source text it references.
width.typical: Identify intertextual references through allusion or quotation in written literary texts; explain how knowledge of the source text is required to understand the full meaning of the reference.
wider: Investigate how a literary text uses allusions to a specific cultural tradition (e.g. classical mythology, the Bible, a particular literary canon) and examine what knowledge that assumes of the reader
Examine how a contemporary author uses intertextual references to classic texts to position their work within a literary tradition
Compare how two authors allude to the same source text differently, examining what each achieves through the reference

modes.reason: Identifying an intertextual reference requires students to distinguish between a text simply mentioning something and deliberately alluding to it — a non-obvious interpretive move. Without explicit scaffolding of what constitutes an allusion and how to trace it to a source, students miss references or over-identify casual mentions as allusions.

nodes.label: Intertextuality and aesthetic quality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how an intertextual reference in a literary text enables new understanding of the text's aesthetic quality — how the reference enriches the reader's appreciation of the text's meaning, craft or effect.
criteria: Explains how a specific intertextual reference enriches the reader's understanding or appreciation of a literary text.
Uses appropriate aesthetic vocabulary (e.g. 'layers of meaning', 'resonance', 'allusion', 'aesthetic effect') in the explanation.

width.minimum: Explain how one intertextual reference in a literary text adds to the reader's understanding or appreciation of the text's aesthetic quality — what the reference enables that a reading without knowledge of the source would miss.
width.typical: Identify intertextual references through allusion or quotation in literary texts and explain how knowledge of other texts influences the reader's understanding and appreciation of the aesthetic quality of the text being read.
wider: Analyse how sustained intertextual allusiveness (multiple references to a single source tradition) shapes the aesthetic identity of a literary text as a whole
Investigate how a parody or creative response to a canonical text generates aesthetic quality through the gap between the original and the imitation
Examine how a First Nations author's use of oral storytelling traditions as intertextual material creates aesthetic qualities not available within Western literary conventions alone

modes.reason: The connection between intertextual reference and aesthetic quality is abstract — students may understand that a reference exists without being able to articulate what it adds aesthetically. Explicit scaffolding of the 'what does this add that the text alone cannot provide?' question is needed to move from identification to aesthetic explanation.

descriptors.title: Sentence patterns, tone and imagery
descriptors.description: analyse how language features such as sentence patterns create tone, and literary devices such as imagery create meaning and effect
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how literary devices and language features create effects in literary texts (AC9E7LE05). They have not yet analysed how sentence-level grammatical choices (active/passive voice, simple vs complex syntax) systematically create tone, or how this connects to the broader operation of imagery in meaning-making.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how sentence patterns create tone and how literary devices such as imagery create meaning and effect in literary texts.

nodes.label: Sentence patterns creating tone
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how sentence-level choices — including active/passive voice, simple vs complex syntax, sentence length and pattern — create tone in a literary text.
criteria: Identifies a specific sentence-level feature (e.g. passive voice, terse syntax) in a literary text.
Explains how that feature creates a specific tone, using appropriate metalanguage.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 analyses how imagery creates meaning and effect — a task requiring the feature→effect reasoning chain built at Node 1. Students who identify sentence features without connecting them to tone arrive at Node 2 unable to analyse images for meaning rather than just label them as devices.

width.minimum: Identify how one sentence-level choice (e.g. active vs passive voice, terse vs elaborate syntax) creates a specific tone in a provided literary passage.
width.typical: Analyse how sentence patterns — including active and passive voice, simple and complex syntax, and varied sentence length — create tone across a literary text; explain how different sentence-level choices produce formal, intimate, urgent or detached tones.
wider: Compare how a short story writer and a poet create contrasting tones using different approaches to sentence structure and length
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use sentence patterns that reflect oral storytelling rhythms to create a tone distinct from written Western prose tradition
Analyse how a single paragraph changes in tone when rewritten using active instead of passive voice, or terse instead of complex syntax

modes.reason: Students often identify sentence features (e.g. 'short sentences') without connecting them to tone (e.g. 'which creates urgency'). The reasoning scaffold — feature → tone → effect — needs to be made explicit and practised before it becomes automatic.

nodes.label: Imagery creating meaning and effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how literary devices including imagery — and specifically how simile, metaphor and sensory imagery — create meaning and effect in literary texts.
criteria: Identifies a specific image in a literary text and names the device (simile, metaphor, personification, sensory image).
Analyses the meaning or effect the image creates, explaining what it suggests beyond its literal content.

width.minimum: Identify an image (simile, metaphor or sensory image) in a literary text and analyse what meaning it creates — what it suggests beyond its literal content.
width.typical: Analyse how imagery and related literary devices create meaning and effect in literary texts; explain how writers use terse or elaborate language choices and how these influence both the meaning created by images and the tone of the text overall.
wider: Analyse how sustained imagery (an extended metaphor or a consistent pattern of images) creates cumulative meaning across a literary text
Compare how imagery operates differently in poetry vs prose — examining how compressed imagery in poetry creates different effects from extended imagery in narrative
Investigate how First Nations Australian authors use imagery connected to Country, place and natural cycles to create meaning not available through imagery drawn from other traditions

modes.reason: Students who only encounter imagery in poetry may not transfer the analytical skill to prose. Encountering imagery across poetry, prose fiction and drama — and seeing how it operates differently in each — builds a genuinely transferable analytical capability.

descriptors.title: Create and edit literary texts
descriptors.description: create and edit literary texts that experiment with language features and literary devices for particular purposes and effects
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create literary texts that use language features and literary devices to create character, setting and mood (AC9E7LE06). They have not yet focused on deliberate experimentation — using devices with conscious intentionality toward a particular effect — or on collaborative and iterative editing of literary writing with peer feedback.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and edit literary texts that experiment with language features and literary devices for particular purposes and effects.

nodes.label: Experimenting with language features and devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a literary text that deliberately experiments with at least one language feature or literary device, and articulate the purpose or effect the experiment is intended to achieve.
criteria: Creates a literary text that uses at least one named literary device or language feature deliberately.
Can explain the purpose or intended effect of the device choice in their own text.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 is editing for effect — a task that requires students to have a created text to edit and, crucially, to have made deliberate device choices in that text to revisit and evaluate. Students who have not built a working repertoire at Node 1 produce undifferentiated writing with no purposeful choices to reflect on or revise.

width.minimum: Create a short literary piece (e.g. a short story opening or poem) that deliberately uses at least one literary device or language feature for a named effect, and explain the choice made.
width.typical: Create literary texts that combine multiple literary devices (e.g. imagery, tone, dialogue choices) to achieve a specific purpose or evoke a specific reader response; make deliberate and reflective choices in the writing process.
wider: Create a short story with a sustained use of a single dominant device (e.g. extended metaphor or unreliable narrator perspective) and reflect on how the constraint shaped the writing
Collaborate with a peer to write a short script focusing on dialogue choices for each character, and reflect on how the dialogue reveals character through language rather than description

Experiment with combining literary devices from different cultural traditions (e.g. First Nations storytelling features with Western narrative conventions) to create a distinctive hybrid literary text

modes.reason: Literary experimentation requires a repertoire of devices to experiment with. Students who have only analysed devices need guided practice deploying them in their own writing across multiple short tasks before the experimental relationship to craft becomes comfortable.

nodes.label: Editing for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit their own literary texts — revising imagery, word choices and structural features — and reflect on how editing decisions change the effect of the text.
criteria: Produces a revised version of a literary text with at least one deliberate and explainable change to imagery, word choice or structure.
Articulates how the revision changes or improves the intended effect of the text.

width.minimum: Edit one piece of own literary writing by revising at least one imagery choice or word choice and explain how the revision changes the intended effect.
width.typical: Edit literary texts with attention to imagery, word choices and structural features; reflect on how editing decisions affect the overall purpose and effect; use peer feedback to inform editing choices.
wider: Conduct a sustained editing cycle on a longer literary piece — draft, peer review, revise, reflect — documenting how the text changed and why each revision decision was made
Compare the draft and final versions of a published author's work (where available) to examine how editing decisions changed the effect of the text
Edit a collaborative script written with a peer, focusing on ensuring each character's dialogue is consistent and distinct in voice

modes.reason: Editing literary writing requires students to hold their authorial intention and the reader's experience simultaneously — seeing the text from outside themselves. This integration of compositional and reader perspectives is the hardest part of the creative editing process and warrants explicit attention.

descriptors.title: Texts reflecting contexts
descriptors.description: identify how texts reflect contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how texts are shaped by the context in which they are created and understand how digital and multimodal contexts influence text forms (AC9E7LY01). They have not yet focused on how specific contemporary text forms — social media texts and speeches for reconciliation — reflect the specific contexts of their creation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how texts reflect the contexts in which they are created, including social media texts and speeches for reconciliation.

nodes.label: Texts as context-shaped artefacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific features of a text and explain how they reflect the context — social, historical, technological or cultural — in which the text was created.
criteria: Identifies specific features of a text (e.g. language choices, structure, format) and names the contextual factors that shaped them.
Explains the connection between at least two textual features and the context in which the text was created.

width.minimum: Identify at least two features of a provided text (e.g. a social media post or speech) and explain how each reflects the context in which it was created.
width.typical: Identify and explain how social media texts and speeches for reconciliation reflect the contexts in which they are created; examine how platform affordances, audience, purpose and historical moment are all visible in textual features.
wider: Compare how a social media text and a formal speech on the same topic reflect different contextual constraints — platform, audience, register, purpose — and what this reveals about how context shapes text
Investigate how speeches for reconciliation reflect specific historical and political contexts and how these contexts have shaped the language and structural choices of those speeches
Examine how a First Nations community text (e.g. a land rights statement or community announcement) reflects the specific cultural and political context of its creation

modes.reason: The abstract claim 'texts reflect contexts' needs multiple concrete examples before it becomes a generalised lens. Social media and reconciliation speeches are the ACARA examples, but encountering multiple diverse text-context pairs builds the transferable insight that this is a universal feature of all texts.

descriptors.title: Interaction skills for challenging meaning
descriptors.description: use interaction skills for identified purposes and situations, including when supporting or challenging the stated or implied meanings of spoken texts in presentations or discussion
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use interaction skills in a range of spoken contexts, including formal and informal discussion, and use active listening to evaluate spoken texts (AC9E7LY02). They have not yet focused specifically on using interaction skills to support or challenge the stated or implied meanings of spoken texts — engaging with the substance of what is said, not just participating in discussion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use interaction skills for identified purposes in a range of contexts, including when supporting or challenging the stated or implied meanings of spoken texts.

nodes.label: Identifying stated and implied meanings in spoken texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen to a conversation or speech, identify the point being made, and explain both the tone and manner of presentation — distinguishing stated from implied meanings.
criteria: Identifies the explicit point being made in a spoken text.
Identifies at least one implied meaning and explains the cues (tone, manner, word choice) that signal it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to use interaction strategies to support or challenge the implied meanings of spoken texts. Students who cannot distinguish stated from implied meaning in the first place can only engage with surface content in discussion — the interaction strategies at Node 2 have no target to work on.

width.minimum: Listen to a spoken text, identify the explicit point being made and one implied meaning, and explain how the tone or manner of presentation signals the implied meaning.
width.typical: Listen to a range of spoken texts; identify stated and implied meanings; explain the tone and manner of presentation; describe how the interaction between explicit and implicit meaning shapes the overall message.
wider: Analyse how a formal speech uses understatement, irony or indirect language to imply positions without stating them directly — examining what the speaker does not say as well as what they say
Compare how stated and implied meanings operate differently in informal conversation vs formal debate, examining how context affects the balance between explicit and implicit communication
Investigate how First Nations or multicultural communication styles may use indirect expression, silence or implied meaning differently from mainstream Australian English interaction conventions

modes.reason: The distinction between stated and implied meaning in spoken language is more challenging than in written text — the cues are prosodic and contextual rather than linguistic alone. Explicit scaffolding of what to listen for — tone, pace, word choice, what's conspicuously absent — is needed before students can do this independently.

nodes.label: Supporting and challenging meaning in discussion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use effective interaction strategies — speaking clearly, asking questions about stated and implied ideas, restating and summarising — to support or challenge the meanings of spoken texts in presentations and discussion.
criteria: Uses at least one named interaction strategy (question, restatement, summary) purposefully during a discussion.
Can explain how the strategy was used to support or challenge a stated or implied meaning.

width.minimum: In a discussion, use at least one strategy (asking a question, restating an idea, summarising) to either support or challenge a meaning expressed by another speaker.
width.typical: Use a range of interaction strategies — speaking clearly at appropriate length, asking probing questions about stated and implied ideas, restating and summarising — to engage constructively in formal and informal discussion, including when supporting or challenging claims.
wider: Participate in a structured debate or Socratic discussion where the explicit goal is to challenge implied as well as stated meanings, using evidence-based questioning strategies
Practise summarising an opposing speaker's argument accurately and fairly before challenging it — developing the discipline of steelmanning before critique
Reflect on own interaction patterns in discussion — what assumptions do you bring? When do you challenge and when do you defer? — and evaluate how your patterns affect the quality of discussion

modes.reason: Effective interaction strategies need to become habitual and varied — students need a repertoire of moves (question types, summary formulations, challenge framings) rather than a single default move. Multiple discussion contexts across different formalities build this repertoire.

descriptors.title: Analyse and evaluate language features and sources
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate the ways that language features vary according to the purpose and audience of the text, and the ways that sources and quotations are used in a text
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how language features are shaped by purpose and audience, and identify how authors use supporting evidence in texts (AC9E7LY03). They have not yet evaluated the effectiveness of language feature choices or the use of sources and quotations — moving from analysis to evaluative judgement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate how language features vary according to purpose and audience, and how sources and quotations are used to support ideas in texts.

nodes.label: Evaluating language features for purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse language feature choices in a text and evaluate whether those choices are effective for the text's purpose and audience — forming and justifying a view.
criteria: Identifies specific language features in a text and analyses their relationship to the text's purpose and audience.
Evaluates whether the language choices are effective, providing reasoned justification with reference to the text.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 applies the same evaluative move to sources and quotations. The criteria-application scaffold — 'effective for what purpose, for which audience, with what reasoning?' — built at Node 1 is required for Node 2 to produce genuine evaluation rather than impressionistic reaction to source presence or absence.

width.minimum: Analyse two language features in a text and evaluate whether they are effective for the text's stated purpose and audience, giving reasons for the evaluation.
width.typical: Analyse and evaluate how language features — including vocabulary, tone, sentence structure and register — vary according to purpose and audience; evaluate an author's language choices and present a reasoned opinion about their effectiveness.
wider: Compare how two different authors addressing the same audience for the same purpose use language features differently, evaluating which approach is more effective and why
Evaluate how language feature choices in a First Nations or culturally specific text are calibrated to their intended community audience — what would be gained or lost for a different audience
Analyse how a text changes when its intended audience changes — taking a formal report and rewriting it for a different audience — and evaluate which version is more effective for each audience

modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to apply criteria (effectiveness for purpose and audience) rather than simply describe what they observe. The evaluative move — 'and this is effective/not effective because' — needs to be explicitly scaffolded and practised.

nodes.label: Evaluating use of sources and quotations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how an author uses sources and quotations in a text — assessing whether sources are used effectively to support ideas — and form and express an opinion about the author's approach.
criteria: Evaluates whether a source or quotation in a text effectively supports the claim it is used to substantiate.
Forms a clear opinion about the author's use of sources and supports that opinion with reference to the text.

width.minimum: Evaluate how one source or quotation is used in a text — explain whether it effectively supports the idea it is meant to substantiate, and give a reasoned opinion about the author's approach.
width.typical: Evaluate the use of sources and quotations across a text, forming and presenting opinions about how effectively the author has used evidence to support ideas; identify cases where source use is strong and cases where it is weak or misleading.
wider: Investigate how the same source or quotation can be used to support opposing claims depending on what surrounding context and interpretation the author provides
Analyse how sources are selected and framed in a biased text — examining what the author's source choices reveal about their perspective and what sources are absent
Evaluate the source use in a student's own argumentative writing and revise for greater effectiveness

modes.reason: Evaluating source use effectively requires students to have encountered a range of approaches — strong integration, weak cherry-picking, selective quotation, absence of sources where sources are needed. Exposure to multiple examples of varying quality builds the comparative benchmark needed for genuine evaluation.

descriptors.title: How authors organise ideas
descriptors.description: analyse how authors organise ideas to develop and shape meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how authors structure texts and organise information to achieve purpose (AC9E7LY04). They have not yet analysed the specific organisational logics — proposition and support, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution — and how these structures shape the meaning a text produces.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how authors organise ideas — using structures such as proposition/support, cause/effect and compare/contrast — to develop and shape meaning.

nodes.label: Idea organisation structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the organisational structure a text uses (e.g. proposition and support, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution) and explain how that structure shapes the text's meaning.
criteria: Names the organisational structure used in a text (proposition/support, cause/effect, compare/contrast, or problem/solution).
Explains how that structural choice shapes what the reader understands or is persuaded of.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to analyse how organisational choices shape and limit meaning — a task that requires being able to name and classify the organisational structure in question. Students who cannot identify whether a text uses cause-effect or problem-solution logic cannot analyse the meaning implications of that structural choice.

width.minimum: Identify the organisational structure used in one provided text (e.g. a news article or argument) and explain how that structure shapes what the reader understands from the text.
width.typical: Analyse how texts structured according to proposition and support, cause and effect, compare and contrast, or problem and solution each shape meaning differently; identify examples of each structure and explain the effect the structural choice has on a reader.
wider: Compare how a news article and an academic essay organise the same information differently and analyse how the structural difference shapes the meaning and credibility each text produces

Investigate how a problem-solution structure can be used persuasively — examining what is at stake in the problem framing and whether the proposed solution addresses all aspects of the defined problem
Analyse how the organisation of a webpage (e.g. a news site or advocacy site) uses non-linear structure and shapes meaning differently from a linearly structured print text

modes.reason: Students may know proposition-support from English but not recognise the same organisational logic appearing as cause-effect in other subjects or as problem-solution in design. Encountering the structures across multiple text types builds a transferable analytical vocabulary.

nodes.label: How organisation shapes and limits meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how an author's organisational choices not only develop meaning but also constrain what meanings are possible — examining what organisational choices include, exclude and imply.
criteria: Identifies the organisational structure of a text and analyses how it develops the author's intended meaning.
Identifies at least one way the structural choice shapes or limits what meanings the text can produce.

width.minimum: Identify one way in which the organisational structure of a text shapes or limits the meaning it can produce — what it makes visible and what it makes invisible.
width.typical: Analyse how authors organise ideas to develop and shape meaning across a range of text types; discuss the effectiveness of different organisational approaches for their stated purpose; examine how texts that organise ideas around a problem can frame the solution in ways that limit alternatives.
wider: Rewrite a section of a text using a different organisational logic (e.g. change from cause-effect to problem-solution) and analyse how the structural change shapes the meaning produced

Investigate how the organisational structure of a web page shapes user behaviour and meaning-making differently from printed text — and what ideological or commercial purposes that structure might serve

Analyse how a First Nations text organises knowledge according to principles that differ from Western logical structures (e.g. relationally, through narrative, through Country) and how this creates different kinds of meaning

modes.reason: The insight that organisational choices are not neutral — that how ideas are arranged shapes what meaning is produced — is a critical thinking integration point. It requires students to hold both the content and the structural logic simultaneously and see that the structure is itself an argument.

descriptors.title: Comprehension strategies for interpretation and evaluation
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring to interpret and evaluate ideas in texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use a range of comprehension strategies to construct meaning from texts and synthesise ideas across texts (AC9E7LY05). They have not yet applied these strategies specifically to interpretation and evaluation — using them to assess the credibility, effectiveness and significance of ideas in texts rather than merely to build comprehension.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies to interpret and evaluate ideas in texts, including assessing credibility and effectiveness of content.

nodes.label: Comprehension strategies for deeper reading
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply comprehension strategies (visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning, inferring) purposefully to interpret ideas in texts — reading for what is implied and inferred, not only what is stated.
criteria: Names at least two comprehension strategies and explains how each was used with a specific text.
Demonstrates inference or questioning as a tool for interpretation — surfacing implied or unstated meaning.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires applying comprehension strategies specifically to evaluation — assessing credibility and effectiveness. Students who only have summarising in their repertoire cannot apply inferring, questioning or monitoring to make evaluative judgements. The full strategy repertoire built at Node 1 is what Node 2 applies in a new evaluative mode.

width.minimum: Apply at least two named comprehension strategies to a text and explain how they helped interpret ideas — specifically naming what the strategy surfaced about implied or inferred meaning.
width.typical: Apply a range of comprehension strategies purposefully to interpret ideas in texts; reflect on and connect information across and between texts; demonstrate inference and questioning as deliberate tools for interpretation.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to a text from a cultural context unfamiliar to the reader — and reflect on which strategies worked, which were less effective, and what gaps in cultural knowledge affected comprehension
Use inferring and questioning strategies specifically to analyse what a text does NOT say — what is conspicuously absent from the text — and why
Compare how different comprehension strategies are required for reading a visual image vs a written text on the same subject

modes.reason: Comprehension strategies become truly useful when students have a full repertoire and can select the most appropriate strategy for a given reading challenge. Students who default to summarising need to experience questioning, inferring and monitoring as equally productive tools across different texts.

nodes.label: Comprehension strategies for evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comprehension strategies to evaluate ideas in texts — assessing the credibility, effectiveness and significance of content, including evaluating the selection and composition of images for their effect on credibility.
criteria: Applies at least one comprehension strategy to evaluate an idea or image in a text.
States a clear evaluative judgement (credible/not credible, effective/not effective) with reasoning that references specific textual or visual evidence.

width.minimum: Apply at least one comprehension strategy to evaluate an idea in a text — assessing whether it is credible, well-supported or effectively communicated.
width.typical: Use comprehension strategies to evaluate the content of texts, including determining criteria for evaluating website content, assessing the credibility of information and evaluating the selection and composition of images for their effect on the credibility or meaning of a text.
wider: Develop and apply explicit evaluation criteria for a class of texts (e.g. websites on a health topic) and use comprehension strategies to systematically evaluate multiple texts against those criteria

Investigate how the selection and framing of images in a news website affects reader credibility judgements — examining which images are selected, how they are cropped and what associations they trigger
Evaluate how cross-referencing information across texts (connecting strategy) can reveal inconsistencies or contradictions between sources — and what to do when reliable sources disagree

modes.reason: Evaluation requires applying criteria, not just responding with a gut reaction. The structured reasoning scaffold — what criteria am I using? what does the evidence show against those criteria? what is my evaluation? — needs to be made explicit before students can evaluate credibly rather than impressionistically.

descriptors.title: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts
descriptors.description: plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising and expanding ideas, and selecting text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features for purposes and audiences in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive and/or analytical
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, create, edit and publish texts for a range of purposes and audiences, making deliberate text structure and language feature choices (AC9E7LY06). They have not yet focused on expanding and organising ideas through the full planning-to-publishing cycle with academic accuracy goals, or on the deliberate use of vocabulary for positioning and persuasion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising and expanding ideas with deliberate structural, language and visual feature choices suited to purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Planning and organising ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a written or multimodal text by organising and expanding ideas — using conceptual maps, journals or equivalent tools — and selecting appropriate text structures for the text's purpose and audience.
criteria: Produces a planning document that organises ideas and identifies a text structure suited to the purpose.
Can explain why the chosen structure is appropriate for the text's purpose and intended audience.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to create texts with deliberate structural and language feature selections — which presupposes a plan that has already organised ideas and identified structural choices. Thin planning means students create reactively rather than deliberately, making the 'deliberate selection' evidence invisible.

width.minimum: Produce a planning document (conceptual map, outline or journal) for a written text that organises and expands at least three ideas and identifies the text structure to be used.
width.typical: Plan written and multimodal texts using conceptual maps or journals to organise and expand ideas; select appropriate text structures and justify how these selections serve the text's purpose and audience; plan for the integration of language features, literary devices and visual features.
wider: Compare different planning approaches (linear outline vs conceptual map vs journal drafting) and evaluate which approach produces better-organised ideas for a specific text type
Plan a multimodal text that requires explicit decisions about how written text, images and visual layout will work together to serve the purpose and audience
Investigate how published authors describe their planning process and compare with own practice — examining whether planning strategies vary by text type or purpose

modes.reason: Planning a text with deliberate structural and language feature choices requires students to separate planning decisions from execution — an unfamiliar metacognitive move. Without explicit scaffolding of what a planning document should contain (ideas, structure, feature selections), students either skip planning or treat it as an outline with no selection rationale.

nodes.label: Creating with deliberate language and feature selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create written or multimodal texts that make deliberate selections from text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features to serve their purposes and audiences.
criteria: Creates a text for a named purpose and audience.
Can identify and explain at least two deliberate structural or language choices made in the text and how they serve the purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 is editing for accuracy and meaning. Effective editing requires a text that was created with deliberate choices — something to evaluate and refine. Students who created without repertoire at Node 2 have only mechanical errors to correct at Node 3, not purposeful revision decisions to make. The editing task collapses to proofreading.

width.minimum: Create a text for a specified purpose and audience that demonstrates at least two deliberate selection choices (e.g. a specific text structure, a vocabulary choice to position the reader, or a literary device for effect) and can explain each choice.
width.typical: Create written and multimodal texts for a range of purposes (imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical) and audiences, making deliberate and explainable selections from text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features; select vocabulary to position and persuade the reader where appropriate.
wider: Create a text that deliberately exploits the conventions of a specific genre for persuasive or satirical effect — using the reader's genre expectations as a rhetorical tool
Create a multimodal text in which visual features and written text work interdependently, and reflect on how each modality contributes differently to the overall purpose

Create a text for an unfamiliar audience (e.g. a First Nations community audience, an academic audience, an international audience) and reflect on what structural and language choices the unfamiliar audience requires

modes.reason: Creating across the range of text purposes (imaginative, informative, persuasive, analytical) requires a repertoire of structural and language strategies associated with each purpose. Students who have only created in one mode cannot transfer confidently to others. Multiple creation tasks across purposes build this repertoire.

nodes.label: Editing for accuracy and meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit own texts for grammatical accuracy, spelling and punctuation, and for clarity and precision of meaning — using experimentation with sentence structure, literary devices and vocabulary to clarify ideas.
criteria: Produces a revised version of own text with identifiable improvements to at least one grammatical feature and at least one meaning clarity issue.
Can explain the rationale for at least two specific editing decisions.

width.minimum: Edit a piece of own writing for at least one grammatical feature (sentence structure, punctuation or spelling) and for at least one meaning clarity revision, and explain the revisions made.
width.typical: Edit written texts for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and for meaning — experimenting with sentence structure order, literary devices and vocabulary to clarify ideas for academic or creative purposes; reflect on how editing decisions change the text.
wider: Conduct a systematic editing cycle — first for accuracy, then for meaning, then for effect — and document the revision history with annotations explaining each change
Edit a peer's writing for meaning clarity and accuracy, providing written justifications for suggested revisions
Examine published author revisions (where available) and compare editorial decisions with own editing practice

modes.reason: Editing fluency requires repeated practice — the habit of reading one's own writing critically for accuracy and meaning does not develop from a single editing task. Multiple edit cycles across varied texts, with explicit attention to different editing foci, build the automaticity that makes editing reliable rather than superficial.

descriptors.title: Plan, create and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations
descriptors.description: plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations for audiences and purposes, selecting language features, literary devices, visual features and features of voice to suit formal or informal situations, and organising and developing ideas in texts in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive and/or analytical
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, create and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations for audiences and purposes, selecting features of voice and language (AC9E7LY07). They have not yet focused on the full planning-rehearsal-delivery cycle with deliberate selection of literary devices and visual features, or on calibrating voice features for specific audience effects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations with deliberate selection of language, literary, visual and voice features for specific purposes and audiences.

nodes.label: Planning and crafting presentations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a spoken or multimodal presentation that makes deliberate selections of language features, literary devices, visual features and voice features, organising and developing ideas for a specific purpose and audience.
criteria: Produces a presentation plan that identifies specific feature selections and explains their purpose.
Can justify why chosen features suit the presentation's purpose and intended audience.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 is rehearsal and delivery — a phase entirely dependent on what was planned and crafted at Node 1. Students with thin planning arrive at rehearsal without deliberate feature choices to practise or multimodal elements to integrate. Delivery becomes improvised rather than purposeful.

width.minimum: Produce a plan for a spoken or multimodal presentation that identifies at least two feature selections (e.g. tone, vocabulary, a simile, visual support) and explains how each will serve the purpose and audience.
width.typical: Plan spoken and multimodal presentations for a range of purposes and audiences; select vocabulary, sentence structures, literary devices and features of voice with deliberate attention to purpose and audience; integrate multimodal features (visual, audio, structural) to support understanding.
wider: Plan a persuasive advertising campaign about a contemporary issue, making explicit decisions about visual design, language choices and voice features for a target audience
Compare how the same ideas require different planning and feature selection choices when delivered as a formal speech vs an informal talk vs a debate speech

Investigate how First Nations Australian oral presentation traditions (e.g. Welcome to Country, formal public speaking) use voice features and structural conventions that differ from Western formal speech conventions

modes.reason: Planning a presentation with deliberate voice, language and visual feature selections requires students to think ahead about audience effect — an intentional design move rather than reactive drafting. Without explicit scaffolding of what presentation planning involves (feature choices, audience considerations, structural decisions), students produce a content outline rather than a delivery plan.

nodes.label: Rehearsing and delivering for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can rehearse and deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation, using features of voice — tone, volume, pitch, pace — with attention to the effects these have on audience reaction and acceptance of ideas.
criteria: Delivers a presentation that demonstrates deliberate use of at least one voice feature (tone, volume, pitch or pace).
Can reflect on the intended and actual effect of voice feature choices on the audience.

width.minimum: Deliver a spoken presentation and demonstrate deliberate use of at least one voice feature (tone, volume, pitch or pace) for an intended audience effect.
width.typical: Rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations, selecting and using features of voice with attention to their effect on audience response; integrate multimodal features in a presentation to support audience understanding; reflect on the effectiveness of delivery choices.
wider: Deliver a debate speech that uses voice features and vocabulary deliberately to persuade an audience and evaluate own performance against intended effect
Create a voiceover for a media presentation, selecting voice features that complement visual elements to construct a persuasive or informative effect
Reflect systematically on own presentation delivery — using video self-review or peer feedback — and identify specific voice feature improvements to rehearse

modes.reason: Confident, controlled presentation delivery is a fluency skill. Understanding which voice features to use does not automatically translate into being able to deploy them under the pressure of performance. Multiple rehearsal and delivery opportunities — in low-stakes and then higher-stakes contexts — build the composure and control the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Applying knowledge to spell accurately
descriptors.description: apply learnt knowledge to spell accurately and to learn new words
