descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply spelling rules and understand word origins and morphemic patterns (AC9E7LY08). They have not yet focused on applying accumulated morphemic and etymological knowledge to the spelling and learning of complex words, or on knowing how to access and use sources for the spelling of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander language words.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply learnt knowledge of morphemic patterns, unusual letter combinations and language-specific resources to spell complex words accurately and learn new words.

nodes.label: Applying morphemic knowledge to complex words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply knowledge of morphemes — prefixes, suffixes, roots — and unusual letter combinations to spell complex words accurately.
criteria: Spells complex words correctly in own writing, demonstrating application of morphemic knowledge.
Can explain how morpheme analysis (prefix, root, suffix) supports accurate spelling of at least two complex words.

width.minimum: Apply morphemic knowledge to spell at least three complex words correctly, explaining how morpheme analysis guided the spelling.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of morphemic patterns, etymology and unusual letter combinations to spell complex words accurately across academic and creative writing; use morphemic analysis as a systematic strategy for approaching unfamiliar words.
wider: Investigate how words from particular language origins (e.g. Latin, Greek, French, Arabic) carry predictable morphemic patterns that can be applied to unfamiliar words
Compare morphemic structures across words from different language families and examine what this reveals about borrowing and language history in English

Limited width — this is a skill with thin variation in contexts at this year band. Extension goes deeper: building awareness of etymological research tools and applying them independently to learn large numbers of new words.

modes.reason: Spelling accuracy is fundamentally a consolidation skill — knowing morphemic patterns intellectually does not automatically produce accurate spelling under writing conditions. Repeated application across multiple writing contexts builds automaticity.

nodes.label: Spelling Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander language words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use appropriate sources (e.g. the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia, local First Nations community resources) to access the correct spelling of Aboriginal language and Torres Strait Islander language words.
criteria: Identifies at least one appropriate source for the spelling of Aboriginal language or Torres Strait Islander language words.
Uses that source to spell at least two words correctly in own writing.

width.minimum: Identify at least one appropriate source for the spelling of Aboriginal language or Torres Strait Islander language words and demonstrate correct spelling of at least two words accessed from that source.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of appropriate sources — including the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia and local First Nations Australian community guidance — to access and use correct spellings of Aboriginal language and Torres Strait Islander language words in own writing.
wider: Investigate how spelling conventions for Aboriginal language words differ from English spelling conventions and what this requires in terms of resource use and cultural respect

Explore how local First Nations community members are the authoritative source for the correct spelling and pronunciation of their community's language words — and what this means for respectful practice
Examine how the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia records language names as a resource for identifying and respecting Country/Place naming conventions

descriptors.title: Vocabulary in familiar contexts
descriptors.description: recognise and develop awareness of vocabulary used in familiar contexts related to everyday experiences, personal interests and topics taught at school
descriptors.knowledge: Students bring oral vocabulary from home and community contexts. They have not yet been asked to consciously attend to vocabulary — to notice, collect and develop awareness of words in relation to specific topics and contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and use vocabulary relevant to everyday experiences, personal interests and school topics — drawing on multiple sources to expand their word knowledge and applying vocabulary in both imaginative and informative contexts.

nodes.label: Topics have words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that topics and contexts have specific vocabulary — particular words that go with particular subjects or activities.
criteria: Student can name at least three words associated with a familiar topic.
Student can identify a word as a 'topic word' when it is introduced in a new context.

width.minimum: Name at least three words that belong to one familiar topic (e.g. words related to families, or words used in a current class topic).
width.typical: Identify and collect vocabulary associated with school topics; recognise learning area–specific words across multiple topics; notice when new words are introduced.
wider: Build a word wall for a current topic and continue adding to it as new vocabulary is encountered across the unit
Compare the vocabulary of two different topics — what words appear in both? What words are unique to each?

modes.reason: Vocabulary acquisition at Foundation is fundamentally about accumulation — students need to encounter and retain many words across many contexts before vocabulary awareness becomes a generative habit.

nodes.label: Vocabulary grows through experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify multiple ways of encountering and learning new vocabulary — through interactions, texts, images, objects and play.
criteria: Student can identify at least two different ways they have encountered new vocabulary.
Student can use a recently acquired vocabulary word appropriately in speech or in a text they are creating.

width.minimum: Identify one new word encountered in class and explain where or how they came across it.
width.typical: Recognise that vocabulary can be expanded through informal interactions, planned experiences, texts, images, artefacts and objects; draw on vocabulary encountered in multiple ways — including imaginative play — to use words in context.
wider: Investigate how role-play activities generate new vocabulary — comparing words used in different dramatic contexts (shopkeeper, scientist, storyteller)
Explore vocabulary from different cultural contexts in the class — including words from First Nations Australian languages or other community languages
Compare vocabulary encountered through visual texts (picture books, films) with vocabulary encountered through oral interaction and real objects

modes.reason: Students may think vocabulary grows only through 'word learning lessons'. Multiple sources — play, objects, images, community language — help build the broader understanding that vocabulary is encountered everywhere.

descriptors.title: Letter formation
descriptors.description: form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt letter formations
descriptors.knowledge: Students may have pre-writing experience (drawing, mark-making) but have not yet been explicitly taught and practised standardised letter formations for most of the alphabet.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt formations — with a functional pencil grip and consistent starting points, direction and size.

nodes.label: Functional grip and starting point
nodes.checkpoint: Students use a functional pencil grip and can demonstrate the correct starting point for a modelled letter.
criteria: Student uses a recognisably functional pencil grip.
Student starts letters at the correct point without prompting for practised letters.
nodes.hinge_reason: Incorrect pencil grip and starting-point habits established here directly impair the accuracy and legibility of letter formation in Nodes 2 and 3 — motor habits are increasingly difficult to correct once established.

width.minimum: Demonstrate a functional pencil grip and correctly start at least one letter from the top.
width.typical: Develop and use a functional pencil grip; follow demonstrations of where to start and in which direction to write letters; apply consistently across practised letters.
wider: Practise grip and formation with different writing tools — pencil, marker, chalk — noting how grip adapts
Use letter formation across different media — sand tray, whiteboard, digital stylus — attending to starting point consistency

modes.reason: Pencil grip and starting-point habits must be established early and consistently — errors in these mechanics become increasingly hard to correct. Repetition across tools and contexts is the remedy, not breadth.

nodes.label: Form lower-case letters accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form most lower-case letters using learnt formations — with correct direction and legible shape.
criteria: Student produces most lower-case letters in a recognisable, legible form.
Student's letter formation is consistent across a short piece of writing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Lower-case letter formation must be sufficiently established before upper-case letters in Node 3, since upper-case letters are used in conjunction with lower-case in all real writing tasks — inconsistent lower-case production undermines legibility in any written work from this point forward.

width.minimum: Form at least fifteen lower-case letters using learnt formations legibly.
width.typical: Form most lower-case letters using learnt letter formations; demonstrate correct directionality and size; produce legible letterforms in writing tasks.
wider: Apply lower-case letter formations in the context of real writing tasks — labelling drawings, writing names, copying short sentences
Compare letter formation consistency across different surfaces and tools
Explore how printed lower-case letters vary in font and compare with handwritten forms — understanding that the letterform has a consistent structure

modes.reason: Letter formation is a motor skill — accuracy and consistency require practice. The width axis is thin here; the issue is reliable production, not contextual breadth.

nodes.label: Form upper-case letters accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can form most upper-case letters using learnt formations.
criteria: Student produces most upper-case letters in a recognisable, legible form.
Student uses upper-case letters correctly in their own name.

width.minimum: Form at least ten upper-case letters using learnt formations legibly.
width.typical: Form most upper-case letters using learnt letter formations; apply in contexts where capitals are required (names, sentence starts).
wider: Use upper-case letters in authentic writing contexts — own name, classmates' names, titles — attending to when capitalisation is required
Compare upper-case and lower-case letter pairs and discuss how formation relates to the letter's identity

modes.reason: As with lower-case, upper-case formation is a motor skill requiring practice. Application in authentic contexts (names, titles) reinforces both formation and the rule for when to use capitals.

descriptors.title: Language empowers relationships and roles
descriptors.description: recognise how language empowers relationships and roles
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how language expresses and creates personal and social identities (AC9E7LA01). They have not yet examined how language functions as a mechanism of power within communities — shaping membership, authority and social roles.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise how specific language choices empower or constrain relationships and define roles within communities.

nodes.label: Community membership through language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language features that signal membership in specific communities, such as family registers, teen slang, technical jargon and classroom interaction patterns.
criteria: Student identifies at least two community-specific language features and names the community each belongs to
Student explains how each language feature signals membership or reinforces belonging in that community

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of community-specific language and explain how they signal belonging to that community.
width.typical: Compare language features across three or more communities (e.g. family, peer group, classroom), explaining how each signals membership and reinforces shared identity.
wider: Analyse how online community language (gaming, fandoms, professional forums) constructs hierarchies of expertise through jargon and access
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use language, including specific greetings in language, to reinforce relationships to Country/Place and community
Investigate how code-switching between community registers positions speakers differently depending on context

modes.reason: Students often conflate all informal language as equivalent; examining different community types reveals that the empowering function varies — jargon in professional contexts differs qualitatively from intimacy markers in family contexts. More community contexts resolve this flattening.

nodes.label: Language and power in roles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise how language choices define and reinforce roles — such as authority, expertise or solidarity — within and across communities.
criteria: Student identifies specific language features (e.g. imperative mode, technical register, terms of address) that construct a role
Student explains how those features empower or position the speaker in relation to others in that context
nodes.hinge_reason: The conceptual move from 'this is a language feature' to 'this feature constitutes power' is prerequisite for N3. Without it, students at N3 cannot explain empowerment as a mechanism — they can only describe features, not explain how those features make power.

width.minimum: Identify a role (e.g. teacher, expert, parent) and explain how specific language features construct or reinforce that role in a given text or interaction.
width.typical: Compare how language constructs authority versus solidarity roles across two or more contexts, explaining how choices position speakers relative to others.
wider: Analyse how the same speaker shifts language to assert or defer authority depending on audience and setting
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use language to assert cultural authority and knowledge in ways that resist mainstream framing
Investigate how gendered or age-related language norms empower some roles and constrain others

modes.reason: The link between language choice and power is abstract — students need scaffolded reasoning to move from observing a language feature to explaining how it constitutes power rather than merely describing it.

nodes.label: Language empowerment as a mechanism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise how language choices function as mechanisms of empowerment — not just markers of identity — actively shaping relationships and roles rather than simply reflecting them.
criteria: Student explains how a language choice actively constructs a relationship or role, not merely reflects it
Student uses appropriate metalanguage (e.g. register, mode, positioning) in their explanation

width.minimum: Explain how a specific language choice in a text actively constructs or reinforces a relationship dynamic, rather than merely describing it.
width.typical: Analyse a text (e.g. a speech, social media post, classroom exchange) and explain how multiple language choices work together to empower particular roles or relationships, using metalanguage appropriately.
wider: Compare how the same relationship is constructed differently across two texts from different cultural or historical contexts
Analyse how First Nations Australian language use in literature creates empowerment through connection to Country and cultural knowledge, rather than through dominance
Examine how disrupting expected language norms can challenge established power relationships

modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate understanding of community membership, role construction and the active/constitutive function of language into a single analytical move. The integration — language doesn't just reflect power, it creates it — is the core insight of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Indirect evaluation devices
descriptors.description: understand how evaluation can be expressed directly and indirectly using devices such as allusion, evocative vocabulary and metaphor
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise evaluative language and understand how evaluations are substantiated by textual evidence (AC9E7LA02). They have not yet examined how evaluation can be embedded indirectly through literary devices that position readers without explicit appraisal language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how evaluation is expressed both directly and indirectly through devices including allusion, evocative vocabulary and metaphor.

nodes.label: Direct vs indirect evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between evaluations expressed directly (explicit appraisal language) and those embedded indirectly through word choice and framing.
criteria: Student identifies at least one direct and one indirect evaluation in a text
Student explains how indirect evaluation positions the reader without using explicit appraisal terms
nodes.hinge_reason: The direct/indirect distinction is a prerequisite for N2 and N3 — students who cannot identify indirect evaluation cannot analyse evocative vocabulary or metaphor as evaluative devices at those nodes.

width.minimum: Identify one example of direct evaluation and one of indirect evaluation in a text, and explain how they differ in the way they communicate the author's position.
width.typical: Compare direct and indirect evaluation across two text types (e.g. editorial and advertisement, podcast and poem), explaining how each mode positions the reader differently.
wider: Analyse how advertising deliberately avoids direct evaluative claims while using indirect devices to position consumers
Compare the evaluative intensity of direct versus indirect appraisal in political speech, examining which is more persuasive and why

modes.reason: Students default to identifying explicit evaluative language ('great', 'terrible') and miss indirect embedding. Comparing diverse text types — especially non-literary ones like advertisements — reveals the fuller range of how evaluation works.

nodes.label: Evocative vocabulary as evaluative device
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how evocative vocabulary choices embed evaluation — directing readers' views without stating an explicit appraisal.
criteria: Student identifies evocative vocabulary and explains the connotations that make the evaluation implicit
Student explains how the word choice directs the reader's view without making the evaluation explicit

width.minimum: Identify evocative word choices in a text and explain how they guide the reader's evaluation of a person, place or idea.
width.typical: Analyse how a range of evocative vocabulary choices in a text work together to build an implicit evaluative position, drawing on examples from print, editorial, talkback or podcast contexts.
wider: Compare evocative vocabulary in texts covering the same event from different publication contexts (broadsheet vs tabloid, mainstream vs community media)
Examine how similes used in evaluative contexts carry embedded judgement through the connotations of the vehicle term

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of evocative vocabulary examples across contexts to understand this as a systematic device rather than an occasional stylistic choice. Range across text types matters here.

nodes.label: Metaphor and allusion as evaluative devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how metaphor and allusion express evaluation by importing connotations from outside the immediate text to position readers toward particular interpretations.
criteria: Student identifies a metaphor or allusion and names the associations it activates
Student explains how those associations constitute an implicit evaluation of a person, event or idea

width.minimum: Identify a metaphor or allusion in a text and explain how it embeds evaluation through the associations it activates.
width.typical: Analyse how metaphor and allusion work as evaluative devices in at least two text types, explaining how the imported associations direct the reader's appraisal.
wider: Analyse how sustained metaphors in editorials or long-form journalism construct an evaluative framework throughout a text
Examine how allusions to shared cultural or literary references position readers who recognise them versus those who don't, as a mechanism of cultural evaluation
Compare how First Nations Australian authors may use allusion to Country and cultural knowledge as evaluative framing in ways that position readers differently

modes.reason: The evaluative function of metaphor is not self-evident — students need a reasoning scaffold to move from 'this is a metaphor' to 'this metaphor imports these connotations which direct the reader toward this evaluation'. The chain from vehicle to association to evaluative effect needs explicit modelling.

This node integrates all three indirect devices — allusion, evocative vocabulary, metaphor — as related members of the same evaluative toolkit. Students are assembling a coherent understanding of indirect evaluation as a system.

descriptors.title: Adapting and subverting text structures
descriptors.description: examine how authors adapt and subvert text structures and language features by experimenting with spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements, and their combination
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify and describe how text structure and language features vary by purpose (AC9E7LA03). They have not yet examined how authors deliberately adapt or subvert expected structures for artistic or rhetorical effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how authors adapt and subvert text structures and language features through experimentation with spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements.

nodes.label: Expected vs adapted structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when an author has adapted a conventional text structure and describe what the expected structure would have been.
criteria: Student names the conventional structure for the genre
Student identifies at least one structural feature that the text has adapted or departed from
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate the conventional structure have no baseline against which to identify adaptation or subversion at N2 and N3 — they cannot explain the effect of deviation without knowing what was deviated from.

width.minimum: Identify one text that departs from conventional structure for its genre and describe what the conventional structure looks like.
width.typical: Compare two texts in the same genre (e.g. two short stories, two feature articles) where one follows convention and one adapts it, explaining how each makes different structural choices.
wider: Examine how digital and multimodal texts (e.g. interactive journalism, social media narratives) extend or adapt print conventions
Analyse how non-linear narrative structures in short fiction create different reading experiences from linear structures

modes.reason: Students need exposure to a range of conventional structures before they can recognise adaptation. Building a repertoire of 'what the convention looks like' in different genres is prerequisite to analysing deviation.

nodes.label: Purpose and effect of structural adaptation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine why an author adapts structure and explain the purpose and effect of the structural choice on the reader.
criteria: Student explains why an author may have chosen a non-standard structure for this text and context
Student identifies a specific effect the structural choice has on the reader or the text's meaning

width.minimum: Examine one structural adaptation (e.g. non-linear narrative, subverted opening) and explain its purpose and effect on the reader.
width.typical: Analyse structural adaptations across at least two text types, explaining both the purpose of each adaptation and its effect on meaning or reader response.
wider: Compare how the same structural device (e.g. in medias res opening, fragmented timeline) is used for different purposes across different genres
Examine how public texts such as feature articles use structural experimentation in their opening paragraphs to position readers, and evaluate the effect of these choices

modes.reason: Students often describe structural features without connecting them to purpose and effect. The reasoning chain 'structural choice → authorial purpose → reader effect' needs explicit scaffolding — especially for the move from describing what is unusual to explaining why and to what end.

nodes.label: Subversion across modes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how authors subvert conventions by experimenting with the combination of spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements.
criteria: Student identifies which conventions are being subverted and in which mode(s)
Student explains the effect of the subversive choice on the text's meaning or audience experience

width.minimum: Examine a multimodal text and identify how it subverts or experiments with the combination of at least two modes (e.g. spoken and visual, written and image), explaining the effect.
width.typical: Analyse how structural subversion operates across spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements in a range of texts, including how the combination itself becomes the subversive device.
wider: Analyse how spoken word poetry or performance poetry subverts the conventions of both written poetry and spoken language simultaneously
Examine how digital storytelling experiments with navigation and reader agency as a structural subversion of linear narrative

modes.reason: Examining subversion across modes requires students to coordinate understanding of conventions in multiple modes simultaneously — written, spoken, visual — and recognise that the combination itself can be the subversive move. This integration is harder than analysing each mode separately.

descriptors.title: Cohesion through nominalisation and connectives
descriptors.description: investigate a range of cohesive devices that condense information in texts, including nominalisation, and devices that link, expand and develop ideas, including text connectives
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how cohesion devices including overviews and paragraph structure guide readers (AC9E7LA04). They have not yet examined nominalisation as a condensing device or the range of text connectives that signal logical relationships between ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how nominalisation condenses information and how text connectives link, expand and develop ideas across extended texts.

nodes.label: Text connectives and logical relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify text connectives and explain the logical relationship each signals — conclusion, reason, expansion, condition.
criteria: Student identifies at least three text connectives in a text and categorises the logical relationship each signals
Student explains how the connectives shape the reader's understanding of how ideas are linked

width.minimum: Identify text connectives in an argument or explanation and explain the logical relationship each signals (e.g. causal, conditional, additive).
width.typical: Investigate how text connectives structure an argument's logic across a full text — sequencing, supporting and qualifying claims — using examples including 'therefore', 'moreover', 'since', 'because', 'if … then'.
wider: Compare how the same logical relationship is signalled differently in academic versus journalistic texts (e.g. formal connectives vs implicit logical flow)
Analyse how a writer's choice of connective can shade the logical force of a claim (e.g. 'however' vs 'nevertheless' vs 'despite this')

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of connective types (causal, conditional, additive, contrastive, conclusive) to see text connectives as a system rather than isolated vocabulary items. Recognition across diverse texts is the goal.

nodes.label: Nominalisation as condensing device
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify nominalisations and explain how they condense prior information into a noun phrase that advances the text's argument or explanation.
criteria: Student identifies a nominalisation and states what process or clause it condenses
Student explains how condensing allows the text to carry that information forward as an established premise

width.minimum: Identify at least two nominalisations in a text and explain what information each condenses and how this allows the text to move forward.
width.typical: Investigate nominalisation across academic and technical texts, analysing how abstract nouns condense clauses or arguments, distil information and allow the text to treat that information as a given as it develops.
wider: Compare nominalisations in scientific and humanistic writing, examining differences in how each discipline uses condensing to build knowledge
Analyse how nominalisation can obscure agency and examine the ideological implications of this choice in journalism or political discourse

modes.reason: Nominalisation is hard to see in familiar contexts because it feels natural. Exposure to academic and technical texts from different disciplines helps students recognise nominalisation as a systematic device rather than an occasional quirk. Cross-discipline examples resolve the 'is this even a device?' confusion.

nodes.label: Cohesive devices as a system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how nominalisation and text connectives work together as a cohesive system, allowing extended texts to develop complex arguments while maintaining coherence.
criteria: Student explains how a nominalisation and a connective in the same text jointly contribute to cohesion
Student shows how the devices allow the text to carry an argument or explanation across multiple paragraphs

width.minimum: Explain how nominalisation and at least one connective type work together in a text to condense and link ideas across paragraphs.
width.typical: Investigate how a range of cohesive devices — nominalisation, text connectives, and their interaction — work together to sustain and develop an argument or explanation across an extended text.
wider: Analyse a complex argumentative text to map how nominalisations are introduced, carried and linked across sections, tracing the cohesive architecture of the whole
Compare the cohesive density of a student text with a published text, identifying where cohesive devices are underused and what effect this has on coherence

modes.reason: The final node requires students to see nominalisation and text connectives as coordinated devices that together achieve cohesion — not independent items on a checklist. The integration of how condensing and linking work together is the analytical target.

descriptors.title: Creative sentence variation for effect
descriptors.description: identify how authors vary sentence structures creatively for effects, such as intentionally using a dependent clause on its own or a sentence fragment
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how complex and compound-complex sentences elaborate, extend and explain ideas (AC9E7LA05). They have not yet examined how authors deliberately violate sentence conventions as a creative device.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how authors use intentional structural violations — dependent clauses as sentences, sentence fragments, interrupting clauses — to achieve deliberate effects.

nodes.label: Identifying intentional structural violations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between unintentional sentence errors and deliberate structural violations used for effect.
criteria: Student identifies a structural violation and names the type (fragment, stand-alone dependent clause, interrupting clause)
Student provides a reason for treating it as intentional (e.g. author, publication context, consistency of device, effect achieved)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish intentional from erroneous violations cannot analyse effects at N2 and N3 — they have no principled basis for treating a fragment as a device rather than a mistake to ignore.

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of a deliberate structural violation (fragment or dependent clause used as a sentence) and explain why it is intentional rather than an error.
width.typical: Identify and distinguish intentional sentence fragments, stand-alone dependent clauses, and interrupting clauses in published texts, explaining the markers that signal deliberate rather than erroneous use.
wider: Compare how structural violations in literary fiction versus advertising create different effects — and different conventions about when violation is acceptable
Examine how spoken language conventions (incomplete sentences, interruptions) are imported into written texts for particular effects

modes.reason: The concept of intentional violation is confusing for students who have been taught that fragments are 'wrong'. Multiple contexts — literary, advertising, journalism — each have different tolerance for structural violation and different effects. Breadth across contexts resolves the apparent rule-violation confusion.

nodes.label: Effect of sentence fragments and stand-alone clauses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how sentence fragments and stand-alone dependent clauses create specific effects — emphasis, rhythm, voice, immediacy.
criteria: Student identifies the structural violation and names a specific effect it creates
Student explains how the effect connects to the surrounding text — not just the fragment in isolation

width.minimum: Identify a sentence fragment or stand-alone dependent clause and explain the specific effect it creates (e.g. emphasis, pause, urgency).
width.typical: Analyse how fragments, stand-alone dependent clauses and their placement in the surrounding prose create effects of emphasis, rhythm or voice in literary or persuasive texts.
wider: Compare the effect of a fragment at the start versus end of a paragraph, and analyse how position interacts with the device
Examine how fragments are used differently in first-person narrative versus third-person, and what this reveals about voice and reader positioning

modes.reason: Students who can identify fragments still often produce generic effect labels ('it creates tension'). Comparing fragment effects across different positions and genres — and examining what changes and what stays constant — builds the analytical precision needed to move beyond generic effect labelling.

nodes.label: Interrupting clauses and their effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how interrupting clauses (embedded inside another clause) create effects of qualification, digression, intimacy or irony.
criteria: Student identifies an interrupting clause (naming the outer and inner clause structure)
Student explains a specific effect the interruption creates — not just that it 'adds detail'

width.minimum: Identify an interrupting clause in a text and explain how its placement within another clause creates a specific effect on pace, voice or meaning.
width.typical: Analyse how interrupting clauses are used across literary and informational texts to create qualification, digression, intimacy or irony, explaining the effect of the interruption on reader experience.
wider: Compare how the same type of interrupting clause (e.g. parenthetical aside) creates very different effects in fiction versus formal academic writing
Examine how writers use interrupting clauses to mimic the rhythms of thought or spoken language in stream-of-consciousness or first-person narrative

modes.reason: This node completes the set — fragments, stand-alone clauses, interrupting clauses — as a coordinated toolkit of intentional sentence variation. Students are building an integrated understanding of structural violation as a legitimate authorial resource, not three separate tricks.

descriptors.title: Abstract nouns and nominalisation for condensing
descriptors.description: understand how abstract nouns and nominalisation can be used to summarise ideas in text
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how complex and compound-complex sentences elaborate, extend and explain ideas (AC9E7LA05). They have encountered nominalisation as a cohesive device (AC9E9LA04). They have not yet focused specifically on how abstract nouns and nominalisation function to summarise and carry forward prior ideas within a text.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how abstract nouns and nominalisation summarise ideas, structure arguments and allow texts to treat prior content as an established premise.

nodes.label: Abstract nouns as summary references
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify abstract nouns used to summarise prior text content and explain what they compress.
criteria: Student identifies an abstract noun used as a summary reference
Student explains what prior text content it compresses into the noun phrase
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify abstract nouns as summary references cannot understand N2 — the argument-structuring function of nominalisation depends on first seeing that noun phrases carry condensed prior content. Without N1, the process→thing transformation at N2 has no conceptual anchor.

width.minimum: Identify two abstract nouns in an academic or informational text (e.g. 'the previous argument', 'the prologue') and explain what content each compresses from earlier in the text.
width.typical: Analyse how abstract nouns in academic and technical texts function as backward-pointing summary references, distilling earlier explanations into a single noun phrase that can be treated as established.
wider: Compare how abstract nouns function differently in scientific texts versus literary criticism — and what this reveals about how different disciplines build knowledge
Examine how the absence of abstract summary nouns affects the coherence of student writing, using concrete examples

modes.reason: Abstract nouns used as summary references are common in academic and technical texts but uncommon in everyday writing. Students need exposure across disciplines to see this as a systematic knowledge-building device rather than incidental usage.

nodes.label: Nominalisation as argument structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how nominalisation structures an argument by transforming processes into things that can be positioned, qualified and built upon.
criteria: Student identifies a nominalised form and states the process verb it derives from
Student explains what grammatical advantage the nominalised form gives the writer (e.g. positioning as subject, adding qualifier, advancing the argument)

width.minimum: Identify a nominalised form in an argument (e.g. 'the destruction of' instead of 'destroying') and explain how treating the process as a noun-thing advances the argument.
width.typical: Analyse how nominalisations structure an argument in an academic or informational text, tracking how transformed processes become the objects of further reasoning.
wider: Compare two versions of the same paragraph — one with nominalisations, one with verb forms — and analyse the effect on argumentative density and register
Examine how nominalisation in political or bureaucratic texts can obscure who is doing what, and evaluate the effect on accountability

modes.reason: The grammatical transformation (process → thing) is abstract. Students need the reasoning scaffold: verb form → nominalised form → what this allows the sentence to do next. Without this chain, students see nominalisations as vocabulary choices rather than structural ones.

descriptors.title: Symbols in still and moving images
descriptors.description: analyse how symbols in still and moving images augment meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how vectors, angle and social distance in visual texts create perspective (AC9E7LA07). They have not yet examined how symbols within images augment meaning through cultural or conventional associations that extend beyond what is literally depicted.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how symbols in still and moving images augment meaning, including how symbolic meanings differ across groups and cultures.

nodes.label: Symbols as meaning beyond the literal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify visual symbols in images and explain the meanings they carry beyond their literal depiction.
criteria: Student identifies a visual symbol and names a meaning it contributes beyond its literal presence
Student connects the symbolic meaning to a cultural or conventional association that grounds it
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify symbols as culturally constructed meanings cannot analyse how the same symbol varies across still versus moving image contexts at N2 — they have no framework for the meaning-augmentation concept.

width.minimum: Identify at least one visual symbol in a still or moving image (e.g. a season, colour, weather element) and explain the additional meaning it contributes beyond its literal presence.
width.typical: Analyse how specific seasons, weather and colours function as conventional symbols in a range of still images, films and picture books, evaluating what meanings they contribute to viewer understanding.
wider: Compare how the same visual symbol (e.g. water, fire, white) carries different connotations across cultural contexts, identifying where meanings converge and diverge
Examine how symbols from First Nations Australian art encode cultural knowledge, where the same symbol may have multiple layered meanings or different meanings across different Nations/communities

modes.reason: Students default to Western conventional symbolism (white = purity, red = danger) and miss cross-cultural variation. Exposure to diverse cultural contexts — particularly First Nations Australian visual symbolism — reveals that symbolic meaning is culturally constructed, not universal.

nodes.label: Symbols augmenting meaning across image types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how symbols augment meaning differently in still versus moving images, explaining how context and sequence affect symbolic interpretation.
criteria: Student analyses how a symbol augments meaning in at least one image type (still or moving)
Student explains how the medium (still vs moving) affects how the symbolic meaning is conveyed or accumulated

width.minimum: Analyse how a symbol in a still image augments meaning, then compare with how the same or similar symbol works in a moving image where sequence and context add further layers.
width.typical: Analyse how symbols augment meaning across both still and moving images, explaining how the temporal dimension of moving images — sequence, juxtaposition, duration — changes how symbols accumulate or transform meaning.
wider: Analyse how a film uses a recurring symbol across its duration, tracing how the symbol's meaning evolves through accumulation and contextual shift
Compare how the same cultural symbol is used in still advertisement images versus moving film contexts, examining how medium shapes symbolic interpretation

modes.reason: Analysing symbols across still and moving images requires students to coordinate understanding of static symbolism with the temporal logic of moving images (repetition, transformation, juxtaposition). The integration — how a symbol's meaning is augmented differently by medium — is the analytical target.

descriptors.title: Vocabulary choices for style, mood and tone
descriptors.description: analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to style, mood and tone
descriptors.knowledge: Students investigate how vocabulary builds specialist knowledge, including terms with everyday and technical meanings (AC9E7LA08). They have not yet analysed how vocabulary choices create a text's distinctive style, mood and tone as interconnected qualities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to style, mood and tone in texts.

nodes.label: Vocabulary and tone
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify vocabulary choices that create a specific tone and explain how the connotations of those choices produce that tone.
criteria: Student identifies specific vocabulary choices and names a tone they contribute to
Student explains how the connotations of those words produce the named tonal quality

width.minimum: Identify vocabulary choices in a text that create a recognisable tone (e.g. sarcastic, reverent, anxious) and explain how the connotations of specific words produce that tone.
width.typical: Analyse how a range of vocabulary choices across a text consistently build a tone, explaining how individual word connotations accumulate into a tonal effect.
wider: Compare how the same subject is treated with different tonal registers in two texts (e.g. a news report vs a satirical piece), and explain what vocabulary shifts produce the tonal difference
Examine how a sarcastic tone is constructed through the gap between vocabulary connotation and implied meaning

modes.reason: Tone is easy to perceive but hard to analyse — students often say 'the tone is sarcastic' without being able to connect it to specific vocabulary features. Multiple text types with contrasting tones help students build the analytical vocabulary for naming how tone is made.

nodes.label: Vocabulary and mood
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how vocabulary choices create and sustain mood — the emotional atmosphere of a text — and distinguish mood from tone.
criteria: Student identifies vocabulary choices contributing to mood and names the mood created
Student distinguishes mood from tone in at least one example — explaining the difference between the atmosphere experienced and the author's attitude
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate mood (reader atmosphere) and tone (author attitude) produce systematically muddled style analyses at N3 — the vocabulary/style node requires the mood/tone distinction to be operative.

width.minimum: Identify vocabulary choices that create a recognisable mood in a text and explain how they create that atmosphere for the reader.
width.typical: Analyse how vocabulary choices across a passage create and sustain mood, distinguishing mood (the atmosphere created for the reader) from tone (the author's attitude).
wider: Analyse how mood shifts are created through vocabulary change within a text, and examine what effect these shifts have on reader response
Compare how mood is created through vocabulary in a written text versus a moving image — examining whether visual and verbal mood-making use equivalent or different devices

modes.reason: Students routinely conflate mood with tone or with character emotion. Seeing mood created across different text types — narrative, poetry, film — where neither the author's attitude nor a character's feeling is the primary effect helps students secure the distinct concept.

nodes.label: Vocabulary and style
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to an author's distinctive style — the recognisable patterns of language use that characterise their writing.
criteria: Student identifies vocabulary features that contribute to a recognisable style
Student explains how the vocabulary choices are effective for this text's purpose and audience

width.minimum: Identify vocabulary features that contribute to a text's style and explain how they characterise that text's distinctive voice or manner.
width.typical: Analyse how vocabulary choices across a text contribute to its stylistic effectiveness — including how the vocabulary's register, precision, rhythm and connotative range define a recognisable style.
wider: Compare the vocabulary styles of two texts by the same author and identify consistent stylistic features that mark authorial identity
Examine how an author's vocabulary style serves their purpose — why a particular style is effective for this text's context and audience

modes.reason: Style, mood and tone are interconnected — a text's vocabulary choices produce all three simultaneously. The integration node asks students to coordinate their understanding of all three into a unified analysis of how vocabulary choices contribute to a text's overall effect.

descriptors.title: Punctuation for referencing and citing
descriptors.description: understand punctuation conventions for referencing and citing others for formal and informal purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how colons and brackets support meaning (AC9E7LA09). They have not yet examined the punctuation conventions specific to referencing and citation — how to integrate others' words and ideas into their own writing with appropriate attribution.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand punctuation conventions for referencing and citing others in formal and informal contexts, including when to use direct quotation and when to report sources.

nodes.label: Direct quotation conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply punctuation conventions for integrating direct quotations into their own writing.
criteria: Student correctly punctuates direct quotations including quotation marks and integration punctuation
Student attributes quotations to their source appropriately
nodes.hinge_reason: Quotation punctuation errors are systemic in formal writing tasks — students who haven't secured the conventions at N1 produce incorrectly formatted citations throughout their assessed analytical writing.

width.minimum: Apply correct punctuation for at least two direct quotations in a piece of writing, including quotation marks, attribution and any necessary punctuation for integration.
width.typical: Apply punctuation conventions for direct quotations across a range of integration contexts — introducing, interrupting and following up quotations in essays, reviews and academic assignments.
wider: Compare how different citation conventions (e.g. APA, MLA, Chicago) handle the punctuation of direct quotation, and explain why standardisation matters in academic contexts
Examine how journalistic quotation conventions differ from academic ones, and what this reveals about different relationships to source attribution

modes.reason: Quotation punctuation is a precision skill — students know the rules in isolation but errors accumulate under compositional pressure. Practice embedding quotations in their own writing matters more here than conceptual breadth.

nodes.label: When to quote vs paraphrase or report
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain when direct quotation is appropriate versus paraphrasing or general source reporting, and apply this judgment in their writing.
criteria: Student makes an attribution choice (quote vs paraphrase) and can explain the reasoning
Student's written attribution correctly signals the relationship between their own ideas and the source

width.minimum: Make and justify one decision to use a direct quotation and one decision to paraphrase or report a source, explaining the reasoning for each choice.
width.typical: Apply and explain decisions about quoting directly versus paraphrasing or reporting sources across a formal writing task, justifying each attribution choice based on purpose and context.
wider: Analyse how over-quoting weakens an argument in student essays, and develop principles for deciding when the author's exact words add value vs when paraphrase serves better
Compare attribution practices in academic writing versus opinion writing, and examine what different conventions reveal about the relationship between writer and source

modes.reason: The judgment about when to quote directly requires explicit reasoning criteria that students rarely develop spontaneously. A scaffold (does the exact wording matter? is the authority of the source relevant? does paraphrase lose something important?) helps students make principled rather than habitual decisions.

descriptors.title: Representations of people and places across contexts
descriptors.description: analyse the representations of people and places in literary texts, drawn from historical, social and cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify and explore ideas, viewpoints and issues in literary texts across historical, social and cultural contexts (AC9E7LE01). They have not yet analysed how representations of people and places are constructed — examining the choices authors make and what those choices reveal about context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how representations of people and places in literary texts reflect and are shaped by historical, social and cultural contexts, across First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Representation as construction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that representations of people and places in literary texts are constructed — the product of authorial choices — not neutral or natural.
criteria: Student identifies authorial choices (not just character attributes) in the representation
Student connects at least one choice to a likely contextual influence (historical, cultural, social)
nodes.hinge_reason: The shift from 'the character is like this' to 'the author has constructed this character this way' is prerequisite for N2 — analysing how context shapes representation only makes sense if representations are already understood as constructed choices.

width.minimum: Identify two choices an author has made in representing a character or place and explain what those choices suggest about the author's perspective or context.
width.typical: Analyse how an author's choices construct a representation of a person or place, examining vocabulary, characterisation and narrative framing as constructed rather than transparent.
wider: Compare two representations of the same type of person or place (e.g. rural Australia, an immigrant community) from different time periods, examining how the construction differs

Examine how First Nations Australian authors construct representations that reflect unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing, and contrast with representations in mainstream Australian literature

modes.reason: The conceptual shift from 'the character is like this' to 'the author has constructed the character this way, and here's why' is a genuine hinge. Students resist this shift because it feels like it undermines the reality of the story. Wider cultural and historical contexts — particularly First Nations Australian authorship — help students see that representations are perspectives, not mirrors.

nodes.label: Context shaping representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how historical, social and cultural contexts shape how people and places are represented in literary texts.
criteria: Student analyses (not just describes) a representation, connecting choices to contextual factors
Student explains how the context makes the representation meaningful — why these choices make sense in this time/place/culture

width.minimum: Analyse one text and explain how a specific contextual factor (historical period, cultural background, social values) is reflected in the representation of a character or place.
width.typical: Analyse representations of values associated with key aspects (e.g. authority, community, family) in literary texts from two or more cultural or historical contexts, explaining how context shapes the representation.
wider: Examine how a recurring Australian motif (e.g. water, landscape, belonging) is represented differently across texts from different time periods, and what this reveals about shifting cultural contexts
Compare how First Nations Australian authors represent relationships with Country/Place in ways that differ structurally from how non-Indigenous authors represent natural settings
Analyse how the same historical period is represented differently by an author writing within it versus one writing retrospectively

modes.reason: Analysing how context shapes representation requires students to coordinate literary analysis with historical and cultural knowledge. The integration — using contextual understanding to interpret representational choices — is the core analytical capability this descriptor develops.

descriptors.title: Personal response and subsequent analysis
descriptors.description: present a personal response to a literary text comparing initial impressions and subsequent analysis of the whole text
descriptors.knowledge: Students form and justify opinions about texts, identifying agreement and difference with others (AC9E7LE02). They have not yet compared their initial impressions with a developed whole-text analysis — the dialectic between first response and considered interpretation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present a personal response to a literary text that compares initial impressions with subsequent analysis of the whole text.

nodes.label: Initial response as legitimate reading
nodes.checkpoint: Students can articulate an initial response to a literary text and recognise that first impressions are a valid starting point for analysis.
criteria: Student articulates at least one specific initial response (not just a general impression)
Student connects the response to a specific textual feature rather than leaving it as an unanchored feeling
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate an initial response have nothing to compare against when asked to present the journey from first impression to analysis at N3 — the comparison is definitionally blocked.

width.minimum: Record an initial response to a literary text — including emotional reactions, questions and confusion — and explain what in the text prompted each response.
width.typical: Articulate initial impressions of a literary text including what the student found compelling, confusing or significant, connecting each response to specific textual features.
wider: Compare how different students' initial responses to the same text vary, and begin to hypothesise what textual features produce those different responses
Examine how initial responses might be shaped by the reader's cultural background or prior experiences

modes.reason: Students often have undifferentiated initial responses ('I liked/didn't like it'). Experiencing varied texts and being asked to record specific reactions — what surprised, confused or interested them — builds the repertoire of response types that makes comparison with later analysis meaningful.

nodes.label: Whole-text analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop an analysis of a complete text that interrogates and makes judgements about its ideas and interpretations.
criteria: Student develops an interpretation that uses textual evidence to support a judgement
Student's analysis demonstrates engagement with the whole text, not just the parts that produced their initial response

width.minimum: Develop an interpretation of a complete text that goes beyond initial impressions, using textual evidence to support a judgement about the text's ideas.
width.typical: Interrogate and make judgements about a text as a whole — comparing their own interpretation with others' ideas and reaching an independent or considered position about the text's meanings and value.
wider: Examine how reading a text a second time, with knowledge of the ending, changes the interpretation of earlier sections
Compare your interpretation of a text's central ideas against a published review or critical reading, explaining where you agree, where you diverge, and why

modes.reason: Moving from response to analysis requires a specific reasoning structure: from personal reaction to textual evidence to interpretation to judgement. Students need explicit scaffolding for this chain, particularly the move from 'I felt X' to 'this is produced by Y device and means Z'.

nodes.label: Comparing initial and developed response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present a personal response that explicitly compares their initial impressions with their subsequent whole-text analysis, explaining what changed and why.
criteria: Student explicitly compares an initial impression with their subsequent analysis
Student explains what the fuller analysis revealed that the initial impression could not have accessed

width.minimum: Present a response that identifies at least one way their initial impression changed after whole-text analysis, and explains what the analysis revealed that the initial impression missed.
width.typical: Present a personal response to a literary text that traces the journey from initial impressions to developed interpretation — explaining what the analysis added, complicated or confirmed, and arriving at an independent position.
wider: Examine how the process of sharing initial responses with others before detailed analysis affects subsequent interpretation — and what this reveals about reading as a social process
Reflect on a text where initial and final response are significantly different, and analyse what this reveals about the text's complexity or the reader's assumptions

modes.reason: Presenting a response that integrates initial impression and subsequent analysis — showing how one led to or was transformed by the other — requires students to hold both simultaneously and articulate the relationship. This is the core capability of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Features that influence text preferences
descriptors.description: analyse how features of literary texts influence readers' preference for texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain how literary devices and language features create character and influence emotions and opinions (AC9E7LE03). They have not yet analysed how the combination of text features shapes readers' preferences and judgements about literary value.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how features of literary texts — characterisation, setting, plot, theme and literary devices — influence readers' preference for texts.

nodes.label: Features that create preference
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific literary features that create a personal preference response and explain why those features appeal or do not appeal.
criteria: Student names specific literary features (not just 'the story') as preference-drivers
Student explains how a feature creates the preference — connecting the feature to a reading experience
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with no analytical vocabulary for literary features cannot contribute substantively to collaborative criteria-building at N2 — discussion collapses to preference assertions without feature-grounded analysis.

width.minimum: Identify at least two literary features (e.g. characterisation, pacing, setting) that contribute to your preference for or against a text, and explain how each feature shapes your response.
width.typical: Reflect on and discuss responses to literature including characterisation, setting, plot events, themes and literary devices — connecting each to factors that influence preference.
wider: Survey peer preferences for the same text and compare which features create different responses — examining whether preference factors are personal, cultural or conventional
Compare the features that create preference in a literary text versus a popular/genre text, examining what different reader communities value

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of analysable literary features to move beyond 'I liked/didn't like it'. Range of feature types — across characterisation, setting, plot, theme, device — matters before students can analyse preference with precision.

nodes.label: Collaborative analysis of literary value
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute to and benefit from collaborative discussion of literary preference, formulating shared or contested criteria for literary value.
criteria: Student contributes at least one preference factor to collaborative discussion with textual grounding
Student can articulate at least one shared or contested criterion that emerged from discussion

width.minimum: In discussion with others, compare factors that influence your preference for a text and identify at least one criterion about what distinguishes literary value that emerges from the discussion.
width.typical: Collaboratively formulate a list of factors that distinguish literary value — through discussion of characterisation, setting, plot events, themes and literary devices — recognising that criteria may vary between readers.
wider: Compare literary value criteria developed by the class with critical criteria used in published literary awards or reviews, examining overlaps and gaps
Examine how different cultural communities may hold different criteria for literary value, and what this reveals about the relationship between culture and aesthetic judgement

modes.reason: Formulating shared criteria from collaborative discussion requires students to integrate their own preference analysis with others' perspectives into provisional shared judgements. The social dimension of literary evaluation — how value is negotiated — is the integrative insight.

descriptors.title: Aesthetic qualities of authorial style
descriptors.description: analyse texts and evaluate the aesthetic qualities and appeal of an author's literary style
descriptors.knowledge: Students discuss the aesthetic and social value of literary texts using appropriate metalanguage (AC9E7LE04). They have not yet analysed and evaluated the aesthetic qualities of a specific author's literary style as a distinctive and comparably assessed set of choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate the aesthetic qualities and appeal of an author's literary style.

nodes.label: Identifying authorial style
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify features of an author's literary style — the consistent patterns of language, structure and technique that characterise their writing.
criteria: Student identifies at least two consistent stylistic features across multiple texts
Student names specific textual evidence for each stylistic feature identified
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating aesthetic quality (N2) requires a catalogue of identified stylistic features to evaluate — students who haven't built that catalogue from multiple texts have no raw material to assess at N2.

width.minimum: Identify at least three consistent stylistic features across two or more texts by the same author, explaining what each feature contributes to the author's style.
width.typical: Compare texts created by the same author to determine literary style — examining vocabulary patterns, sentence structure, narrative techniques, and thematic concerns as consistent stylistic markers.
wider: Investigate how an author's style changed over their career, and evaluate what drove the evolution
Compare an author's fiction style with their non-fiction (where available) and examine what remains consistent

modes.reason: Identifying style requires students to have accumulated enough features from enough texts to recognise patterns rather than isolated choices. Two texts minimum; three is better. Building a catalogue of features before evaluating is necessary.

nodes.label: Evaluating aesthetic qualities and appeal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the aesthetic qualities of an author's literary style — making and supporting judgements about what makes the style effective, distinctive or appealing.
criteria: Student makes a specific evaluative claim about the author's style (not just description)
Student supports the evaluation with at least two pieces of textual evidence

width.minimum: Evaluate the aesthetic appeal of one aspect of an author's style, explaining what makes it effective and how it contributes to the overall literary experience.
width.typical: Analyse and evaluate the aesthetic qualities of an author's literary style — assessing its appeal, explaining its distinctiveness, and presenting comparisons to others.
wider: Present a comparison of two authors' styles, evaluating the relative aesthetic appeal of each and arguing for a judgement about which is more effective for a particular literary purpose
Examine how cultural background and context shape what readers find aesthetically appealing in literary style — analysing where aesthetic preferences are culturally situated

modes.reason: Evaluating aesthetic quality requires students to move from 'I find this appealing' to 'this has aesthetic quality because...' — a reasoning move from subjective response to grounded evaluation. The criteria for aesthetic judgement need explicit scaffolding to produce substantiated evaluation rather than preference assertion.

descriptors.title: Complex literary devices and intertextuality
descriptors.description: analyse the effect of text structures, language features and literary devices such as extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextual references
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify and explain how literary devices create layers of meaning in texts including poetry (AC9E7LE06). They have not yet analysed the more complex devices that operate across whole texts or invoke meaning from outside the text — extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextuality.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse the effect of text structures, language features and literary devices including extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextual references.

nodes.label: Extended metaphor and allegory
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify extended metaphor or allegory in a literary text and explain how the sustained comparison or parallel narrative generates meaning across the whole text.
criteria: Student identifies the vehicle of the extended metaphor/allegory and the tenor it represents
Student explains how at least two details of the text derive meaning from the extended comparison
nodes.hinge_reason: Extended metaphor and allegory are the foundational devices — students who cannot identify sustained figurative layering at N1 have no basis for analysing symbolism, metonymy or intertextuality at N2 and N3, which all depend on recognising that literary meaning operates beyond the literal.

width.minimum: Identify an extended metaphor or allegory in a text and explain how the extended comparison generates meaning that a single metaphor could not.
width.typical: Analyse how extended metaphor or allegory structures meaning across a text — examining how the sustained vehicle shapes interpretation of individual details and the overall significance.
wider: Compare how two texts use allegory for different purposes (e.g. political critique, moral instruction, psychological exploration) and evaluate the effect of each
Examine how identifying an extended metaphor or allegorical layer changes interpretation of a text previously read as literal

modes.reason: Extended metaphor and allegory are easy to recognise in obvious examples (Animal Farm) but hard to identify in more subtle texts. Multiple examples across genres — prose, poetry, film — help students develop a flexible pattern for what sustained figurative layering looks like.

nodes.label: Symbolism and metonymy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how symbols and metonymy create meaning in literary texts by substituting part for whole, or associating object with concept.
criteria: Student identifies a symbol or metonymic usage and names the concept or whole it represents
Student explains the specific meaning-effect the device creates — not just labels it

width.minimum: Identify a symbol or metonymy in a literary text and explain the meaning it creates through association rather than direct statement.
width.typical: Analyse how symbolism and metonymy operate in a range of literary texts — identifying imagery, examining examples of authors' use of devices to create meaning, and explaining the effect on audiences.
wider: Compare how the same symbol carries different meanings across cultural contexts — examining where symbolic meanings are shared and where they diverge
Analyse how a poet's use of metonymy creates compressed meaning by asking what the part stands for and what it omits

modes.reason: Symbols and metonymy are easiest to recognise in explicit literary examples but harder to spot in subtler texts. Encountering them across poetry, prose and visual contexts builds pattern recognition that prevents students from treating each instance as isolated rather than as a device type.

nodes.label: Intertextual references
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify intertextual references in literary texts and explain how they augment meaning by invoking associations from another text or tradition.
criteria: Student identifies an intertextual reference and names the source text or tradition being invoked
Student explains the specific meaning-effect that the intertextual reference creates in this text

width.minimum: Identify an intertextual reference in a literary text and explain what meaning it imports from the referenced text or tradition.
width.typical: Analyse how intertextual references — literary, cultural, mythological or historical — contribute to meaning in literary texts, explaining both what is imported and what effect the invocation has on the reader's interpretation.
wider: Examine how intertextual references create a two-tier reading experience — accessible to readers who recognise the reference, different for those who don't — and evaluate the implications for audiences
Analyse how a text subverts or ironises an intertextual reference, creating meaning through the gap between original and adaptation

modes.reason: Recognising intertextual references requires a repertoire of cultural, literary and mythological knowledge. Students with wider reading can identify more references — this is a strand where the width of prior reading directly enables the analytical work.

Intertextuality integrates all the complex device analysis — extended metaphor, allegory, symbol, metonymy can all be deployed intertextually. The final node coordinates the range of complex devices as a system of meaning-making tools that operate across texts.

descriptors.title: Create and edit experimental literary texts
descriptors.description: create and edit literary texts, that may be a hybrid, that experiment with text structures, language features and literary devices for purposes and audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit literary texts experimenting with language features and literary devices (AC9E7LE07). They have not yet created hybrid texts that experiment specifically with text structures, or focused editing on structural integration of experiments.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and edit literary texts, including hybrids, that experiment with text structures, language features and literary devices for purposes and audiences.

nodes.label: Experimenting with text structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a literary text that makes a deliberate structural experiment and can explain what the experiment is intended to achieve.
criteria: Student makes at least one identifiable structural experiment in the text
Student can articulate what effect the structural experiment is intended to create
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have only experienced linear prose structures default to them — without a repertoire of structural options, 'experimentation' at N1 is impossible, and N2 editing for structural coherence has nothing to edit.

width.minimum: Create a short literary text that makes one deliberate structural experiment (e.g. non-linear timeline, subverted genre opening, hybrid form) and explain the purpose of the choice.
width.typical: Create and draft a literary text that experiments with at least one text structure element and one language feature or device, explaining how the choices serve purpose and audience.
wider: Create a text that adapts an existing short story, poem, play or speech into a different form (e.g. print to short film, poem to spoken word piece), examining what is preserved and what must change
Experiment with prequel or sequel writing as a form of textual intervention — examining how the original text constrains and enables the new one

modes.reason: Creative experimentation requires a repertoire of structural options to choose from. Students who have only experienced linear prose structures will default to them. Building familiarity with a range of structural possibilities — non-linear, hybrid, genre-subversive — enables genuine experimentation.

nodes.label: Editing for structural and device coherence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit a literary text to ensure that structural experiments, language features and devices work together coherently, including checking that repetition and detail are purposeful.
criteria: Student's edited text shows evidence of deliberate revision decisions (not just surface error correction)
Student can identify at least one editing decision that improved the text's coherence or the effectiveness of an experiment

width.minimum: Edit a draft literary text to address at least one coherence issue — checking that detail or repetition is purposeful, that paragraphs are linked, and that run-on sentences are controlled.
width.typical: Edit a literary text by checking for run-on sentences, ensuring detail and repetition are used for effect, ensuring paragraphs are linked in ways that develop the narrative, and ensuring that structural and device experiments serve rather than undermine the text.
wider: Engage in peer editing with attention to whether another writer's experiments are achieving their stated purpose — developing evaluative criteria for creative editing
Edit across multiple drafts and reflect on what each round of editing reveals about the gap between intention and effect

modes.reason: Editing is a precision skill — students can understand the principles but need practice under compositional conditions. Editing for structural and device coherence (not just error correction) requires fluency with both the craft and the revision process.

Effective editing requires students to coordinate attention to grammar, structure, devices and audience simultaneously — holding the text's purpose in mind while attending to local decisions. This is the most demanding compositional capability of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Representations reflect contexts
descriptors.description: analyse how representations of people, places, events and concepts reflect contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain how current technology affects reading, creating and responding to texts (AC9E7LY01). They have not yet analysed systematically how representations across media reflect the contexts in which they are produced.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how representations of people, places, events and concepts in texts reflect the contexts in which those texts are produced.

nodes.label: Representations vary across contexts
