nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how representations of people, places or events vary across texts from different contexts and explain what produces the variation.
criteria: Student identifies at least two representations of the same subject from different contexts
Student explains at least one contextual factor that produces the difference in representation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat representations as accurate-or-inaccurate (rather than contextually positioned) cannot analyse language features as context-reflective devices at N2 — the N2 analytical task presupposes representations are understood as constructed.

width.minimum: Identify two representations of the same person, place or event from different contexts (e.g. different publications, time periods or cultural positions) and describe how they differ.
width.typical: Examine how representations of public figures in media vary across different contexts — identifying specific differences in language, emphasis and framing, and explaining what contextual factors might produce them.
wider: Compare how a news event is represented in media from different national contexts, examining how national perspective shapes framing
Analyse how the same historical figure is represented differently across texts from different time periods, tracing how changing social values shape the representation

modes.reason: Students often treat representations as either accurate or inaccurate, missing the contextual logic that makes each representation coherent in its own terms. Multiple contexts — across time, culture, publication type — are essential for the insight that all representations are contextually positioned.

nodes.label: Analysing language features in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how specific language features are used to represent individuals or groups in ways that reflect the text's context.
criteria: Student analyses specific language features (not just general register) used to represent a person or group
Student connects the language choices to at least one contextual factor — not just noting that the text is old or comes from a different culture

width.minimum: Analyse how language features (e.g. word choice, grammar, framing) are used in a text to represent a person or group in a particular way, and connect the choices to the text's context.
width.typical: Analyse language features used across texts from different time periods to represent individuals or groups — identifying how language choices shift with changing contexts and what this reveals about the relationship between language and social values.
wider: Analyse how language that was normalised in historical texts to represent a group is recognised as problematic today, examining what this reveals about how contexts shape representation

Compare the representation of the same concept (e.g. 'progress', 'freedom') across texts from different political or cultural contexts, examining how the same word carries different representational freight

modes.reason: Analysing how language features reflect context requires students to integrate language analysis (specific features, choices) with contextual understanding (historical period, publication context, social values). These two competencies need to be coordinated rather than applied sequentially.

descriptors.title: Analyse how language positions listeners
descriptors.description: listen to spoken texts that have different purposes and audiences, analysing how language features position listeners to respond in particular ways, and use interacting skills to present and discuss opinions regarding these texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students use interaction skills to discuss and present ideas, evaluating features of spoken texts (AC9E7LY02). They have not yet analysed how language features specifically position listeners — the mechanism through which spoken texts direct response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students listen to spoken texts, analyse how language features position listeners to respond in particular ways, and use interaction skills to present and discuss opinions about those texts.

nodes.label: How language positions listeners
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language features in a spoken text that position listeners toward particular responses and explain the positioning mechanism.
criteria: Student identifies a language feature in a spoken text
Student explains how that feature positions the listener — naming the expected or likely response it encourages
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain the positioning mechanism of a language feature cannot present a grounded opinion about a spoken text at N2 — they can only describe the text, not analyse how it acts on listeners.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language features in a spoken text (e.g. inclusive pronouns, emotive language, stereotypes) and explain how each positions the listener to respond in a particular way.
width.typical: Analyse how language features in spoken texts — including stereotype creation, emotive language and speaker positioning devices — direct listeners toward particular responses.
wider: Compare how the same topic is positioned differently for listeners in two spoken texts from different contexts (e.g. a community radio program versus a commercial broadcast)
Examine how podcasts use para-linguistic features alongside language to create intimacy and position the listener as an in-group member

modes.reason: The mechanism of positioning — how a language feature makes a listener more likely to respond in a particular way — is abstract. Students need a reasoning scaffold: feature → mechanism → listener effect. Without this chain, students describe the feature without explaining the positioning.

nodes.label: Presenting and discussing opinions about spoken texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use interaction skills to present and discuss opinions about spoken texts, including speaking clearly, presenting a reasoned opinion and responding to others.
criteria: Student presents an opinion about a spoken text with at least one specific piece of evidence
Student demonstrates at least one interaction skill (e.g. responding to another's view, inviting others' contributions, building on a point)

width.minimum: Present an opinion about a spoken text, including at least one specific language feature as evidence, speaking clearly for an appropriate length of time.
width.typical: Use effective dialogue and discussion strategies in formal and informal contexts — presenting opinions about spoken texts with specific evidence, listening to and responding to others' views, and speaking with clarity and appropriate pacing.
wider: Conduct a formal discussion of a spoken text using structured dialogue protocols, evaluating how the structure itself affects the quality of opinion exchange
Compare how the same opinion about a text lands differently when presented orally versus in writing — examining what the spoken mode adds or limits

modes.reason: Oral discussion skills require repeated practice under real discussion conditions. The skills — speaking clearly, responding to others, maintaining coherence under conversational pressure — develop through practice, not conceptual extension.

descriptors.title: Evaluate perspective representation through language
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate how language features are used to represent a perspective of an issue, event, situation, individual or group
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how language features shape meaning and vary according to audience and purpose (AC9E7LY03). They have not yet evaluated language features as perspective-representing devices — moving from describing what features do to evaluating how effectively they represent a perspective.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate how language features represent perspectives on issues, events, situations, individuals or groups.

nodes.label: Language features as perspective devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how specific language features represent a perspective — identifying the choices and explaining the perspective they embed.
criteria: Student identifies a language feature and names the perspective it represents
Student explains how the feature represents the perspective — not just that it 'shows the author's opinion'
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating representation at N2 requires being able to identify which language features represent a perspective and how — students who haven't built this analytical move have no basis for evaluative judgement beyond personal agreement or disagreement.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language features in a text and analyse how each represents a particular perspective on the text's subject.
width.typical: Analyse how language features across a text work together to represent a perspective — examining how language in news and social media coverage of a contentious issue is used to convey opinions and represent ideas.
wider: Compare language features across coverage of the same contentious issue in two media contexts with different editorial positions
Examine how language features in inspirational or advocacy speeches position the audience toward a perspective — identifying techniques that influence listener response

modes.reason: Perspective representation is easiest to see in obviously biased texts. Students need to encounter subtler uses — in news reporting, in ostensibly neutral descriptions — to understand that all language represents perspective, not just intentionally persuasive texts.

nodes.label: Evaluating perspective representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how effectively or fairly language features represent a perspective — making and supporting judgements about language choices as representational tools.
criteria: Student makes a supported evaluative judgement about a language choice as a representation tool
Student's evaluation goes beyond agreeing or disagreeing with the perspective — it assesses how the language works as representation

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one language choice as a representation tool — making a judgement about whether it represents the perspective fairly, effectively or misleadingly, and supporting the judgement with evidence.
width.typical: Evaluate how language features are used to represent perspectives across a range of text types — comparing campaign speeches, journalism and social media, and making supported judgements about the effectiveness and fairness of representational choices.
wider: Evaluate how language in a historical text represents a group in ways that are now recognised as problematic, and assess the impact of such representations
Examine advocacy speeches from films or media and evaluate how language features influence the listener — assessing both effectiveness and ethical dimensions of the techniques used

modes.reason: Evaluating language representation requires criteria for judgement — students need reasoning scaffolds for what makes a representation fair, effective or misleading. Without criteria, evaluation collapses into agreement or disagreement with the perspective rather than analysis of the representation.

descriptors.title: Evaluate idea organisation and its impact
descriptors.description: analyse the organisation of ideas in paragraphs and extended texts, and evaluate its impact on meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain how ideas are structured using taxonomies, cause and effect, metaphors and chronology (AC9E7LY04). They have not yet evaluated the impact of organisational choices on meaning — moving from describing organisation to assessing its effectiveness.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse the organisation of ideas in paragraphs and extended texts and evaluate its impact on meaning.

nodes.label: Techniques for organising ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify organisational techniques used in texts and explain what each technique does to the reader's experience of the ideas.
criteria: Student names an organisational technique and explains its function (not just describes the content sequence)
Student identifies how the technique shapes what the reader experiences — not just what information is present
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating impact at N2 requires named technique types — students without a repertoire of organisation techniques evaluate by intuition rather than evidence, which means the N2 evaluative judgement cannot be substantiated.

width.minimum: Identify at least two organisational techniques in a text (e.g. juxtaposition, chronological reversal, exaggeration) and explain what each does to the arrangement of ideas.
width.typical: Analyse the techniques used in extended texts to organise ideas — examining comparison, contrast, exaggeration, juxtaposition, chronological manipulation, and expansion/compression of time.
wider: Compare how two texts covering the same event use different organisational techniques and assess which arrangement is more effective for their respective purposes
Examine how a text's organisation creates emotional effects — analysing how the sequence of information is designed to evoke particular responses

modes.reason: Students need a repertoire of organisational technique names and functions to analyse organisation at the level of choice rather than just sequence. Building this repertoire across diverse text types enables the evaluative work at node 2.

nodes.label: Evaluating impact on meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the impact of organisational choices on meaning — making judgements about whether the arrangement conveys meaning effectively and supporting those judgements.
criteria: Student makes a specific evaluative claim about an organisational choice (not just describes it)
Student supports the evaluation with reference to the text's purpose and the effect on meaning or reader response

width.minimum: Evaluate the impact of one organisational choice in a text — making a supported judgement about whether it effectively conveys meaning.
width.typical: Evaluate techniques used in texts to organise ideas and evoke emotional responses — explaining whether the author conveys meaning effectively through the sequence of information and evidence, and making supported judgements.
wider: Reorder a section of a text and evaluate how the reorganisation changes the meaning or emotional impact — using the exercise to illuminate the effect of the original choices
Evaluate the organisational coherence of a student text and provide targeted feedback on one structural improvement

modes.reason: Evaluating organisational impact requires criteria — students need scaffolding for what makes an arrangement effective (does it serve the purpose? does it lead the reader through the argument? does it create the intended effect?). Without criteria, evaluation is preference rather than analysis.

descriptors.title: Compare ideas across texts using comprehension strategies
descriptors.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring to compare and contrast ideas and opinions in and between texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies including inferring to analyse and summarise information and ideas (AC9E7LY05). They have not yet deployed strategies specifically to compare and contrast ideas and opinions across multiple texts simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use comprehension strategies to compare and contrast ideas and opinions in and between texts.

nodes.label: Comprehension strategies for comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and apply comprehension strategies specifically for the purpose of comparing ideas and opinions within and across texts.
criteria: Student applies at least two named comprehension strategies and explains how each supported comparison
Student identifies at least one similarity and one difference between ideas or opinions in the texts compared
nodes.hinge_reason: Cross-text comparison at N2 depends on being able to deploy multiple strategies flexibly — students defaulting to one strategy produce shallow comparisons that miss the multiple dimensions needed for the descriptor's comparison task.

width.minimum: Apply at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. summarising, questioning, inferring) to compare ideas or opinions in two texts, explaining how each strategy supported the comparison.
width.typical: Apply a range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring — to compare and contrast visual representations, print and digital sources, and current event representations.
wider: Develop a comparison protocol: which strategies are most useful for comparing visual versus verbal texts, and why?
Apply comprehension strategies to compare texts with conflicting interpretations of the same event, evaluating the quality of the evidence each presents

modes.reason: Students often default to one or two favoured comprehension strategies. Building a full repertoire of all seven named strategies — and matching strategy to comparison purpose — expands the analytical toolkit for cross-text comparison.

nodes.label: Comparing and contrasting across texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast ideas and opinions in and between texts, identifying positions, evaluating evidence and summarising the relationship between them.
criteria: Student identifies specific ideas or opinions from each text and explains how they compare
Student's comparison goes beyond listing — it explains what the similarities and differences reveal about the texts' positions or purposes

width.minimum: Compare ideas or opinions from two texts on the same topic, identifying how they are similar, how they differ, and what the difference reveals about the texts' positions.
width.typical: Compare and contrast representations of an event in print and digital sources — summarising qualities, identifying opinions and analysing evidence — and compare articles representing a current event, contrasting ideas and opinions across texts.
wider: Compare visual representations of the same issue across online news sources and evaluate how the visual choices support or contradict the verbal argument
Compare three or more texts on the same issue and map the ideological positions they represent — evaluating whether any positions are absent

modes.reason: Cross-text comparison requires students to hold multiple texts in mind simultaneously, coordinate their respective positions, and synthesise a view of their relationship. This integration — across texts, modes and positions — is the core challenge of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Create critical written and multimodal texts
descriptors.description: plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising, expanding and developing ideas, and selecting text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features for purposes and audiences in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical and/or critical
descriptors.knowledge: Students plan, create and publish texts selecting structures, language features and literary devices for purpose (AC9E7LY06). They have not yet developed analytical and critical text types, or focused on multi-element selection across structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts selecting text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features for purposes and audiences across imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical and critical modes.

nodes.label: Planning and structuring for analytical/critical purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a written text with an argument structure: contention, sequenced supporting points and conclusion.
criteria: Student's plan includes a clear contention and at least two supporting points that develop a line of argument
Student can explain how the planned structure serves the argument's purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot produce a planned argument structure with contention and linked supporting points cannot attempt N2 text creation — the creation task presupposes an understood structural scaffold to populate with language and device choices.

width.minimum: Plan and draft a text with a clear contention, at least two sequenced supporting points and a conclusion — demonstrating that the structure serves the argument.
width.typical: Plan and develop an argument with a contention followed by a series of linked and sequenced paragraphs that develop a line of argument, ending with a conclusion that summarises the main argument.
wider: Plan a complex argument that includes acknowledgement and refutation of a counter-position, evaluating how this strengthens the argument structure
Compare effective planning strategies across text types — argument, analysis, explanation — identifying what changes and what stays the same

modes.reason: Argument structure is a reasoning scaffold as much as a text structure. Students who understand what a contention, supporting point and conclusion do — not just what they are — can plan arguments that actually argue. The logical architecture needs explicit modelling.

nodes.label: Creating with selected language and device choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts selecting appropriate text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features for their specific purpose and audience.
criteria: Student makes at least two deliberate selection decisions (structure, language, device or multimodal) and can explain why
Student's text demonstrates — not just states — the intended purpose and audience awareness

width.minimum: Create a text that makes deliberate selections of at least one structural and one language/device choice, and can explain why each choice suits the purpose and audience.
width.typical: Create informative or analytical texts with well-chosen facts and precise language; or imaginative/persuasive texts with deliberate literary and structural device selections; discussing literary device choices and evaluating their potential effects on an audience.
wider: Create a text that deliberately subverts a conventional structure for this text type, and evaluate the effect of the subversion on purpose and audience
Create a multimodal text and evaluate how the multimodal choices expand or complicate what could be achieved in written mode alone

modes.reason: The descriptor names four simultaneous selection dimensions: text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features. Coordinating deliberate selections across all four — rather than making one choice at a time — is the compositional integration this node targets.

nodes.label: Editing and publishing for accuracy and effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit written and multimodal texts for grammatical accuracy, spelling and punctuation, and to improve clarity and organisation for specific purposes and audiences.
criteria: Student corrects at least one accuracy error and makes at least one effectiveness revision
Student can explain the reasoning for at least one revision decision

width.minimum: Edit a draft text addressing at least one accuracy issue (grammar, spelling or punctuation) and one effectiveness issue (clarity, organisation, or device choice), explaining the reasoning for each revision.
width.typical: Review and edit texts for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and to achieve particular purposes and address specific audiences — improving clarity and control through organising, developing, extending and linking ideas.
wider: Develop a personal editing checklist calibrated to your own known error patterns, and apply it to produce a publishable draft
Peer-edit a classmate's text and provide targeted feedback on both accuracy and effectiveness — distinguishing between non-negotiable errors and matters of style

modes.reason: Editing requires mechanical fluency — the ability to attend to accuracy while also holding the text's purpose in view. Students improve through repeated editing practice across different text types, not through additional conceptual instruction.

descriptors.title: Plan and deliver analytical presentations
descriptors.description: plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations for purpose and audience, using language features, literary devices and features of voice such as volume, tone, pitch and pace, and organising, expanding and developing ideas in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical and/or critical
descriptors.knowledge: Students plan, create and deliver presentations selecting structures, devices and voice features for purpose and audience (AC9E7LY07). They have not yet developed analytical and critical spoken modes, or deliberately coordinated literary devices, language features and voice features simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations using language features, literary devices and voice features for purposes and audiences across analytical and critical modes.

nodes.label: Planning for spoken analytical and critical purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a spoken presentation with a clear structure that develops and expands ideas analytically or critically for a specific audience.
criteria: Student produces a plan with a clear purpose and structure suited to the spoken form
Student can explain at least one planning decision in terms of what the audience needs
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot plan a spoken text for audience cannot meaningfully rehearse voice features at N2 — without a planned structure there is nothing to rehearse against, and delivery at N3 is unfocused.

width.minimum: Plan a spoken presentation with a clear purpose, a structure that develops ideas, and deliberate selection of at least one text structure suited to the purpose.
width.typical: Plan a spoken presentation that organises, expands and develops ideas — selecting text structures and adapting literary devices to meet the needs of the audience when debating, presenting a seminar or creating a voiceover.
wider: Compare planning strategies for a formal seminar versus a debate — identifying what structural choices differ and why the audience and form demand different organisation
Plan a collaborative imaginative recreation of a text or key idea, identifying how collaboration requires explicit structural negotiation

modes.reason: Planning analytical spoken texts requires students to reason about how ideas should be organised for an audience that cannot re-read. The reasoning scaffold — what the audience needs to hear first, how to signal transitions, how to use voice to mark structure — differs from written planning and needs explicit modelling.

nodes.label: Rehearsing voice features for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can rehearse a presentation using voice features — volume, tone, pitch and pace — for specific effects and can articulate the relationship between voice choice and purpose.
criteria: Student demonstrates deliberate variation of at least one voice feature in delivery
Student can explain the intended effect of at least one voice feature choice

width.minimum: Rehearse a section of a presentation varying at least one voice feature (volume, tone, pitch or pace) for effect, and explain what effect the variation is intended to create.
width.typical: Select voice features — tone, volume, pitch and pace — for their specific effects to create tone or persuade an audience, demonstrating deliberate rehearsal decisions.
wider: Compare how the same words land differently with different voice feature choices — conducting a side-by-side rehearsal and evaluating the effect
Analyse how professional speakers (e.g. in the elaboration examples: news voiceovers, debates) use voice features, and evaluate which choices could be transferred to a student presentation

modes.reason: Voice feature control develops through rehearsal practice. Students know conceptually that pace and tone create effects but the skill of deploying them consistently under performance conditions requires rehearsal repetition, not additional conceptual knowledge.

nodes.label: Delivering with integrated multimodal and language choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation that integrates language features, literary devices, voice features and multimodal elements for purpose and audience.
criteria: Student delivers a presentation that demonstrates deliberate integration of at least two of the four element types
Student can evaluate the success of at least one integrative choice — did it serve the purpose and audience?

width.minimum: Deliver a presentation that integrates at least two of the four elements (language features, literary devices, voice features, multimodal elements) in ways that serve the purpose.
width.typical: Deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation integrating language features, literary devices, voice features and multimodal elements — including graphics, text animations or images to accompany and influence viewer response.
wider: Deliver a news-style current affairs presentation that uses images with spoken text to influence viewer response, then evaluate how effectively the multimodal combination achieved the purpose
Collaborate with peers to deliver an imaginative recreation of part of a text — evaluating how the group's delivery decisions collectively represent the key idea

modes.reason: Delivery integrates all four elements simultaneously under performance conditions. Coordinating language choices, device deployment, voice features and multimodal elements while maintaining audience connection is the fullest expression of the descriptor's demand.

descriptors.title: Spelling for stylistic effect
descriptors.description: understand how spelling is used in texts for particular effects; for example, characterisation, humour and to represent accents and distinctive speech
descriptors.knowledge: Students use spelling rules and word origins including Greek and Latin roots to learn and spell new words (AC9E7LY08). They have not yet examined spelling as a deliberate authorial device used for characterisation, humour and accent representation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how spelling is used deliberately in texts to create effects including characterisation, humour and representation of accents and distinctive speech.

nodes.label: Spelling as characterisation device
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify deliberate spelling variations used to represent character speech and explain the characterisation effect they create.
criteria: Student identifies a deliberate spelling variation and names the characterisation effect it creates
Student explains how the spelling variation represents spoken features (accent, dialect, distinctiveness) that standard spelling would mask

width.minimum: Identify at least one example where an author has varied spelling to represent a character's speech and explain what the variation reveals about the character.
width.typical: Analyse how authors drop letters or use non-standard spelling to emulate the sound of spoken words, examining what the spelling choices contribute to characterisation — accent, dialect, education level, personality.
wider: Compare how different authors represent similar accents through spelling — examining the range of conventions and what is gained or risked by each approach
Examine the ethics of using non-standard spelling to represent a character's speech, considering who makes such choices and what effects they have on readers from that community

modes.reason: The intent-versus-error distinction is the central challenge here — students need to see that deliberate spelling variation is an authorial choice, not a mistake. Multiple author examples across genres and character types help resolve this.

nodes.label: Spelling for humour and neologism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how unconventional spelling is used in media texts for humour or to create neologisms, and explain the effect.
criteria: Student identifies a spelling effect (humour, neologism, accent) and names what creates it
Student explains how the unconventional spelling generates its effect — why it works rather than just noting that it does

width.minimum: Identify a neologism or humorous spelling in a media text and explain what effect the unconventional spelling creates.
width.typical: Analyse how spelling is used in media texts such as online posts for humour and neologism creation — examining how spelling variation signals register, in-group knowledge and cultural currency.
wider: Trace how a digital neologism ('selfie', 'binge-watch', 'photobomb') entered mainstream usage, examining how its spelling and form stabilised or shifted
Compare how intentional misspelling functions in advertising versus social media — examining what different communities accept and why

modes.reason: Neologism and humorous spelling are most visible in digital and media texts that students already encounter. Seeing multiple examples across online posts, advertising and social media — where spelling deviation is normalised for different purposes — builds the analytical habit of asking what the non-standard spelling is doing, not just noting it.

descriptors.title: Punctuation and capital letters
descriptors.description: identify punctuation as a feature of written text different from letters; recognise that capital letters are used for names, and that capital letters also signal the beginning of sentences while punctuation marks signal the end
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise some letters and have encountered written text. They have not yet been asked to distinguish punctuation marks from letters or to understand the systematic roles of capital letters and end-of-sentence punctuation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can identify punctuation marks as distinct from letters, recognise capital letters in names and at sentence beginnings, and identify end-of-sentence punctuation marks — understanding that these are consistent, rule-based conventions in written English.

nodes.label: Punctuation is not letters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify punctuation marks in a text and distinguish them from letters.
criteria: Student can reliably point to punctuation marks and identify them as distinct from letters.
Student can name at least one punctuation mark by name (e.g. full stop, question mark).
nodes.hinge_reason: Without reliably distinguishing punctuation from letters, students cannot identify what capital letters or end punctuation marks are — both Nodes 2 and 3 depend on punctuation marks being already separated from the letter system.

width.minimum: Point to at least one punctuation mark in a written text and say it is not a letter.
width.typical: Identify punctuation marks as distinct features of written text; sort punctuation marks from letters across several familiar examples; begin to name common punctuation marks.
wider: Collect and classify all punctuation marks encountered in a class text — grouping them and counting how many of each type appear
Explore punctuation marks in digital texts — including emoji — and discuss which ones follow the same rules as print punctuation

modes.reason: Students need reliable letter–punctuation discrimination as a prerequisite for all subsequent print literacy. This is a precision skill: errors (treating punctuation as letters) cascade into reading and writing. Practice with a range of texts is the remedy.

nodes.label: Capital letters signal names and sentence starts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify capital letters used for names and at the beginning of sentences, and explain the rule behind each use.
criteria: Student can identify a capital letter used for a name and say why it is capitalised.
Student can identify a capital letter at the start of a sentence and say why it is capitalised.
Student can explain that capital letters follow rules — they are not placed randomly.

width.minimum: Identify a capital letter in a familiar word and say why it is capitalised (name, or start of sentence).
width.typical: Recognise that capital letters are used for proper names (people, places, school names); recognise that capital letters signal the beginning of sentences; identify these in everyday and classroom texts.
wider: Investigate capital letters across a wide range of text types — books, signs, labels, digital texts — and confirm consistency of the rules
Compare own name, classmates' names, the school name and the class name — noting that the capital letter rule applies consistently
Explore how capital letters appear in other alphabetic writing systems and compare with English conventions

modes.reason: The two uses of capitals (names and sentence starts) can be confused — students may think only one rule exists. Multiple contexts showing both uses, alongside consistent exceptions (mid-sentence common nouns), help build a complete schema.

nodes.label: Punctuation signals sentence endings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify end-of-sentence punctuation marks (full stop, question mark, exclamation mark) and understand that they signal the end of a sentence.
criteria: Student can identify a full stop, question mark and exclamation mark in a text.
Student can explain that each of these signals the end of a sentence.
Student can use a full stop in their own writing at the end of a sentence.

width.minimum: Identify a full stop in a text and say that it means the sentence has ended.
width.typical: Identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks as sentence-end signals; recognise the rule that punctuation marks — not new lines — signal sentence endings; apply this in reading and beginning writing.
wider: Compare sentences ending with different punctuation marks and discuss how each affects how the sentence is read or spoken
Investigate how punctuation functions differently in digital informal writing (texts, posts) vs formal written texts
Sort sentences by end punctuation type and read each aloud — exploring how punctuation signals prosody

modes.reason: Students may know full stops but not question marks or exclamation marks as sentence-enders — each requires its own contextual exposure before the general 'punctuation ends sentences' concept is robust.

descriptors.title: Recognise rhyme, alliteration and phonemes
descriptors.description: recognise and generate rhyming words, alliteration patterns, syllables and sounds (phonemes) in spoken words (phonological awareness)
descriptors.knowledge: Students may have heard rhymes and songs. They have not yet been asked to consciously attend to, name and generate the phonological patterns in spoken words — rhyme, alliteration, syllables and phonemes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and generate rhyming words, identify alliteration patterns, identify syllables in spoken words, and isolate phonemes — demonstrating phonological awareness across multiple word types.

nodes.label: Rhyming words share endings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a rhyming pair and produce a rhyming word when given a target.
criteria: Student can identify whether two words rhyme when heard.
Student can generate at least one rhyming word when given a target word.
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable rhyme recognition signals that phoneme-level auditory discrimination is developing — without this, phoneme isolation in Node 4 and the blending and segmenting tasks in LY10 will be unreliable, as they all depend on the ability to hear and attend to sounds within words.

width.minimum: Identify whether two words rhyme; generate one word that rhymes with a given word.
width.typical: Recognise and produce rhyming words; identify rhyming patterns in familiar stories and rhymes; generate rhyming strings.
wider: Generate rhyming strings across multiple word families — exploring how many words share the same rime
Compare rhyming conventions in English with other languages or First Nations Australian language patterns known to students
Create simple rhyming couplets orally — applying rhyme generation to creative language play

modes.reason: Reliable rhyme recognition and production is foundational to phonological awareness — errors here indicate the phoneme-level awareness needed for decoding is not yet secure. Practice across many word pairs is the remedy.

nodes.label: Alliteration is repeated initial sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify alliteration patterns in spoken words — recognising that initial sounds repeat.
criteria: Student can identify two words that start with the same sound.
Student can produce at least one alliterative phrase orally.

width.minimum: Identify an alliteration pattern in two words (e.g. 'helpful Henry').
width.typical: Identify alliteration patterns in spoken words and familiar texts; produce simple alliterative phrases; understand that alliteration is about the initial sound, not the initial letter.
wider: Create alliterative name phrases for each class member — exploring alliteration productively
Identify alliteration in poems, picture book titles and tongue twisters across a range of texts
Compare alliteration in English with sound-play patterns in other languages

nodes.label: Words have syllables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the number of syllables in spoken words by clapping, tapping or counting.
criteria: Student can clap the correct number of syllables in a spoken word.
Student correctly distinguishes one-syllable and two-syllable words.

width.minimum: Correctly identify the number of syllables in at least five words of varying length (one to three syllables).
width.typical: Identify syllables in spoken words by clapping or tapping; segment multi-syllable words; understand that every syllable contains a vowel sound.
wider: Clap syllables across names of class members, local area names and topic words — exploring syllable patterns in real vocabulary
Compare syllable counts in familiar words across different languages — noting that syllable structure differs across languages
Sort word cards by syllable count — building a syllable-based word awareness

nodes.label: Words are made of phonemes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can isolate individual phonemes in spoken words — hearing the discrete sounds that make up a word.
criteria: Student can isolate the first phoneme in a spoken word.
Student can isolate the final phoneme in a spoken CVC word.
Student understands that words are made of more than one sound.
nodes.hinge_reason: Phoneme isolation is a prerequisite for blending and segmenting in LY10 — students cannot blend phonemes they cannot yet isolate, and cannot segment words into phonemes they cannot hear as discrete units.

width.minimum: Identify the first phoneme in at least three spoken words.
width.typical: Recognise individual phonemes in spoken words; isolate initial, medial and final phonemes; understand that words are made of discrete sounds.
wider: Practise phoneme isolation across a range of word types — varying initial, medial and final positions
Compare phonemes in English words with sounds in other languages or names familiar to students — noticing sounds that English does and doesn't have
Use phoneme awareness as a bridge to letter-sound knowledge — connecting isolated phonemes to their grapheme representations

modes.reason: Phoneme isolation is a prerequisite for blending and segmenting (AC9EFLY10) — without reliable phoneme isolation, decoding will be unreliable. Practice to accuracy is required before width is productive.

descriptors.title: Inclusive and exclusive language effects
descriptors.description: understand how language can have inclusive and exclusive social effects, and can empower or disempower people
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise how language empowers relationships and roles (AC9E9LA01). They have not yet analysed the inclusive/exclusive social effects of language — how it can empower or disempower people through alignment, inclusion and marginalisation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how language can have inclusive and exclusive social effects, and can empower or disempower people.

nodes.label: Alignment and distancing devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language devices that seek to align or distance the listener/reader, including inclusive pronouns and assumptive phrases.
criteria: Identifies specific language devices (pronoun choices, assumptive phrases) that seek to align or distance an audience
Explains the intended social effect of at least one alignment device on a specified audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to identify language that references shared assumptions — a concept built on understanding how alignment devices position readers as insiders or outsiders. Without this, shared assumption analysis has no linguistic basis.

width.minimum: Identify at least two alignment devices (e.g. ‘of course’, ‘we’) in a provided text and explain the intended effect on the audience.
width.typical: Identify and explain a range of alignment and distancing devices across print and multimodal texts, explaining how each positions the audience as insider or outsider.
wider: Analyse alignment devices across texts from different political or cultural contexts, comparing how ‘we’ and ‘you’ function differently in each
Examine how digital texts (social media posts, comment threads) use alignment language to construct in-group identity
Investigate how First Nations Australian speakers or writers use pronoun and alignment strategies in advocacy or community contexts

modes.reason: Students commonly assume alignment is always intentional and positive; encountering texts where alignment devices are used to exclude or manipulate broadens understanding of how these devices function across contexts.

nodes.label: Shared assumptions and cultural knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language that references shared assumptions and appeals to shared cultural knowledge, values and beliefs, and explain its inclusive or exclusive effect.
criteria: Identifies language that references or assumes shared cultural knowledge or values
Explains the inclusive effect on one audience group and the potentially exclusive effect on another
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to analyse how language empowers or disempowers people — a move that depends on understanding how shared assumption and exclusion operate. Students who cannot identify assumed cultural knowledge will miss the mechanism through which disempowerment occurs.

width.minimum: Identify one example of language appealing to shared cultural knowledge in a provided text and explain who is included and who may be excluded.
width.typical: Analyse how texts use references to shared cultural knowledge, values and beliefs to construct insider and outsider positions, across at least two different text contexts.
wider: Compare how texts targeting different cultural communities deploy different shared knowledge assumptions, examining what is taken for granted in each
Analyse examples where assumed shared knowledge marginalises particular groups — such as gendered or culturally specific references in media texts
Examine how First Nations Australian community communications draw on shared cultural knowledge to create solidarity and speak past mainstream gatekeeping

modes.reason: The inference required — identifying what is assumed rather than stated — needs explicit scaffolding for most students; the reasoning move from ‘what the text says’ to ‘what the text assumes’ is the core challenge here.

nodes.label: Empowerment and disempowerment through language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how language choices can empower or disempower people, identifying examples of marginalising or inclusive language and explaining their social effects.
criteria: Identifies specific language that empowers or disempowers people in a given text
Explains the social effect of the language choice on the people named or referenced, with reference to context

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of language that is inclusive or marginalising in a provided text and explain the social effect on the people named or referenced.
width.typical: Analyse how language in a range of texts empowers or disempowers people, considering how naming, labelling and inclusion/exclusion choices shape social effects across different contexts.
wider: Compare how empowering and disempowering language has been used historically and currently in relation to the same group — e.g. changing language around disability, First Nations identity, or gender
Examine political or media texts to trace how language choices have been used to disempower particular groups, and evaluate the social consequences
Analyse how communities have reclaimed previously marginalising language as an act of empowerment

modes.reason: Whether language is empowering or disempowering is highly context-dependent; students need to encounter multiple contexts to understand that the same word or phrase can have opposite effects depending on who uses it and in what setting.

This node integrates the alignment devices and shared assumptions from nodes 1–2 with broader social analysis — students coordinate their linguistic analysis with awareness of power and social context.

descriptors.title: Evaluative language reveals values
descriptors.description: understand that language used to evaluate, implicitly or explicitly reveals an individual’s values
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how evaluation is expressed directly and indirectly through allusion, vocabulary and metaphor (AC9E9LA02). They have not yet examined how evaluative language — whether implicit or explicit — reveals the underlying values of the person using it.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand that language used to evaluate, implicitly or explicitly, reveals an individual’s values.

nodes.label: Explicit evaluation and values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify explicit expressions of evaluation and explain what values are revealed by the word choices made.
criteria: Identifies explicit evaluative language in a text
Names the value revealed by at least one evaluative word or phrase and explains the connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to identify implicit evaluation — a harder inference that depends on first being able to recognise and trace explicit evaluation to values. Without this foundation, the move to implicit detection is unsupported.

width.minimum: Identify at least one explicit evaluative statement in a provided text and explain what value it reveals about the writer or speaker.
width.typical: Analyse explicit evaluative language across a range of texts (reviews, speeches, opinion pieces), identifying the values revealed and explaining how word choice signals those values.
wider: Compare explicit evaluative language across texts from different time periods or cultural contexts, examining how the values revealed differ
Analyse how evaluative language in media reviews or editorials reveals institutional as well as individual values
Examine how First Nations Australian writers use explicit evaluation to assert cultural values in public texts

modes.reason: Evaluative language signals values differently across text types — what counts as an explicit evaluative statement in a review differs from a speech or a social media post; students need varied contexts to build reliable identification.

nodes.label: Implicit evaluation and hidden values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify subtle or implied evaluative language and explain the values it reveals, including how labelling and word choice communicate attitude without stating it explicitly.
criteria: Identifies an example of implicit or subtle evaluation in a text
Explains what value is implied by the language choice without the text stating it explicitly

width.minimum: Identify one example of implicit evaluation in a text (e.g. use of a label like ‘teenager’ rather than a person’s name) and explain the value it implies.
width.typical: Analyse how implicit evaluation operates through labelling, word choice, and framing in a range of texts, explaining the values revealed without being stated.
wider: Compare implicit evaluation in texts representing the same event or person from different perspectives — e.g. news reports from different outlets — to identify how different values shape the framing
Examine how political language uses implicit evaluation to position audiences without making values explicit
Analyse how implicit evaluation in texts about First Nations Australians has reflected and reinforced colonial values, and contrast with contemporary First Nations-authored texts

modes.reason: Implicit evaluation is harder to see in isolation; students need a range of examples — especially contrasting texts on the same topic — to develop the inference skill reliably.

The reasoning move from ‘what word was chosen’ to ‘what value that implies’ requires explicit scaffolding — students tend to notice explicit evaluation but miss how word choice silently signals attitude.

descriptors.title: Text structure and language feature effectiveness
descriptors.description: analyse text structures and language features and evaluate their effectiveness in achieving their purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students examine how authors adapt and subvert text structures by experimenting with multimodal elements (AC9E9LA03). They have not yet analysed and evaluated the effectiveness of text structures and language features in achieving their purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse text structures and language features and evaluate their effectiveness in achieving their purpose.

nodes.label: Identifying text structures and language features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the text structure and key language features of a text and describe how they are used.
criteria: Identifies the text structure of a provided text by name or description
Names at least two language features and describes their function in the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate the effectiveness of text structures and language features — a judgement that depends on being able to accurately identify and name those structures and features. Without this, evaluation is untethered from the text.

width.minimum: Identify the main text structure and at least two language features in a provided text and describe their function.
width.typical: Identify and describe the text structure and a range of language features across at least two text types, explaining how each is used to organise or convey meaning.
wider: Compare how the same text purpose (e.g. review, argument) is structured differently in print versus online environments
Examine how multimodal texts integrate graphics, text and sound, identifying how each mode contributes to the overall structure
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors structure texts that incorporate oral storytelling conventions

modes.reason: Accurate identification of text structures and features requires familiarity with a range of text types; students who have not encountered sufficient examples need practice across contexts before they can evaluate effectiveness.

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness in achieving purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of text structures and language features in achieving the text's purpose, making a supported judgement.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about the effectiveness of a text structure in achieving its purpose
Supports the judgement with specific evidence from text structures or language features

width.minimum: Make a supported judgement about whether the text structure and at least one language feature are effective in achieving the text’s purpose.
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of text structures and language features across different sources (e.g. reviews, multimodal texts), making a reasoned judgement with textual evidence.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of the same text transposed between media formats (e.g. print article to online version) and evaluate how the change affects purpose achievement
Evaluate texts from different cultural contexts against their stated purposes, examining how purpose is culturally shaped
Evaluate how documentary or media report structures achieve their purposes through combinations of graphics, text and sound

modes.reason: Effectiveness is relative to purpose and audience; students who only evaluate effectiveness in one context may apply a narrow or default standard — multiple contexts build understanding that the same feature may be effective in one context and not another.
Evaluation requires students to hold purpose, feature and audience in mind simultaneously — this reasoning structure needs explicit scaffolding before students can produce independent evaluations.

descriptors.title: Paragraph structure, cohesion and image integration
descriptors.description: understand how paragraph structure can be varied to create cohesion, and paragraphs and images can be integrated for different purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students investigate cohesive devices including nominalisation and text connectives (AC9E9LA04). They have not yet analysed how paragraph structure can be varied to create cohesion or how paragraphs and images integrate for different purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how paragraph structure can be varied to create cohesion, and how paragraphs and images can be integrated for different purposes.

nodes.label: Varying paragraph structure for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how authors vary paragraph structures and explain the cohesive or rhetorical effect of those variations.
criteria: Identifies a specific paragraph structure variation in a text
Explains the cohesive or rhetorical effect of the variation

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of varied paragraph structure in a text (e.g. short single-sentence paragraph, delayed topic sentence) and explain the effect.
width.typical: Examine how authors vary paragraph structures for rhetorical or cohesive effect across a range of text types, explaining what each variation achieves.
wider: Compare paragraph structure variations in literary and non-literary texts, analysing how variation serves different purposes in each
Examine how digital and online texts use unconventional paragraph structures to aid navigation and engagement
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors vary paragraph structure to incorporate oral storytelling rhythms

nodes.label: Integrating paragraphs and images for purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how paragraphs and images are integrated in texts, and explain how integration serves different purposes for different audiences.
criteria: Identifies how paragraphs and images are integrated in a specific text
Explains the purpose the integration serves for the intended audience

width.minimum: Identify how a paragraph and image are integrated in a provided text and explain the purpose of that integration.
width.typical: Examine the integration of paragraphs and images across different multimodal texts (websites, graphic novels), explaining how different integration strategies serve different purposes and audiences.
wider: Compare image-text integration in graphic novels versus news websites, evaluating how the relationship between modes creates meaning differently in each
Examine how the placement and relationship of paragraphs and images on a webpage guides reader attention and serves a navigational or persuasive purpose
Analyse how First Nations Australian visual artists integrate text and image in community or activist publications

modes.reason: Image-text integration operates very differently across text types — the relationship in a graphic novel is fundamentally different from a webpage or infographic; students need multiple contexts to understand the range of integration strategies.

descriptors.title: Sentence structures to express and craft ideas
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate the effectiveness of particular sentence structures to express and craft ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students identify how authors vary sentence structures creatively including deliberate fragments (AC9E9LA05). They have not yet analysed and evaluated the effectiveness of particular sentence structures to express and craft ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate the effectiveness of particular sentence structures to express and craft ideas.

nodes.label: Identifying deliberate sentence structure choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify deliberate sentence structure choices in texts — including passive voice, verbless clauses, and sentences beginning with conjunctions — and describe their effect.
criteria: Identifies at least one deliberate sentence structure choice by name or description
Describes the effect the structure creates in the context of the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate the effectiveness of sentence structures — a judgement that depends on being able to reliably identify and name specific structures. Students who cannot identify the structure cannot evaluate its purposeful use.

width.minimum: Identify at least one deliberate sentence structure choice (e.g. passive voice, verbless clause) in a provided text and describe its effect.
width.typical: Identify and describe a range of deliberate sentence structure choices across literary and non-literary texts, explaining how each creates a different effect.
wider: Compare how different authors use the same sentence structure (e.g. passive voice) to different effect across contexts
Examine how sentence structure choices in journalism shape how responsibility is attributed in news reports
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use sentence structure deliberately to assert voice or perspective in their texts

modes.reason: Recognition of specific sentence structure types (passive voice, verbless clause, conjunction-opening) requires practice across examples before students can reliably identify them in novel texts.

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness of sentence structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of particular sentence structures in achieving the author’s purpose, making a supported judgement.
criteria: Identifies the sentence structure and its intended effect
Makes a supported judgement about whether the structure is effective for its purpose, with textual evidence

width.minimum: Make a supported judgement about whether a specific sentence structure choice is effective in expressing or crafting an idea in a provided text.
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of a range of sentence structure choices in texts across different purposes and audiences, making reasoned judgements with textual evidence.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of active versus passive constructions in legal, scientific and journalistic texts, evaluating how each serves the text’s purpose
Evaluate how authors’ sentence structure choices shape characterisation or mood in literary texts across different genres
Examine published author interviews or commentary about their sentence-level craft choices and evaluate whether the effects claimed are achieved

modes.reason: Evaluation of sentence-level craft requires students to connect micro-level form (the structure) to macro-level effect (purpose, characterisation, persuasion) — this bridging reasoning needs explicit scaffolding.

descriptors.title: Meaning and style through syntax
descriptors.description: analyse how meaning and style are achieved through syntax
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand how abstract nouns and nominalisation summarise ideas in texts (AC9E9LA06). They have not yet analysed how meaning and style are achieved through syntax including nominalisations, clause combinations and noun group abstraction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how meaning and style are achieved through syntax.

nodes.label: Nominalisation and the construction of events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify nominalisation in texts and analyse how it affects the way events are constructed and what information is made explicit or implicit.
criteria: Identifies at least one nominalisation in a text
Explains how the nominalisation affects what information about the event or agent is made explicit or hidden
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 (clause combinations) and Node 3 (noun group abstraction) both depend on students understanding how nominalisation packages information — without this, analysis of complex clause and noun group structures has no grounding in how syntactic choice constructs meaning.

width.minimum: Identify at least one nominalisation in a provided text and explain how it affects what information about the event is made explicit or hidden.
width.typical: Analyse how nominalisation across a range of academic, journalistic or political texts constructs events, making some actors and causes explicit and others implicit.
wider: Compare how nominalisation is used in scientific texts versus political texts, analysing how each uses nominalisation to construct authority and objectivity
Examine how nominalisation in news reports can obscure agency and responsibility for events
Analyse how nominalisation functions in First Nations Australian legal or advocacy documents to establish formal register and conceptual authority

modes.reason: Nominalisation’s effect on meaning is highly context-dependent — its function in political language (obscuring agents) differs from its function in science (creating technical vocabulary); students need contrasting contexts to see the range.

nodes.label: Clause combinations and logical relations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how logical relations between ideas are built through combining independent and dependent clauses, identifying the type of logical relation expressed.
criteria: Identifies a clause combination and names the logical relation it expresses (e.g. cause, concession, condition)
Explains how the clause combination contributes to the meaning or style of the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to analyse noun group abstraction and generalisation — a move that draws on understanding how complex clause patterns package and condense ideas into nominal forms. Without clause combination analysis, Node 3 syntactic analysis lacks its prerequisite scaffolding.

width.minimum: Identify one clause combination in a provided text that expresses a logical relation (e.g. cause, concession, condition) and explain the relationship it establishes.
width.typical: Analyse how clause combinations across a range of texts build different logical relations — cause, result, concession, condition — and explain how these shape meaning and style.
wider: Compare clause combination strategies in literary and academic texts, analysing how each uses dependent clauses to build different kinds of argument or narrative logic
Examine how clause combinations in historical documents construct cause-effect relationships that shape interpretation of events
Analyse how complex clause combinations in First Nations Australian political or legal texts establish sophisticated chains of reasoning

modes.reason: Identifying the logical relation expressed by a clause combination (particularly concession and condition) requires explicit instruction in the reasoning structure — students tend to identify clauses but not the logical work they do.

nodes.label: Noun group abstraction and generalisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how abstraction in a noun group allows for generalisation of complex ideas and explain its effect on meaning and style in academic texts.
criteria: Identifies an abstract noun group in an academic or analytical text
Explains how the noun group enables generalisation and contributes to formal style

width.minimum: Identify one abstract noun group in a provided text and explain how it allows the text to generalise a complex idea.
width.typical: Analyse how noun group abstraction operates across academic and analytical texts, explaining how it enables generalisation and contributes to formal style.
wider: Compare how noun group abstraction differs between student-written and published academic texts, identifying where students struggle to achieve the generalisation that abstraction enables
Examine how abstract noun groups are used in philosophical or theoretical writing to construct conceptual frameworks
Analyse how abstraction functions differently in persuasive political texts compared with academic analysis

modes.reason: Noun group abstraction draws on both nominalisation (node 1) and clause combination patterns (node 2) — at this node students coordinate all syntactic tools to analyse how meaning and style are constructed holistically.

descriptors.title: Features of still and moving images
descriptors.description: evaluate the features of still and moving images, and the effects of those choices on representations
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how symbols in still and moving images augment meaning (AC9E9LA07). They have not yet evaluated the features of still and moving images and the effects of those choices on representations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate the features of still and moving images, and the effects of those choices on representations.

nodes.label: Visual feature identification and analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific visual features of still and moving images (e.g. lighting, angle, colour, framing) and analyse their effect on meaning.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific visual features in a still or moving image
Explains the effect of each feature on how the subject is represented
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate the effects of visual feature choices on representations — a judgement that depends on having a working vocabulary of visual features. Without this, evaluation cannot be grounded in specific technical choices.

width.minimum: Identify at least two visual features in a still or moving image and analyse the effect of each on how a subject is represented.
width.typical: Analyse a range of visual features in still and moving images across different media contexts, explaining how each feature contributes to the representation of the subject.
wider: Compare how the same visual features (e.g. high angle shot, low-key lighting) function differently in film noir, documentary and advertising contexts
Examine how visual features in news photography construct representations of events and people
Analyse how First Nations Australian visual artists use features such as light, colour and framing to create representations that challenge dominant visual conventions

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of visual feature vocabulary (shot type, angle, lighting, colour temperature, framing) before they can analyse novel images effectively — accumulating cases across image types is the pedagogical work here.

nodes.label: Evaluating effects on representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how visual feature choices create nuance in representations, making supported judgements about the effect of those choices.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about how at least one visual feature choice affects the representation of the subject
Uses specific visual evidence to support the evaluation

width.minimum: Evaluate how at least one visual feature choice (e.g. use of light and dark) creates nuance in a representation, making a supported judgement.
width.typical: Evaluate how a range of visual feature choices work together to create complex or nuanced representations in still and moving images, making supported judgements with visual evidence.
wider: Evaluate how visual feature choices in political imagery have shaped representations of power or vulnerability across different historical periods
Compare the representation of the same subject in different media (e.g. film still, news photograph, artwork) and evaluate how different visual choices construct different meanings
Evaluate how documentary filmmakers use visual features to position audiences in relation to their subjects, examining ethical dimensions of those choices

modes.reason: Students often evaluate visual features as if they have fixed meanings (e.g. ‘darkness = evil’); encountering the same feature used to different effect in different contexts resolves this misconception and builds genuine evaluative flexibility.

descriptors.title: Technical and academic vocabulary for precision
descriptors.description: use an expanded technical and academic vocabulary for precision when writing academic texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to style, mood and tone (AC9E9LA08). They have not yet applied an expanded technical and academic vocabulary for precision when writing academic texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use an expanded technical and academic vocabulary for precision when writing academic texts.

nodes.label: Recognising technical and academic vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the meaning of an increasing range of technical and academic vocabulary relevant to literary and textual analysis.
criteria: Correctly identifies the meaning of at least two technical or academic vocabulary terms in context
Can explain how the terms are used to describe specific textual features
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to use technical vocabulary with precision in their own writing — a capability that depends on first having a working recognition-level understanding of those terms. Students who cannot identify terms accurately cannot deploy them precisely.

width.minimum: Identify the meaning of at least two technical vocabulary terms relevant to literary analysis (e.g. ‘iambic pentameter’, ‘alliteration’) in context.
width.typical: Identify and explain the meaning of a range of technical and academic vocabulary across literary, grammatical and rhetorical analysis, including terms specific to poetry, prose and multimodal texts.
wider: Compare technical vocabulary across different analytical disciplines (e.g. film analysis vocabulary versus literary criticism vocabulary) to examine how field-specific terminology shapes what can be said
Examine how academic vocabulary is used differently in student writing versus published criticism — identifying where precision is achieved or where general language replaces precision
Analyse how First Nations Australian scholars and critics have developed or reclaimed technical vocabulary for analysing their own literary and cultural traditions

modes.reason: Technical vocabulary for literary and textual analysis must be accumulated across text encounters — students need to build a working repertoire of terms that they can deploy in novel analytical contexts.

nodes.label: Using technical vocabulary for precision in academic writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use an expanded technical and academic vocabulary with precision in their own academic writing, selecting terms that accurately describe textual features and effects.
criteria: Uses at least two technical vocabulary terms accurately in own analytical writing
Demonstrates that the technical term is more precise than everyday language would be in the same context

width.minimum: Use at least two technical or academic vocabulary terms accurately and precisely in a short piece of analytical writing about a text.
width.typical: Produce academic writing that consistently uses technical vocabulary to describe textual features (structural, grammatical, literary) with precision, selecting terms that are more accurate than everyday language would allow.
wider: Write analysis of a poetry text using specific prosodic terminology (iambic pentameter, caesura, enjambment) with precision, evaluating how accurate vocabulary enables more exact analysis
Compare own analytical writing before and after deliberately expanding technical vocabulary, examining where vocabulary precision strengthens argument
Write analytical response on a First Nations Australian text using both standard literary critical vocabulary and any specific terminology from First Nations critical traditions

modes.reason: Using technical vocabulary with genuine precision — not just inserting terms — requires practice across writing tasks; students commonly recognise terms but deploy them inaccurately or superficially in their own writing.

descriptors.title: Authors’ use of punctuation
descriptors.description: understand how authors use and experiment with punctuation
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand punctuation conventions for referencing and citing sources formally and informally (AC9E9LA09). They have not yet analysed how authors use and experiment with punctuation for stylistic and rhetorical effects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students understand how authors use and experiment with punctuation.

nodes.label: Punctuation for detail and extension
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how authors use specific punctuation (colons, semicolons, ellipses) to add detail, extend ideas or create particular effects in texts.
criteria: Identifies a specific punctuation mark and names the effect it creates
Explains how the punctuation choice contributes to meaning or style in the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to understand experimental and unconventional punctuation — a move that depends on understanding conventional use first. Students who cannot identify standard punctuation effects cannot recognise or evaluate deliberate departures from those conventions.

width.minimum: Identify at least one use of a specific punctuation mark (colon, semicolon or ellipsis) in a provided text and explain the effect it creates.
width.typical: Identify and explain the use of colons, semicolons and ellipses across expository and literary texts, explaining how each punctuation choice creates a different effect.
wider: Compare how the same punctuation mark (e.g. the colon) creates different effects in academic versus literary versus dialogue contexts
Examine how authors use colons and semicolons differently from the standard rules to create expressive effects in literary prose
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use punctuation experimentally to represent oral speech patterns or cultural storytelling rhythms in print

modes.reason: Recognition and explanation of specific punctuation marks (colon, semicolon, ellipsis) and their effects requires practice across examples — students need familiarity with conventional use before they can meaningfully analyse experimentation.

nodes.label: Punctuation for emotion, tentativeness and experiment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand how authors experiment with punctuation to represent emotions, create tentativeness or achieve stylistic effects, including unconventional uses.
criteria: Identifies an example of experimental or expressive punctuation in a text
Explains the intended effect of the unconventional punctuation choice
