width.minimum: Identify one example of experimental or expressive punctuation use in a text and explain the effect the author intended.
width.typical: Examine how authors use ellipses for tentativeness, multiple exclamation marks for emotion, and other unconventional punctuation for effect, across a range of literary and digital texts.
wider: Compare how digital communication contexts (social media, messaging) have expanded the expressive use of punctuation emojis and unconventional marks, and evaluate whether these are ‘experimental’ in the same sense as literary punctuation
Examine how Modernist authors (e.g. Virginia Woolf, Samuel Beckett) used unconventional punctuation as part of their literary style — compare to contemporary experimental writers
Analyse how punctuation experimentation in poetry (e.g. Emily Dickinson’s dashes) creates unique rhythm and meaning

modes.reason: Experimental punctuation looks very different in literary prose, poetry and digital communication — students who only encounter one context may think experimentation means informality rather than deliberate craft; contrasting contexts resolve this.

descriptors.title: Representations in literary texts reflect context
descriptors.description: analyse representations of individuals, groups and places and evaluate how they reflect their context in literary texts by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how people and places are represented in literary texts across historical, social and cultural contexts (AC9E9LE01). They have not yet evaluated how representations reflect the specific context in which they were produced.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse representations of individuals, groups and places and evaluate how they reflect their context in literary texts by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Analysing representations of individuals and groups
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how individuals and groups are represented in a literary text, identifying specific textual choices that construct those representations.
criteria: Identifies specific textual choices that construct the representation of at least one individual or group
Analyses how those textual choices contribute to the representation
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate representations as reflections of context — a judgement that is only coherent if students can first identify and analyse what the representation is. Thin treatment here leaves Node 2 without the analytical foundation it depends on.

width.minimum: Analyse how at least one individual or group is represented in a provided literary text, identifying specific language and structural choices that construct the representation.
width.typical: Analyse how individuals, groups and places are represented across a literary text, examining a range of textual choices and explaining how each contributes to the representation.
wider: Analyse representations of the same group (e.g. the underdog, the outsider) across multiple literary texts from different authors, comparing how the representation differs
Examine representations of First Nations Australians in texts by non-First Nations Australian authors and compare with representations in texts by First Nations Australian authors
Analyse how representations of places in literary texts construct cultural or national identity

modes.reason: Students often assume that a text's representation is neutral or obvious; encountering contrasting representations of the same group from different author positions resolves this and builds critical reading of representation.

nodes.label: Evaluating representations as reflections of context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how the representations in a literary text reflect the context in which it was produced, making a supported judgement.
criteria: Identifies the context relevant to a representation in a literary text
Makes a supported judgement about how the representation reflects that context, with textual evidence

width.minimum: Evaluate how at least one representation in a literary text reflects the social, cultural or historical context of its production, with supporting evidence.
width.typical: Evaluate how representations across a literary text reflect the context in which it was written — including social, cultural and historical context — making reasoned judgements with textual evidence.
wider: Evaluate how texts that retell or adapt traditional stories (e.g. the anti-hero, the underdog) reflect their contemporary context differently from the original
Evaluate how First Nations Australian authors contemporise or modernise traditional stories, examining what choices reflect contemporary context and what choices maintain tradition
Compare how the same event or social issue is represented in literary texts from different time periods and evaluate what each reflection reveals about its context

modes.reason: Evaluating a representation as a reflection of context requires students to hold both the text and the context in mind simultaneously and reason about the relationship — this inference structure needs explicit teaching.

descriptors.title: Extending others' interpretations of literature
descriptors.description: reflect on and extend others' interpretations of and responses to literature
descriptors.knowledge: Students present personal responses comparing initial impressions with subsequent analysis (AC9E9LE02). They have not yet reflected on and extended others' interpretations of literature.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and extend others' interpretations of and responses to literature.

nodes.label: Engaging with others' interpretations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and reflect on how others have interpreted a literary text, comparing another's interpretation with their own.
criteria: Identifies another's interpretation of a text and reflects on how it compares with their own
Can articulate at least one reason why interpretations might differ
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to extend an interpretation — a move that is only available if students have first identified and reflected on what another interpretation is and where it differs from their own. Without this, Node 2 collapses into restating a single reading.

width.minimum: Identify one interpretation of a text from a published source or peer response and reflect on how it compares with their own reading.
width.typical: Engage with multiple interpretations of a literary text (published critics, peers, class discussions), reflecting on points of agreement, difference and the reasons for different readings.
wider: Debate whether a text possesses universal qualities and consider how different reader positions produce different claims about universality
Examine critical responses to a First Nations Australian text from both First Nations and non-First Nations critics, reflecting on how reader position shapes interpretation
Research how a text's critical reception has changed over time and reflect on what changed interpretations reveal about shifting contexts

modes.reason: Students need to encounter multiple different interpretations of the same text — from peers, published critics and culturally diverse readers — before the concept that interpretations differ and why becomes visible rather than abstract.

nodes.label: Extending interpretations through close textual analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can extend an interpretation of a text by presenting arguments based on close textual analysis, going beyond initial responses.
criteria: Presents an argument based on close textual analysis that extends or deepens an interpretation
Uses textual evidence to support the extension of the interpretation

width.minimum: Present at least one argument based on close textual analysis that extends or deepens an existing interpretation of a text.
width.typical: Present a developed interpretation of a literary text, using close textual analysis to extend beyond surface readings and engage with complexity — through an essay, director's notes or similar form.
wider: Write a critical essay that synthesises personal interpretation with engagement with at least one published critical reading, extending the published reading through own analysis
Create a set of director's notes or adaptation rationale that reflects on and extends interpretive possibilities for a text
Create a personal reading list that includes texts across genres and cultures and justify how each text earns its place through close reading

modes.reason: Extending rather than merely summarising or agreeing with another's interpretation requires students to identify the limits or gaps in a reading and build from there — this moves students beyond 'I agree/disagree' into genuine analytic extension.

descriptors.title: Aesthetic qualities and audience response
descriptors.description: analyse how the aesthetic qualities associated with text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features, and the context in which these texts are experienced, influence audience response
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how features of literary texts influence reader preferences (AC9E9LE03). They have not yet analysed how aesthetic qualities, context and text features combine to influence audience response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how the aesthetic qualities associated with text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features, and the context in which these texts are experienced, influence audience response.

nodes.label: Identifying aesthetic qualities and their sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify aesthetic qualities in a literary text and trace them to specific text structures, language features, literary devices or visual features.
criteria: Identifies at least one aesthetic quality in a text
Traces that quality to a specific text feature (structural, linguistic, literary or visual)
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to analyse how context of experience shapes response — a move that depends on being able to connect features to effects. Students who cannot trace aesthetic qualities to their sources will analyse context as separate from the text rather than interacting with it.

width.minimum: Identify at least one aesthetic quality in a provided text and trace it to the specific feature (language, structural or visual) that creates it.
width.typical: Identify a range of aesthetic qualities in a literary text and analyse how different features — structural, linguistic, literary and visual — combine to produce those qualities.
wider: Compare the aesthetic qualities of texts experienced in different modes (e.g. a poem read silently versus read aloud versus set to music) and analyse how mode of experience affects aesthetic response
Examine how the aesthetic qualities of First Nations Australian texts may be constructed through features not typically foregrounded in Western literary analysis (e.g. oral performance conventions)
Analyse how the aesthetic qualities of a text change when adapted from one medium to another

modes.reason: Students tend to describe aesthetic responses ('I found it powerful') without identifying the specific features producing those responses — the reasoning from effect back to cause needs explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Context of experience and audience response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how the context in which a text is experienced shapes audience response, including how narrative position or other contextual factors affect reader sympathy or engagement.
criteria: Identifies a specific contextual factor that influences audience response to a text
Analyses how that contextual factor interacts with text features to shape the response

width.minimum: Analyse how the context of a text's reception (e.g. narrative position, audience expectation) influences how the audience responds to the text.
width.typical: Analyse how both text features and the context of experience (narrative position, audience expectations, cultural context) combine to influence audience response.
wider: Examine how the same text produces different responses in different audience contexts — e.g. comparing responses to a First Nations Australian text from First Nations and non-First Nations audiences
Analyse how a text experienced in a community or ceremonial context produces a different response than the same text read individually
Compare audience responses to a text in its original context and in a contemporary context, analysing how time and cultural shift affect response

modes.reason: The relationship between text and audience response is context-dependent — the same text features can evoke different responses in different audience contexts; students need contrasting audience contexts to understand this variability.

descriptors.title: Ethical positions and world views in literary texts
descriptors.description: evaluate literary texts from a range of contexts about ethical positions and world views that are challenged, presented, reinforced or privileged
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse texts and evaluate the aesthetic qualities and appeal of an author's literary style (AC9E9LE04). They have not yet evaluated the explicit ethical positions or world views that may be challenged or reinforced by literary texts from a range of contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate literary texts from a range of contexts about ethical positions and world views that are challenged, presented, reinforced or privileged.

nodes.label: Identifying ethical positions and world views
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the ethical positions and world views present in a literary text, distinguishing between those challenged, presented, reinforced or privileged.
criteria: Identifies at least one ethical position or world view in a literary text
Describes whether the text challenges, reinforces or privileges that position
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of ethical positions — a move that presupposes students have identified and distinguished the text's relationship to those positions. Without this, evaluation has no object.

width.minimum: Identify at least one ethical position or world view in a provided literary text and describe whether it is challenged, reinforced or privileged.
width.typical: Identify and analyse the ethical positions and world views across a literary text, explaining how the text positions each — what is challenged, what is reinforced, what is taken for granted.
wider: Compare the ethical positions presented in texts from different cultural contexts about the same issue (e.g. justice, loyalty, belonging)
Examine how First Nations Australian literary texts challenge or reframe ethical positions that are privileged in mainstream Australian literature
Analyse how a text's genre or form shapes which ethical positions it is capable of challenging or reinforcing

modes.reason: Distinguishing between positions that are challenged versus reinforced versus merely presented requires explicit reasoning scaffolding — students tend to identify positions but struggle to analyse the text's relationship to each position.

nodes.label: Evaluating ethical positions across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the ethical positions and world views in literary texts from a range of contexts, making supported judgements about the strengths and weaknesses of those positions.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about the ethical position(s) in a literary text
Evaluates at least one strength or weakness of an ethical position with reference to the text

width.minimum: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of at least one ethical position in a literary text, with supporting analysis.
width.typical: Evaluate ethical positions and world views across literary texts from different cultural, historical and social contexts, making supported judgements with reference to the text and relevant context.
wider: Evaluate conflicting ethical positions presented across two literary texts from different cultural contexts on the same issue, making a reasoned assessment of each
Examine a significant ethical issue treated in First Nations Australian literature and evaluate the position(s) the text takes, considering the cultural and political context
Evaluate how the same ethical position is treated differently across literary texts from different time periods, assessing what each treatment reveals about its historical moment

modes.reason: Evaluation of ethical positions requires students to encounter positions from outside their own cultural frame — texts from First Nations, non-Western and other diverse contexts are essential to prevent students evaluating all positions by a single cultural standard.

descriptors.title: Text features and intertextuality shape interpretations
descriptors.description: analyse how text structure, language features, literary devices and intertextual connections shape interpretations of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse the effect of complex literary devices including extended metaphor, allegory, symbolism and intertextuality (AC9E9LE05). They have not yet analysed how text structure, language features, literary devices and intertextual connections combine to shape interpretations of texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how text structure, language features, literary devices and intertextual connections shape interpretations of texts.

nodes.label: How language devices layer meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how language devices in a text layer meaning and influence the responses of listeners, viewers or readers.
criteria: Identifies at least two language devices in a text
Analyses how the devices interact to layer meaning or shape audience response
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to analyse how intertextual connections shape interpretation — a move that depends on understanding how devices layer meaning. Students who cannot coordinate multiple devices will treat intertextual references as isolated facts rather than meaning-shaping connections.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language devices in a text and analyse how they work together to layer meaning or shape a reader's response.
width.typical: Analyse how multiple language devices interact across a text to create layered meaning, examining how combinations of devices produce effects that no single device would achieve.
wider: Compare how the same literary device (e.g. extended metaphor) operates differently across poetry, prose and film, examining how medium shapes the device's effect
Examine how language devices in a satirical text shape the reader's interpretation of the issue being satirised
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use language devices to layer cultural knowledge and meaning that may not be immediately visible to all readers

modes.reason: Students need to coordinate multiple device identifications into a coherent analysis of how they interact — the challenge is not identifying individual devices but understanding how they compound and layer.

nodes.label: Intertextual connections and interpretation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how intertextual connections shape interpretations of a text, identifying how references to other texts or traditions enrich or complicate meaning.
criteria: Identifies at least one intertextual connection in a text
Analyses how the connection shapes interpretation of the text

width.minimum: Identify at least one intertextual connection in a text and analyse how it shapes interpretation of the text.
width.typical: Analyse how intertextual connections across a text — to other literary works, traditions, genres or cultural references — shape how the text can be interpreted, examining what knowledge is required to activate those connections.
wider: Examine how satirical texts use intertextual references to shape interpretation and what happens to interpretation when readers lack the referenced knowledge
Analyse how First Nations Australian literary texts create intertextual connections to traditional narratives and evaluate how those connections shape meaning differently for different readers
Compare how two texts that reference the same canonical source use that intertextual connection for different interpretive purposes

modes.reason: Intertextual analysis requires students to understand that interpretation is reader-positioned — different readers activate different intertextual connections; encountering texts with diverse intertextual references makes this visible.

descriptors.title: Voice as a literary device
descriptors.description: compare and evaluate how 'voice' as a literary device is used in different types of texts, such as poetry, novels and film, to evoke emotional responses
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit literary texts including hybrids, experimenting with structures, features and devices for purpose (AC9E9LE06). They have not yet compared and evaluated how voice as a literary device evokes emotional responses across different text types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare and evaluate how 'voice' as a literary device is used in different types of texts to evoke emotional responses.

nodes.label: Understanding voice as a literary device
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how voice operates as a literary device in a text, explaining how the author constructs voice and what it contributes to the text.
criteria: Identifies how voice is constructed in a text through specific literary choices
Explains what the constructed voice contributes to the text's meaning or tone
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to compare and evaluate voice across text types — a move that collapses without the conceptual precision about what 'voice as a literary device' means. Students who retain colloquial uses of 'voice' cannot make meaningful cross-text-type comparisons.

width.minimum: Identify how voice is constructed in a provided text and explain what it contributes to the text's meaning or effect.
width.typical: Analyse how voice is constructed as a literary device across at least two different text types (poetry, prose, film), explaining how voice choices shape meaning and tone in each.
wider: Examine how protest voice in poems or songs constructs a sense of collective identity and emotional urgency
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors use voice as a literary device to assert identity and challenge dominant narratives
Examine how unreliable narrators in novels construct a voice that evokes both sympathy and unease

modes.reason: Voice is a conceptually slippery term — students need explicit scaffolding to distinguish 'voice' as a literary device (constructed textual persona) from colloquial uses of 'voice'; the reasoning move from textual choices to constructed voice needs support.

nodes.label: Comparing and evaluating voice across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and evaluate how voice as a literary device evokes different emotional responses across poetry, novels and film.
criteria: Compares how voice as a literary device operates in at least two different text types
Evaluates how each use of voice evokes a different emotional response, with textual evidence

width.minimum: Compare how voice is used in at least two different text types and evaluate how each evokes a different emotional response.
width.typical: Compare and evaluate how voice as a literary device evokes emotional responses across a range of text types — poetry, prose and film — making supported judgements about the effectiveness of each.
wider: Compare the voice of protest across a range of poems, songs and speeches and evaluate how different voices evoke different emotional responses from different audiences
Evaluate how voice in a film creates a different emotional response than the same story told through prose, analysing what the medium change does to the voice
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use voice across text types to evoke emotional responses that challenge or illuminate dominant perspectives

modes.reason: Voice functions very differently across poetry, prose and film — students who only analyse voice in one text type may assume it works the same way everywhere; cross-text-type comparison is the essential context variation here.

descriptors.title: Aesthetic qualities of texts
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate the aesthetic qualities of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse the effect of complex literary devices and evaluate an author's literary style (AC9E9LE04, AC9E9LE05). They have not yet analysed and evaluated the aesthetic qualities of texts using literary analysis terminology.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate the aesthetic qualities of texts.

nodes.label: Identifying aesthetic qualities and valued aspects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify aesthetic qualities in a text using appropriate literary analysis terminology, explaining what is valued about those aspects.
criteria: Identifies at least two aesthetic qualities using appropriate literary analysis terms
Explains why those qualities are valued in the context of the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate aesthetic qualities using literary analysis terms — without an adequate vocabulary repertoire, evaluative claims cannot be articulated with precision and collapse into vague impressions.

width.minimum: Identify at least two aesthetic qualities in a text using appropriate literary terms and explain why those aspects are valued.
width.typical: Identify and describe a range of aesthetic qualities across a literary text — using terms such as 'stanza', 'figurative language', 'symbolism', 'soundtrack' — explaining what is valued about each aspect.
wider: Compare aesthetic qualities across texts from different cultural traditions, examining how different traditions value different aesthetic qualities
Examine how First Nations Australian aesthetic traditions are expressed in literary texts and what criteria of value apply
Analyse how aesthetic judgements about a text have shifted over time as cultural values have changed

modes.reason: Literary analysis terminology must be accumulated through encounters with diverse texts — students need to build a working repertoire of aesthetic vocabulary they can deploy with precision in novel analytical contexts.

nodes.label: Evaluating aesthetic qualities with supported analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the aesthetic qualities of a text, making supported judgements about the use and effect of specific literary devices.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about the use and effect of at least one literary device
Uses specific textual evidence to support the aesthetic evaluation

width.minimum: Evaluate the use and effect of at least one literary device (e.g. symbolism) in a text, making a supported judgement.
width.typical: Evaluate the aesthetic qualities of a literary text, analysing and evaluating the use of multiple literary devices and making supported judgements about their contribution to the text's overall aesthetic effect.
wider: Evaluate how an author's aesthetic choices across a text create a distinctive style, comparing with other authors' approaches to the same genre or form
Evaluate the aesthetic qualities of a First Nations Australian text on its own terms, considering the aesthetic traditions from which it draws
Write a published-style review of a literary text that evaluates aesthetic qualities for a specific audience

modes.reason: Evaluation of aesthetic qualities requires students to articulate a reasoned basis for their judgement — not just whether they found something effective but why, with reference to specific textual evidence and literary criteria.

descriptors.title: Create and edit literary texts with sustained voice
descriptors.description: create and edit literary texts with a sustained 'voice', selecting and adapting text structures, literary devices, and language, auditory and visual features for purposes and audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students create and edit literary texts including hybrids (AC9E9LE06). They have not yet created and edited literary texts with a sustained voice, deliberately selecting and adapting text structures, literary devices and multimodal features for specific purposes and audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and edit literary texts with a sustained voice, selecting and adapting text structures, literary devices, and language, auditory and visual features for purposes and audiences.

nodes.label: Constructing and sustaining a voice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a deliberate authorial voice in a literary text and sustain it across the text through consistent language and structural choices.
criteria: Creates a literary text with a discernible and consistent authorial voice
Can identify the specific language or structural choices that construct and sustain the voice
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to select and adapt text structures for a sustained voice — without a functional understanding of how voice is constructed and maintained, structural and device choices in Node 2 have no coherent purpose to serve.

width.minimum: Create a short literary text with a clearly constructed voice — evidenced by consistent language register, tone and perspective choices — and sustain it across the whole piece.
width.typical: Create a literary text with a sustained voice, using deliberate language, structural and literary device choices to construct and maintain a consistent authorial persona, register and perspective.
wider: Experiment with a range of voice types across different short texts (e.g. collective voice, unreliable narrator, protest voice) to develop fluency with voice construction
Create a suite of short texts on the same key idea expressed in different voices, comparing how voice shapes what can be said and how
Experiment with First Nations Australian authorial voice conventions in a short piece, reflecting on the choices made and their cultural significance

modes.reason: Students who only attempt one voice type may produce technically correct but thin voice construction; experimenting with multiple voice types builds genuine understanding of how voice is constructed rather than accidentally achieved.

nodes.label: Selecting and adapting text structures and literary devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and adapt text structures and literary devices for a specific purpose and audience, explaining their choices.
criteria: Makes at least two deliberate choices of text structure or literary device for a specific purpose
Can explain the intended effect of each choice on the intended audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 (editing) requires students to evaluate and revise their structural and device choices — without having made deliberate choices in Node 2, there is nothing purposeful to edit or reflect on.

width.minimum: In a literary text, make and describe at least two deliberate choices of text structure or literary device for a specific purpose, with an explanation of the effect intended.
width.typical: Create and edit a literary text that demonstrates deliberate selection and adaptation of text structures, literary devices, and language and visual features for a specific purpose and audience, with reflection on choices made.
wider: Experiment with adapting aesthetic features encountered in mentor texts into own writing, explaining what was borrowed and how it was adapted
Create a literary text for a specific real audience (school community, competition) and reflect on how purpose and audience shaped every structural and device choice
Create a literary text that incorporates or responds to a First Nations Australian text, reflecting on the choices required to do so responsibly

modes.reason: Students need to develop the habit of reasoning from purpose and audience backward to structural and device choices — moving from 'I want to create X effect' to 'therefore I will use Y structure/device'; this reasoning chain is the core capability move here.

nodes.label: Editing and reflecting on literary craft choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can edit their literary texts to refine voice and craft, describing choices made and reflecting on the effect of those choices on the text.
criteria: Makes at least two revisions to a literary text with a stated reason for each change
Reflects on how at least one revision improved the voice, structure or device choices

width.minimum: Edit a literary text by making at least two revisions to improve voice consistency or craft, and describe what was changed and why.
width.typical: Edit and refine a literary text, revising choices of structure, literary devices and language features to strengthen voice and purpose; reflect on how choices may be developed further.
wider: Share a literary text with a peer reader and use their response to guide a further editing round, reflecting on how reader feedback informs craft decisions
Produce a writer's commentary alongside a literary text, documenting the editing process and reflecting on how each revision strengthened the text
Compare two drafts of the same piece and analyse specifically what editing decisions improved the voice and craft

modes.reason: Editing integrates all the craft elements from nodes 1–2 — sustained voice, structure, device choices — into a coherent whole; the editing phase is where students demonstrate they can coordinate all elements rather than managing each in isolation.

descriptors.title: Representations reflect contexts
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate how people, places, events and concepts are represented in texts and reflect contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how representations of people, places, events and concepts reflect their contexts (AC9E9LY01). They have not yet evaluated how those representations are constructed and what they communicate about the context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate how people, places, events and concepts are represented in texts and reflect contexts.

nodes.label: Analysing representations in texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how people, places, events or concepts are represented in a text, identifying specific textual choices that construct those representations.
criteria: Identifies specific textual choices that construct a representation
Analyses how those choices contribute to the representation of the person, place, event or concept
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate how representations reflect context — a judgement that depends on first identifying the specific textual choices that construct the representation. Without analysis, evaluation has no evidential basis.

width.minimum: Analyse how at least one person, place, event or concept is represented in a text, identifying specific textual choices that construct the representation.
width.typical: Analyse how a range of people, places, events and concepts are represented across a text, examining how language, visual and structural choices each contribute to the representation.
wider: Compare how stereotypes of people, places or events are constructed across a range of texts and evaluate the assumptions underlying each
Analyse representations of events and issues in First Nations Australian media, examining how representations differ from mainstream media
Compare representations of the same event from texts produced for different audiences and analyse how the intended audience shapes the representation

modes.reason: Students tend to accept representations as natural or accurate; encountering contrasting representations of the same subject (especially First Nations Australian media versus mainstream media) makes the constructed nature of representation visible.

nodes.label: Evaluating representations as reflections of context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how representations in texts reflect the contexts in which they are created, making supported judgements.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about how a representation reflects the context of its production
Identifies at least one aspect of context (social, cultural, historical) that shapes the representation

width.minimum: Evaluate how a representation in a text reflects the context in which it was created, with a supported judgement.
width.typical: Evaluate how representations across a range of texts reflect their contexts, making supported judgements about how social, cultural and historical context shapes what is represented and how.
wider: Evaluate how representations of First Nations Australians in Australian media have changed over time and assess what those changes reveal about shifting contexts
Compare representations of the same concept in texts from different countries or cultures and evaluate what each reveals about its context
Evaluate how the context of a text's production — who made it, for what purpose — shapes its representations and what is left out

modes.reason: Evaluating a representation as a reflection of context requires students to reason from what is shown and how, to what that reveals about the context of production — this two-step inference needs explicit support.

descriptors.title: Spoken text analysis and opinion presentation
descriptors.description: listen to spoken texts and explain the purposes and effects of text structures and language features, and use interaction skills to discuss and present an opinion about these texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse how language positions listeners and use interaction skills to present and discuss opinions about spoken texts (AC9E9LY02). They have not yet explained the purposes and effects of text structures and language features in spoken texts, using interaction skills to present a developed opinion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students listen to spoken texts and explain the purposes and effects of text structures and language features, and use interaction skills to discuss and present an opinion about these texts.

nodes.label: Analysing spoken text structures and features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the purposes and effects of text structures and language features in spoken and multimodal texts.
criteria: Identifies at least one text structure feature and one language feature in a spoken text
Explains the effect of each feature on the audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to present an opinion about a spoken text grounded in analysis of its features — without feature analysis, opinions are disconnected from textual evidence and the interaction skill becomes mere assertion.

width.minimum: Identify at least one text structure feature and one language feature in a spoken text and explain their effect.
width.typical: Analyse the spoken and multimodal features of a media text (e.g. documentary, podcast, political speech), explaining how text structure and language features create effects such as mood, authority or persuasion.
wider: Compare spoken text features across different genres (interview, documentary, political speech) and analyse how genre shapes structure and language choices
Examine how spoken features of First Nations Australian storytelling or oratory function differently from Western speech conventions
Analyse how multimodal features (combination of words and sound) in a media text create effects that neither mode achieves alone

modes.reason: Spoken text features vary substantially across genres — students who have only analysed one genre may not recognise structural and language features in unfamiliar spoken text types; genre breadth builds reliable identification.

nodes.label: Presenting an opinion using interaction skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use interaction skills to discuss and present a developed opinion about a spoken text, drawing on their analysis of its features and effects.
criteria: Presents a clear opinion about a spoken text connected to analysis of its features
Uses at least one interaction skill (turn-taking, building on others' contributions, supporting claims with evidence from the text)

width.minimum: Present an opinion about a spoken text using at least one interaction skill (e.g. structured turn-taking, referencing evidence from the text) and connect the opinion to analysis of the text's features.
width.typical: Use interaction skills to discuss and present a well-developed opinion about a spoken text, drawing on analysis of its text structures and language features, including combination of words and sound.
wider: Participate in a structured discussion where multiple opinions about a spoken text are presented and debated, using interaction skills to build on and respond to others
Present an opinion about a First Nations Australian media text in a class discussion, using interaction skills to engage with differing perspectives on the text
Compare two spoken texts presenting contrasting opinions on the same issue and present an opinion about which is more effective, using interaction skills in a seminar format

modes.reason: Interaction skills in formal discussion contexts require practice — students need repeated structured discussion opportunities to develop the fluency to present opinions clearly while also engaging responsively with others.

descriptors.title: Language features represent values, beliefs and attitudes
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate how language features are used to implicitly or explicitly represent values, beliefs and attitudes
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse and evaluate how language features represent perspectives of issues, events and groups (AC9E9LY03). They have not yet analysed how language features implicitly or explicitly represent values, beliefs and attitudes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate how language features are used to implicitly or explicitly represent values, beliefs and attitudes.

nodes.label: Explicit and implicit representation of values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify language features that explicitly or implicitly represent values, beliefs or attitudes and analyse how they do so.
criteria: Identifies at least one language feature that represents a value, belief or attitude
Distinguishes whether the representation is explicit or implicit and explains how the feature achieves it
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate how language features represent values — a judgement that depends on the ability to identify and distinguish between explicit and implicit representation. Without this distinction, evaluation collapses into surface-level comment.

width.minimum: Identify one language feature in a text that explicitly or implicitly represents a value, belief or attitude, and analyse how it does so.
width.typical: Analyse how a range of language features across a text represent values, beliefs and attitudes both explicitly and implicitly, distinguishing between the two modes of representation.
wider: Analyse social or political cartoons to identify the implicit and explicit values, beliefs and attitudes expressed through visual and language features
Compare how the same value is represented explicitly in one text and implicitly in another, examining what the different strategies achieve
Examine how language features in First Nations Australian activist texts explicitly assert values that mainstream texts represent only implicitly or not at all

modes.reason: The distinction between explicit and implicit representation is context-dependent — what is explicit in one cultural context may be implicit or absent in another; students need contrasting text contexts to see this clearly.

nodes.label: Evaluating how language represents values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how language features are used to represent values, beliefs and attitudes, making supported judgements about the effectiveness or significance of the choices.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about how a language feature represents a value, belief or attitude
Explains the significance of that representation for the text's purpose or audience

width.minimum: Evaluate how at least one language feature is used to represent a value or attitude in a text, making a supported judgement.
width.typical: Evaluate how language features across a text represent values, beliefs and attitudes, making supported judgements about the significance of those choices for the text's purpose and audience.
wider: Evaluate how the representation of values in political texts (e.g. election advertisements, parliamentary speeches) shapes audience understanding of what is at stake
Evaluate how values represented in media texts about First Nations Australian communities have changed over time, and assess the significance of those changes
Compare how different texts covering the same event evaluate values differently and assess what that reveals about the values of the text producers

modes.reason: Evaluation of how language represents values requires students to reason from specific language choices through their implicit assumptions to broader value positions — this multi-step inference needs explicit scaffolding.

descriptors.title: Organisation of ideas to achieve purpose
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate how authors organise ideas in texts to achieve a purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students analyse idea organisation in paragraphs and extended texts (AC9E9LY04). They have not yet analysed and evaluated how authors organise ideas in texts to achieve a specific purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate how authors organise ideas in texts to achieve a purpose.

nodes.label: Analysing organisation of ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how ideas are organised in a text and explain the purpose and effect of the organisational choices.
criteria: Identifies how ideas are organised in a text
Explains the purpose the organisational structure serves for the audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to evaluate the effectiveness of idea organisation — a judgement that depends on first being able to identify and explain the organisational structure and its intended purpose. Without this, evaluation has no object.

width.minimum: Identify how ideas are organised in a text and explain the purpose of that organisation.
width.typical: Analyse how the organisation of ideas in a range of texts — print, digital and multimodal — achieves different purposes, examining how structure guides the reader's attention and understanding.
wider: Compare how ideas are organised in texts designed for different platforms (print versus web page) and analyse how the platform shapes organisational choices
Examine how the organisation of ideas in political pamphlets or advocacy texts achieves persuasive purposes
Analyse how First Nations Australian authors organise ideas in ways that reflect non-linear or culturally specific narrative or argumentative structures

modes.reason: Organisational patterns vary substantially across print, digital and multimodal texts — students who have only analysed one text type may not recognise how purpose shapes organisation in other formats; breadth across text types builds reliable identification.

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness of organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how the organisation of ideas in a text achieves its purpose, making supported judgements.
criteria: Makes a supported judgement about the effectiveness of a text's organisational structure
Connects the evaluation to the text's specific purpose and intended audience

width.minimum: Make a supported judgement about whether the organisation of ideas in a text is effective in achieving its purpose.
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of idea organisation across a range of texts and purposes, comparing how different organisational strategies succeed or fail in achieving their intended purposes.
wider: Compare the organisation of ideas in two online reviews of the same product or text and evaluate which achieves its purpose more effectively and why
Evaluate how the organisation of ideas in a political pamphlet shapes reader response, assessing whether the structure achieves the intended persuasive effect
Evaluate how ideas organised in a non-linear structure (e.g. a web page with navigation, or a non-linear narrative) achieve effects not possible through linear organisation

modes.reason: Effectiveness of organisation is purpose- and platform-dependent — what works on a webpage may not work in print; students need contrasting contexts to evaluate organisation in relation to purpose rather than applying a single standard.

descriptors.title: Comprehension strategies for complex and abstract ideas
descriptors.description: integrate comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning and inferring to analyse and interpret complex and abstract ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students use comprehension strategies to compare and contrast ideas and opinions within and between texts (AC9E9LY05). They have not yet integrated multiple comprehension strategies to analyse and interpret complex and abstract ideas.
descriptors.endpoint: Students integrate comprehension strategies to analyse and interpret complex and abstract ideas.

nodes.label: Applying strategies to complex ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply comprehension strategies to analyse complex ideas in texts, selecting appropriate strategies for the type of complexity encountered.
criteria: Applies at least two named comprehension strategies to analyse a complex idea in a text
Can explain what each strategy contributes to their understanding
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to integrate multiple strategies — a move that depends on having a working repertoire of strategies that can be applied to complex ideas. Students who cannot apply strategies individually cannot coordinate them.

width.minimum: Apply at least two comprehension strategies to analyse a complex idea in a provided text, explaining what each strategy reveals.
width.typical: Apply a range of comprehension strategies — including visualising, questioning and inferring — to analyse complex and abstract ideas across different text types.
wider: Monitor comprehension while reading a text with complex abstract concepts (e.g. justice, identity) and use questioning and connecting strategies to build interpretation across the text
Apply comprehension strategies to interpret the role of a character archetype across a range of texts, summarising the archetype's function and analysing its importance
Use visualising and connecting strategies to interpret how abstract concepts (e.g. parenthood, freedom) are represented in visual advertising

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate fluency with multiple comprehension strategies before they can select and integrate them — practice across text types builds the repertoire needed for integrative use.

nodes.label: Integrating strategies to interpret abstract ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can integrate multiple comprehension strategies to interpret complex and abstract ideas, producing a developed interpretation.
criteria: Integrates at least two comprehension strategies in producing an interpretation
Produces a developed interpretation of a complex or abstract idea supported by evidence from the text

width.minimum: Integrate at least two comprehension strategies to produce an interpretation of an abstract idea in a text, explaining how the strategies worked together.
width.typical: Integrate comprehension strategies to develop a sustained interpretation of complex and abstract ideas across a text, explaining how different strategies contributed to the interpretation.
wider: Interpret the representation of an abstract concept (e.g. justice, belonging) by integrating monitoring, inferring and connecting strategies across multiple texts
Apply integrated comprehension strategies to interpret abstract concepts in First Nations Australian texts, considering how prior connecting knowledge shapes interpretation
Use integrated strategies to interpret how a character archetype functions across different cultural contexts, analysing what the archetype's variation reveals

modes.reason: The integrative use of multiple strategies — not just applying them in sequence but coordinating them to build a cumulative interpretation — is the core challenge here and requires explicit teaching of how strategies inform each other.

descriptors.title: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts
descriptors.description: plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising, expanding and developing ideas through experimenting with text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features for specific purposes and audiences in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical and/or critical
descriptors.knowledge: Students plan, create and publish texts developing ideas critically, selecting features for complex purposes and audiences (AC9E9LY06). They have not yet planned, created, edited and published written and multimodal texts that experiment with text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features across the full range of text purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising, expanding and developing ideas through experimenting with text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features for specific purposes and audiences.

nodes.label: Planning for purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a written or multimodal text by identifying purpose, audience and key ideas, and selecting appropriate text structures and features for those choices.
criteria: Identifies the purpose and audience of the planned text
Selects at least two structural or language feature choices with a rationale connected to purpose and audience

width.minimum: Produce a plan for a text that identifies purpose, audience, key ideas and at least two structural or feature choices with a rationale for each.
width.typical: Develop a detailed plan for a written or multimodal text that organises and expands ideas, selects text structures and features appropriate to the purpose and audience, and previews the argument or structure.
wider: Plan a persuasive text that previews the argument structure explicitly — outlining major points, evidence and conclusion — before drafting
Plan a multimodal text that integrates navigation, text, sound and moving/still images, considering how each mode serves the audience
Plan a text that addresses a First Nations Australian community audience, considering how purpose, audience and cultural context shape structural and feature choices

nodes.label: Creating texts with developed ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create written and multimodal texts that develop and expand ideas through deliberate use of text structures, language features, literary devices and multimodal features.
criteria: Creates a text that develops ideas through deliberate feature choices
Demonstrates experimentation with at least one text structure, language feature or multimodal element
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 (editing and publishing) requires students to have a created text to review, revise and reflect on — without a substantive creation, editing is reduced to surface error-correction rather than purposeful revision.

width.minimum: Create a text that develops ideas through at least two deliberate feature choices (structural, language or multimodal), with evidence of experimentation.
width.typical: Create a written or multimodal text that organises, expands and develops ideas through deliberate experimentation with text structures, language features, literary devices and/or multimodal features for a specific purpose and audience.
wider: Create a written text that compels readers to empathise with ideas and emotions expressed or implied, using deliberate literary and structural choices
Design a webpage that combines navigation, text, sound, and moving and still images for a specific audience, making deliberate structural choices about how the modes work together
Create a multimodal text that addresses a complex real-world issue for a specific audience, experimenting with how different modes contribute to an analytical or critical purpose

modes.reason: Students who only create in one mode or for one purpose develop a narrow repertoire — experimentation across written and multimodal contexts builds transferable understanding of how features serve different purposes.

nodes.label: Editing and publishing with reflection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can review, edit and refine texts for accuracy and purpose, and reflect on choices made and how they might develop further.
criteria: Makes at least two specific editing revisions with a stated reason
Reflects on at least one choice made in the text and how it might be developed further

width.minimum: Edit a text making at least two specific revisions to grammar, spelling, vocabulary or structure, and reflect on at least one choice made.
width.typical: Review and edit a written or multimodal text for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation and to achieve specific purposes and address particular audiences, reflecting on how choices may be changed or developed in future texts.
wider: Conduct a structured self-editing process using an editing checklist that covers grammar, vocabulary precision, structural effectiveness and audience impact
Share a draft with a peer and use their response to guide a revision round, reflecting on how reader feedback informed editing decisions
Publish a final text to a real audience (school publication, competition) and reflect on how the publishing context shaped final editing decisions

modes.reason: Editing integrates the planning and creation phases — students must coordinate their original intentions with what the text actually achieves; this phase collapse risk is real if students treat editing as merely correcting errors rather than purposeful revision.

descriptors.title: Plan, create and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations
descriptors.description: plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations by experimenting with rhetorical devices, and the organisation and development of ideas, to engage audiences for different purposes in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical and/or critical
descriptors.knowledge: Students plan, create and deliver presentations developing ideas analytically and critically (AC9E9LY07). They have not yet planned, created, rehearsed and delivered presentations experimenting with rhetorical devices to engage audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations by experimenting with rhetorical devices, and the organisation and development of ideas, to engage audiences for different purposes.

nodes.label: Planning presentations with rhetorical awareness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a spoken or multimodal presentation that identifies purpose, audience and at least two rhetorical devices to be used, with a rationale.
criteria: Identifies purpose and audience for the presentation
Names at least two rhetorical devices and explains how each will engage the audience

width.minimum: Produce a plan for a spoken presentation that identifies purpose, audience, rhetorical devices to be used and how they will engage the audience.
width.typical: Develop a detailed plan for a spoken or multimodal presentation that organises and develops ideas for a specific purpose and audience, identifying rhetorical devices and explaining how they will engage the audience.
wider: Plan a persuasive presentation that manipulates rhetorical devices to compel the audience to act, explaining specifically how each device will achieve the intended response
Plan a panel discussion or debate on an issue related to a text, considering how the interactive format shapes rhetorical choices
Plan a reflective monologue as a character from a studied text, considering how character voice and rhetorical choices serve the narrative and analytical purpose

nodes.label: Creating and rehearsing the presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and rehearse a spoken or multimodal presentation, using rhetorical devices and refining delivery through rehearsal.
criteria: Creates a presentation that includes at least two rhetorical devices
Shows evidence of rehearsal in the delivery — timing, delivery choices, responsiveness to audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to deliver the presentation — without sufficient rehearsal, the rhetorical choices planned and created cannot be executed effectively in real time and the delivery fails to achieve its purpose.

width.minimum: Create and rehearse a spoken presentation that uses at least two rhetorical devices, with evidence of rehearsal reflected in delivery.
width.typical: Create and rehearse a spoken or multimodal presentation that develops and organises ideas for a specific purpose, using rhetorical devices with evidence of deliberate preparation and rehearsal.
wider: Create a multimodal presentation that manipulates rhetorical devices across visual and spoken modes to compel the audience to act
Create and rehearse a reflective character monologue from a studied text, experimenting with how rhetorical choices support both characterisation and argument
Create a spoken text that incorporates the rhetorical strategies of First Nations Australian oratory or storytelling conventions

modes.reason: Delivery of rhetorical devices in real time requires rehearsal — students who have not practised sufficiently cannot execute their rhetorical choices effectively; rehearsal fluency is the threshold capability here.

nodes.label: Delivering to engage the audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation that engages the audience for a specific purpose, using rhetorical devices effectively.
criteria: Delivers a presentation that uses at least two rhetorical devices
Demonstrates audience engagement through at least one observable delivery choice (pacing, eye contact, rhetorical question, etc.)

width.minimum: Deliver a spoken presentation that uses at least two rhetorical devices and demonstrates awareness of audience engagement.
width.typical: Deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation that engages the audience through effective use of rhetorical devices, appropriate organisation and clear development of ideas for a specific purpose.
wider: Deliver a persuasive multimodal presentation intended to compel the audience to act, using a range of rhetorical devices across spoken and visual modes
Participate in a debate or panel discussion about a text-related issue, using interaction skills and rhetorical devices to present and defend a position
Deliver a character reflective monologue that engages the audience through both rhetorical performance and analytical insight about the character's choices

modes.reason: Live delivery integrates planning, creation and rehearsal — students must coordinate rhetorical choices, organisational structure and audience responsiveness in real time; phase collapse here means the presentation fails to achieve its purpose despite adequate preparation.

descriptors.title: Spelling system and spelling for effect
descriptors.description: use knowledge of the spelling system to spell words and to manipulate standard spelling for particular effects
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain how spelling is used deliberately for effects such as characterisation, humour and accent representation (AC9E9LY08). They have not yet used knowledge of the spelling system both to spell words correctly and to manipulate standard spelling for particular effects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use knowledge of the spelling system to spell words and to manipulate standard spelling for particular effects.

nodes.label: Applying spelling system knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their knowledge of the spelling system to spell words accurately, including technically complex vocabulary.
criteria: Spells a range of technical and academic vocabulary accurately in own writing
Can apply spelling knowledge to unfamiliar words using system knowledge (morphology, etymology)
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to manipulate standard spelling for deliberate effect — a move that depends on knowing what standard spelling is and why it exists. Students without secure spelling system knowledge cannot distinguish deliberate manipulation from error.

width.minimum: Accurately spell a range of technical and academic vocabulary in context, applying knowledge of the spelling system.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of the spelling system to spell words accurately across a range of text types and registers, including technical and academic vocabulary.
wider: Examine how knowledge of word etymology and morphology supports spelling of unfamiliar technical vocabulary across different subject areas
Analyse how spelling conventions differ across Australian, British and American English, and explain when each is appropriate
Limited width — this node has limited context variation; enrichment at this node is primarily through applying accurate spelling in increasingly sophisticated and technical texts.

modes.reason: Accurate spelling of technical vocabulary requires practice and consolidation — students need repeated exposure and use in context to internalise correct forms, particularly for domain-specific vocabulary.

nodes.label: Manipulating spelling for particular effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate standard spelling deliberately to achieve particular effects, understanding how the departure from standard spelling creates meaning.
criteria: Identifies a deliberate spelling manipulation in a text
Explains the effect the manipulation creates and how it differs from standard spelling

width.minimum: Identify one example of deliberate spelling manipulation in a text (e.g. a homophone used for effect, a respelling for humour) and explain the effect it creates.
width.typical: Identify and analyse a range of deliberate spelling manipulations in texts, explaining how each departure from standard spelling achieves its intended effect.
wider: Examine how homophones and deliberate misspellings are used in advertising, brand names and product marketing (e.g. 'lite') and evaluate their effectiveness
Analyse how spelling manipulation is used in digital communication contexts (e.g. internet vernacular, memes) to create new meaning or group identity
Examine how authors have used spelling manipulation to represent dialect, accent or characterisation, and evaluate the ethics of such representations for different communities

modes.reason: Spelling manipulation operates very differently across literary characterisation, advertising and digital communication — students need multiple contexts to understand that manipulation is deliberate craft, not just error.

descriptors.title: Segment and blend phonemes
descriptors.description: segment sentences into individual words; orally blend and segment single-syllable spoken words; isolate, blend and manipulate phonemes in single-syllable words (phonological awareness)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise phonemes (AC9EFLY09). They have not yet been explicitly taught to blend phonemes into words, segment words into phonemes, or manipulate individual phonemes by substitution, addition or deletion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can blend phonemes into words, segment single-syllable words into phonemes, and manipulate phonemes by addition, deletion and substitution — demonstrating secure phoneme-level awareness across a range of single-syllable word types.

nodes.label: Sentences are strings of words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment a spoken sentence into its individual words — identifying where word boundaries fall.
criteria: Student correctly segments a spoken sentence into its individual words.
Student can count the number of words in a spoken sentence.

width.minimum: Segment a spoken sentence of three to four words into individual words by clapping or tapping.
width.typical: Segment sentences into individual words; understand that words are the units within sentences; count words in short spoken sentences.
wider: Apply word segmentation to sentences of varying length — including sentences with contractions and function words
Connect spoken word segmentation to written word spaces — matching oral and print word boundaries

nodes.label: Blending: sounds into words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can blend a sequence of separately spoken phonemes into a recognisable word.
criteria: Student blends three separately spoken phonemes into a recognisable word.
Student can blend words of varying CVC, CVCC and CCVC patterns.
nodes.hinge_reason: Blending fluency is the core decoding mechanism in LY04 and LY12 — students who cannot reliably blend phonemes into words cannot read connected text using phonics, and their decoding will remain halting and inaccurate.

width.minimum: Blend three phonemes into a CVC word when given the sounds separately (e.g. /l/-/i/-/p/ → 'lip').
width.typical: Blend phonemes of single-syllable spoken words — including CVC, CVCC and CCVC patterns; produce the target word correctly from the phoneme sequence.
wider: Blend phoneme sequences across a wide range of single-syllable word types — varying vowels, clusters and codas
Apply blending to words containing digraphs once grapheme knowledge is established
Practise blending through word games, oral riddles and chants — building fluent blending as a reading tool

modes.reason: Blending fluency is the core decoding mechanism — it must become fast and accurate. Slow or inaccurate blending limits reading. Practice to fluency across word types is required before width adds value.

nodes.label: Segmenting: words into sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can segment a single-syllable spoken word into its constituent phonemes — saying each sound separately.
criteria: Student segments a CVC word into three separate phonemes.
Student can segment both onset and rime of a word.
nodes.hinge_reason: Segmenting is the prerequisite for spelling — students who cannot segment a spoken word into phonemes cannot apply letter-sound knowledge to encode it in writing (LY12, LY13). Segmenting errors propagate directly into misspelling.

width.minimum: Segment a CVC word into three phonemes (e.g. 'can' → /c/-/a/-/n/).
width.typical: Segment single-syllable spoken words into phonemes — including CVC, CVCC and CCVC patterns; say each phoneme distinctly; understand this as the inverse of blending.
wider: Segment words across a wide range of single-syllable types — varying onset, vowel and coda
Apply segmenting to words with digraphs (once grapheme knowledge supports this) — recognising that 'sh' is one phoneme
Connect segmenting to spelling — use segmentation to support encoding in writing tasks

modes.reason: Segmenting is the inverse of blending and equally foundational for spelling. Consistent accuracy across word types is required — errors propagate directly into misspelling.

nodes.label: Phoneme manipulation: add, delete, substitute
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate phonemes in single-syllable words by addition, deletion and substitution — generating new words.
criteria: Student can substitute the initial phoneme to make a new word.
Student can delete the initial phoneme and say what remains.
Student can add a phoneme to generate a new word.

width.minimum: Substitute the initial phoneme in a given word to make a new word (e.g. 'run' → 'fun').
width.typical: Manipulate phonemes by addition, deletion and substitution at initial, medial and final positions; generate new words through each manipulation type; understand that changing one phoneme changes the word.
wider: Practise phoneme manipulation across all positions — initial, medial, final — systematically exploring minimal pairs
Apply phoneme manipulation to generate a range of words for a rime family — building awareness of word families as phonemic units
Explore phoneme manipulation through word games, chants and minimal pair comparisons

modes.reason: Phoneme substitution and deletion can feel arbitrary without multiple examples — students need to work across initial, medial and final positions, and across addition/deletion/substitution, before the principle that phonemes are independently manipulable is secure.
